name: Orphan Patent Evidence-of-Use (bankrupt estates, FCC/teardown proof; incl. semiconductor, photonics, mature-node)
one_line_reason: This is a real ML discovery edge on cheap, illegible orphan patents. But the hit only becomes an opinion, the step-up is about 10-30x into a thin NPE/aggregator market that discounts for PTAB risk, and the ladder caps at a few-billion-dollar patent fund.
fatal_flaw: The proving step does not actually prove anything. An evidence-of-use chart is a contestable opinion whose value is only realised after years of licensing or litigation (about $2-5M per case to trial, with roughly 65-70% of instituted PTAB final decisions invalidating all challenged claims). So buyers pay roughly 10-30x, not 10^3-10^4x, and the market is thin. The ladder tops out at a few-$B NPE or fund, not a trillion-dollar chain.
step_up: Unproven: patents from distressed estates, lapse-bound owners and bulk ABC sales typically clear at roughly $2k-$30k each (my estimate from memory of bankruptcy 363 sales and broker lots; not verified this run). Proven: brokered US patents have averaged about $100k-$250k asking per asset in Richardson Oliver Insights market reports across 2013-2022 (from memory), and only roughly 25-30% of listed packages sell. A strong EoU-charted asset reading on a large product might reach $250k-$1M. Realistic step-up is about 10-30x, with outliers at 100x. The "unproven" asset is not near zero; it already trades at four to five figures. That is far from Terranox's 10^4.
hit_rate_capex: My estimates, not verified this run: perhaps 1-5% of random orphan patents read on a currently shipping product with enough remaining term and damages to be worth charting. A manual attorney chart costs about $3k-$15k, and a teardown or SEM cross-section adds $5k-$20k. Cost per hit today is therefore roughly $100k-$1M. ML triage could plausibly cut that 5-20x, which is a real lever, capped at 1/base rate (about 20-100x). Charting is already being automated by several AI patent-analytics startups, so the lever is not proprietary.

name: Cryptic Clusters / Legacy Actinomycete Libraries: orphaned natural-product collections re-read for novel clusters
one_line_reason: Cheap-to-buy rights and a genuinely low base hit rate, but the BGC novelty "answer" is already precomputed in public databases by antiSMASH and incumbents like Ginkgo/Fraunhofer/Naicons, the physical proving step dominates cost and time instead of being trivial, and the proven asset clears at low single-digit millions (Basilea/Spexis, CHF 2M) — so it scores 13/25 and fails C1 and C4, the two that matter.
fatal_flaw: The outcome is already summarised in a legible public field: antiSMASH / antiSMASH-DB / BiG-FAM / MIBiG already auto-annotate and novelty-score essentially every public BGC, so there is no illegible-data edge to exploit — and the proving step is the dominant cost and the dominant failure mode (11-32% of expressed clusters yield any detectable compound at all; $50-200k and 6-24 months each), which inverts Terranox's 95-5 ratio into roughly 30-70. ML can re-rank the cheap part and cannot fix the expensive part. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure: building the plant is harder than finding the mine.
step_up: Unproven right: physical legacy libraries have changed hands for storage costs or effectively nothing — Sanofi transferred ~110,000 strains (~80,000 actinomycetes, 70 years of industrial effort) to Fraunhofer IME in 2020 as a shared-resource transfer, no sale price; Ginkgo bought Warp Drive Bio's genome-mining platform including >135,000 bacterial strains and >4M predicted BGCs in 2019 with terms undisclosed (plausibly low single-digit millions given it was a cast-off asset of Revolution Medicines). Deinove licensed access to 400 of Naicons' 45,000 strains, price undisclosed. So call the right $10k-low-7-figures (my estimate anchored on those three). Proven right: a single validated novel scaffold with in vivo activity transacts at roughly CHF 2M (Basilea/Spexis, whole program, up to, incl. milestones) to maybe $10-50M upfront for a strong antifungal/ADC payload (my estimate). That is ~10-100x on a per-asset basis, up to ~1000x only if you bought the library for storage costs AND got a best-case oncology payload — but the capex consumed to get there ($50-200k x many clusters, likely $5-20M to one validated scaffold) eats most of the multiple. Unlike the uranium case, the step-up is NOT immediate on a hit and NOT a market-observable repricing of the asset you own; the library does not reprice because one cluster worked.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is genuinely low, which is the candidate's best feature. Detection of any compound from a heterologously expressed cluster: 11-32% (four large-scale studies, 2023 review PMC10727000). Of 50 studies over Jan 2018-Jun 2023, only 63 new natural product families emerged. Probability a given silent cluster yields a novel compound with commercially relevant potency/selectivity/developability: my estimate <1-2%. Cost per proving attempt: $50-200k and months per cluster (candidate's own figure, consistent with CRO/biofoundry pricing; my estimate for a full isolate-to-structure-to-assay cycle is $80-250k). Theoretical ML lever = 1/base rate = 50-100x, so the ceiling is attractive. The problem is that ML can only improve the *selection* term, not the expression/fermentation failure term — and the 11-32% detection failure is overwhelmingly host/regulatory/pathway biology, not picking the wrong cluster. Realistic achievable capex reduction: 2-3x, not 10x. That caps C3 at 3.

name: Hand Match / Marginalia: unrecognised historic letters and annotated books
one_line_reason: Cheap bought rights and a real 10^2-10^3x step-up, but attempts already cost little, so the ML lever saves little money. Proving depends on paleographers, and the thin collector market has no ladder.
fatal_flaw: Value at the top comes from expert and scholarly consensus plus provenance, not from the ML match, and the supply of valuable unrecognised hands is tiny and fixed. The result is a boutique dealer with a few lucky finds a year in a market of about $1-2B a year (estimate), with no ladder to a large company.
step_up: Unproven: a $50-5k estate lot or book catalogued as "unidentified hand" (candidate figure, plausible). Proven comparables: an Edgar Allan Poe letter (a plea for $40) sold for $125,125 in 2020 (Inquirer). A Kerouac letter to Robert Lax sold for $11,000. Tolkien letters went for $2.7k-13k each in 2018 (Locus). A John Steinbeck letter sold for $32k at RR Auction. Taking a $50-500 lot to $10k-125k gives roughly 10^2-10^3x. A Milton- or Shakespeare-class association copy would be over 10^4x, but those are once a decade. Most real hits are minor figures at about 3-30x.
hit_rate_capex: I found no published base rate. My estimate is well under 0.1% of "unidentified hand" lots belonging to anyone with market value, and under 0.01% for a famous writer. The cost per attempt is already low: buying a $50-500 lot plus photography. The lever is therefore not "10x cheaper drills". It is triage across inventory, and that is limited by how many lots exist and by expert sign-off time ($500-5k per opinion, my estimate), not by discovery capex. The lever exists, but the money it saves is small.

name: Reuse-Rights Pipeline Easements: abandoned-in-place pipelines for CO2, H2 and fiber
one_line_reason: The reading is illegible and the ladder is real, but discovery is under half the rung, the required hit rate collapses across a whole corridor, the physical requalification is bespoke and hard, and the step-up waits for a thin, stalled buyer pool.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is not where the value or the difficulty is. Corridors that look cheap are often legally void (the easement lapsed on abandonment, or its scope has to be litigated per parcel), every parcel in the chain must pass (one gap kills the corridor), and turning a proven corridor into value still needs bespoke physical requalification and a CO2 or hydrogen buyer that is currently stalled. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode, and owners who can read their own easements already do the good conversions themselves.
step_up: On paper the ratio is huge because the basis is near zero or negative: the operator is carrying an abandonment liability, and abandoning in place costs about $10-50k/mile (my estimate). Proven value per mile, all my estimates and not sourced (searches unavailable): new CO2 pipeline build cost is about $2-4M/mile, with right-of-way about 10-20% of that, so a clean reusable corridor could be worth about $100k-1M/mile to a CO2 developer if the pipe also requalifies. For fiber, a right-of-way license is about $1-10k/mile per year, or a few $k-$50k/mile capitalised. The value is not realised when the scope is proven, though. It only appears after the buyer's inspection and requalification and only if a buyer exists. Navigator CO2 cancelled in 2023, Summit has stalled on permits and eminent-domain bans (South Dakota 2025), and that buyer pool is thin. Realistic step-up from a verified paper corridor to a sale is about 10-100x, not 10^4.
hit_rate_capex: Proving is cheap, not expensive and mostly failing. Title and abstract review is about $300-2,000 per parcel (my estimate), and a corridor has hundreds to thousands of parcels. The base hit rate per parcel for broad, assignable language ("oil, gas and other substances", no reversion on non-use) might be 20-50% (my estimate). The rate that matters is whether every parcel in a 50-300 mile corridor passes. That is the per-parcel rate raised to the power N, close to zero for long runs, so the binding constraint is holdouts and gaps, not finding the right corridor. ML cuts the cost of reading parcels, but that cost was never the dominant capex. Curative work (buying new rights to fill gaps) and requalifying the pipe dominate, and ML does not cut those 10x.

name: Powered-Land Options: farmland options proven by utility load studies
one_line_reason: The farmland purchase discount is real and the ladder is big, but capacity belongs to whoever signs the ESA and posts collateral, not to whoever reads the grid data first. Incumbents already screen headroom, and the step-up needs capital and utility commitments rather than discovery. It fails the 80%-discovery frame much like the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
fatal_flaw: Proving here is not a cheap discovery event that the landowner then owns. Utility capacity is allocated to whoever signs the ESA and posts collateral, not to whoever reads the data first. The study result is non-binding and decays as others queue. Rising tariffs specifically target speculative flippers. And well-funded incumbents (Tract, Cloverleaf, EdgeCore, brokers) already screen the same public grid data. So the 10^3x step-up needs heavy capital commitment and network upgrades, not an ML-found hit: discovery is a minority of the rung.
step_up: Unproven: Midwest/Southeast cropland is roughly $5-10k/acre (USDA 2025 national cropland average about $5.8k/acre, from memory), and options run about $50-300/acre/yr (candidate's figure, plausible). Proven: powered or entitled data-center land trades at roughly $300k-2M/acre in hot markets (Loudoun reported at $1-4M/acre; secondary markets $100-500k/acre, from memory of 2024-25 press). So land goes about 30-100x and the option premium goes 10^3x or more. But the jump needs a firm capacity commitment, not just a study. A study or a non-binding will-serve letter alone probably gets about 2-5x (estimate), because buyers have been burned by phantom capacity. All numbers here are recalled or estimated: the search budget was exhausted, so none were verified this run.
hit_rate_capex: Study cost is $50-250k per site (candidate's figure; Texas SB6 of 2025 sets a roughly $100k large-load study fee, from memory). Base hit rate, meaning the study shows usable headroom on an acceptable timeline: I estimate 15-30% in constrained RTOs. AEP Ohio's large-load queue fell from about 30 GW to about 13 GW after its 2025 tariff required minimum-demand commitments, which shows most requests are speculative (from memory). The lever is capped at roughly 3-6x, not 10x. A proving attempt also costs only about $100k against a $10-100M exit, so capex is not the binding constraint.

name: Masterless: defunct-label masters via MMA
one_line_reason: Clean frame and illegible data, but the step-up is a revenue multiple on tiny royalties (mostly 1-5x, rarely 100x). The valuable outcomes are already visible in public play counts and SoundExchange unpaid lists, and the ladder tops out at a catalogue fund. Figures are estimates because the search budget was exhausted.
fatal_flaw: Unit economics on the typical hit are too small. Buyers price defunct small-label masters at 5-15x trailing royalties, and those royalties are usually hundreds of dollars a year. So the step-up is mostly 1-5x, not 10^3. The few high-value orphans are already revealed by public play counts and SoundExchange unpaid lists, so they are contested. The binding cost is legal chain-of-title closure, which ML cannot cut.
step_up: These figures are my estimates from memory; the search budget was used up and no live search ran. Master catalogues trade at about 8-15x net label share for clean, growing catalogues (about 15-20x at the 2021 peak) and about 5-10x for small or illiquid ones. A typical defunct small-label master earns perhaps $100-$2,000 a year (estimate). Bought at $1-5k, the expected sale value is about $1-15k, so most hits are 1-5x. A rare breakbeat or sampled master with heavy sync or streaming use could reach 100x. The step-up is fat-tailed, not a reliable 10^3, and the claimed 10^2-10^3x holds only for outliers.
hit_rate_capex: These figures are estimates; no searches ran. A title-reconstruction attempt (archival research, contacting heirs and trustees, legal opinion on chain of title) costs perhaps $2-10k in labour and legal fees. The base hit rate for 'provably clean title plus meaningful revenue' is maybe 5-15%. That caps the ML lever at about 7-20x, which on paper matches the rubric's ~10x. In practice, the legal closing work (signatures from heirs, releases from bankruptcy trustees, termination-right exposure under 17 USC 203) is human and not ML-reducible. Realistically ML cuts the cost of a hit by about 2-4x.

name: Continuation Forge: live patent families with pending continuations
one_line_reason: Real frame and real buyers, but the step-up is only ~10-50x and depends on litigation. Continuation status is legible, incumbents already run this playbook, and the ladder ends in an NPE business worth billions at most.
fatal_flaw: This is already the standard NPE playbook. IP Edge, Dominion Harbor, IV and Acacia, plus brokers who screen for live continuations, already buy families with pending continuations and draft claims to read on shipping products. Pending status is a legible field, and LLM claim-charting tools are commoditising the matching. The proven value is not realised on allowance: it depends on years of litigation exposed to IPR and Alice. That caps the immediate step-up at about 10-50x rather than 10^3-10^4 and leaves no illegible-data moat.
step_up: From memory, not verified this run (the search budget was used up): Richardson Oliver Insights brokered-market reports put average asking prices around $100-250k per US asset, and older reports were higher. Small-inventor, auction and bankruptcy patents often clear at $5-50k. A family with an allowed claim that a strong EoU chart shows reading on a high-volume product might sell for $250k-$2M to an NPE or a defensive aggregator such as RPX or AST. Outlier litigation outcomes can be 10^4x, but those take years and a contingency trial. Realistic immediate step-up: about 10-50x on a hit, not the claimed 50-1000x and nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: Allowance itself is easy. Continuations are allowed at high rates (my estimate: 70-90%, consistent with overall USPTO allowance rates). The real hit is an allowed claim that is both valid and infringed by a shipping product and that survives a buyer's diligence. Commonly cited figures say only about 1-5% of issued patents are ever licensed or asserted (my estimate, not sourced this run). Cost per attempt: $5-100k to buy plus $3-60k to prosecute, so roughly $20-150k. ML could plausibly raise the hit rate 3-5x. The ceiling is set by the 1/base-rate cap and by legal-validity risk that ML cannot reduce. Capex falls maybe 3-5x, not 10x.

name: Tracebird / Back-to-Birth: records-orphaned engines and LLPs
one_line_reason: The rung is clean (cheap scrap title, capitalised buyers, 20-300x step-up), but the proving step relies on private documents and regulatory acceptance, not on reading public data, so ML gives only a lead-ranking edge, and records specialists and USM incumbents already work these parts.
fatal_flaw: The proof sits in private records, not public ones. Back-to-birth cycle history is either documented in operator and OEM files or it cannot be rebuilt, and regulators and buyers will not accept ML-inferred cycles for safety-critical LLPs. The ML can find leads but cannot prove a part, so the 10x capex lever falls apart.
step_up: These figures are my estimates from prior knowledge, because the shared web-search budget ran out before any search returned. An LLP with broken back-to-birth trace sells at scrap or metal value, roughly $2-20k. A serviceable CFM56-7B or V2500 LLP with remaining life is worth roughly $100k-$1M; a new CFM56-7B full LLP stack lists around $4-5M. That puts the step-up at roughly 20-300x on a hit, in line with the candidate's claim. It is not 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: These are estimates; none were found. Trace recovery by specialist records firms and MRO records teams probably costs $5-20k per part in labour, OEM or operator data requests and sworn statements. My guess is that most recoveries fail when a gap in the operator's records cannot be closed, with a base success rate perhaps 10-30%. That would cap the lever at about 3-10x. Even then, ML can only rank which parts are likely to be recoverable. It cannot make a recovery succeed, because the missing link is a private document that either exists or does not.

name: ShelfClear: rescuing compounds shelved for species-specific tox findings
one_line_reason: This is the stranded-drug-rescue idea that was already killed. The data asymmetry runs toward the seller, the proving step is costlier than pitched, and the step-up depends on efficacy and patent life, not on the tox flag.
fatal_flaw: The signal is not in public, illegible data. A shelved compound's tox package is private and held by a seller who can read it, and clearing the tox flag is not what a buyer pays for: efficacy, competitive position and remaining patent life set the price. So there is no frame where discovery from public data is 80%+ of the work and the output is sellable on its own.
step_up: Unproven: shelved assets from TTOs or biotech estates can be had for nominal upfront ($0-1M) plus royalties. But big pharma rarely out-licenses at nominal prices, and it often holds rights back (estimate). Proven: in 2024 the median upfront to preclinical biotechs was $47M, down from $75M in 2022 (JP Morgan via BioStock). Upfronts were about 6% of headline deal value in 2024, and early-stage upfronts were 1.5-3.7% of deal value in 2024-2025 (Goodwin). Those medians come from selected, efficacy-differentiated assets, often in hot modalities. A small-molecule rescue with a historical tox flag and a shortened patent life would more realistically get $2-15M upfront (estimate). On a hit, that is about 10-100x on total invested capital ($0.5-1M acquisition plus proving), not 100-500x.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate of the proving step: if the target compound is well chosen, a mechanistic package showing a rodent-specific effect probably works 30-50% of the time. Rodent PPAR-alpha and alpha-2u-globulin mechanisms are textbook and already accepted (estimate). The real failure rate comes after: the share of tox-cleared shelved compounds that actually get licensed for meaningful money is probably 5-15% (estimate). Shelving is often driven by strategy or efficacy and the tox flag is just the stated reason. Cost per attempt: $0.1-0.3M as pitched, realistically $0.5-3M with in vivo bridging, plus acquisition and diligence costs (estimate). With a 30-50% base hit rate on the tox step, ML can lift it at most about 2-3x (lever capped at 1/hit rate). The uncertainty that dominates, licensability, cannot be predicted from public tox data.

name: DeadPatent Hits: re-proving unlicensed university compound patents against new targets
one_line_reason: Rights are cheap and the ladder is real. But the patent data is already legible through SureChEMBL/ChEMBL, hits are commoditised by make-on-demand libraries, and buyers pay little for a re-validated hit, so the step-up is about 3-30x and not 10^3.
fatal_flaw: Hit substitution. Validated hits are close to a commodity, available from Enamine REAL plus docking or from DEL providers for about $100 per compound with no IP encumbrance. So an old university composition-of-matter patent on a re-validated hit commands little premium, and the valuable step-up happens later, in medicinal-chemistry optimisation, which is not discovery-dominated.
step_up: Unproven: a TTO option or licence on an unlicensed patent at about $10-50k (candidate's figure; plausible, since around 60-70% of US university patents are never licensed out, IPWatchdog/LESI). Proven: Harvard-Merck paid $20M upfront for preclinical small-molecule inhibitors, but BioCentury called that atypical. UT-CSPC paid $4.5M upfront for two preclinical candidates, and those were mAbs. My estimate for a re-validated hit with no in vivo data is $0-1M upfront, and many get $0 beyond milestones. That puts the realistic step-up at about 3-30x, not 100-500x, and the value is back-loaded into milestones that only pay if someone else spends the clinical capital.
hit_rate_capex: The candidate puts cost per proving attempt at $50-150k and 6-10 weeks for resynthesis plus an assay panel, which is reasonable for CRO pricing. Published virtual-screening hit rates against a target are typically about 5-30% at the micromolar level (estimate from the literature). Clearing potency plus selectivity plus ADME is lower, perhaps 2-10%. ML already supplies much of the current hit rate, because incumbents dock these same ChEMBL/SureChEMBL compounds. So there is limited room to lift it further. The lever over the existing computational baseline is perhaps 2-3x, not 10x (estimate).

name: Freezer Estate / Liquidation Strains / Strain Salvage: bankrupt synbio and fermentation strain banks
one_line_reason: Rights can be bought and the ladder is real. But the proving step is not the step-up event: buyers pay for scaled, cost-competitive production, not titers, and the outcome data is private inside the lot, so the public-data ML edge is small.
fatal_flaw: A bench-proven strain is not the valuable asset. The value appears only after scale-up and techno-economic de-risking, which is the expensive, bespoke and mostly failing part, so discovery is never 80% of any sellable rung. Industrial synbio's graveyard (Amyris, Zymergen) consists of companies with good strains that failed at scale and cost.
step_up: Unproven: lots from trustees, mostly my estimate of $10k to low $100ks. The candidate's own figure is not sourced. Zymergen's Chapter 11 (Del. 23-11661) sold assets to Ginkgo and Pivot Bio, but I found no public per-asset price. Proven precedent: Givaudan paid $200M upfront plus up to $150M in earnouts for Amyris cosmetic ingredients (Amyris 8-K, 2023). That was a commercial portfolio with about $30M of 2022 sales plus a manufacturing deal, not a freezer of strains, so it is not a valid comparable for a bench-proven strain. A shake-flask titer probably moves the value of one strain from about $10k to about $50-300k at most (3-30x, my estimate). The 100-1000x only shows up after scale-up and commercial offtake (a buyer contracted to take the output), which takes years and $10-100M+.
hit_rate_capex: No published base rate for revival plus a commercially relevant titer from shelved industrial strains. My estimate: maybe 5-20% of annotated strains revive and reproduce their recorded titers, and under 1-2% are commercially relevant at today's ingredient prices. Bench proving costs $10-100k per strain at CROs (the candidate's figure; plausible). The ML lever is weak. The debtor's own notebooks and LIMS (lab database) already record which strains hit which titers. Once the lot is bought, triage is a matter of reading the records, not prediction, and before the purchase the data isn't public. Realistic capex cut: about 2-3x, not 10x.

name: Extremo Rights / Nagoya Enzymes: exclusive ABS site rights mined from public metagenomes
one_line_reason: Best-in-class on illegible public data (petabases of unannotated SRA reads with no regulator-written answer field) and on hit-rate lever, but fails the core test: the ABS permit confers no exclusivity over an already-public sequence, so nothing re-rates on a hit, and the rung where discovery is 95% has no capitalised buyer because value only appears after years of protein engineering and scale-up. Total 12/25.
fatal_flaw: The purchased right is not excludable. Because the sequence is already in public SRA, an ABS site permit blocks no competitor from finding and using the same enzyme, and DSI is being pulled out of bilateral site-level ABS into a multilateral fund, so the permit's scarcity value is trending to zero rather than appreciating on a hit. There is no mineral-title analogue: you cannot buy the thing that re-rates. Compounding it, the one rung where discovery is 80%+ of the work has no buyer, because the value-recognising step (engineering, expression, scale-up to industrial conditions) is the expensive bespoke build — the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern the rubric explicitly rejects.
step_up: Claimed $10-100k ABS agreement to $1-50M enzyme deal (10^2-10^3x). My read: the step-up is real in headline terms but is not attached to the purchased right. Industry in-licensing of a *validated* enzyme/platform runs roughly $0.5-5M upfront plus mid-single-digit royalties for early-stage assets, with $20-50M+ upfronts reserved for clinical-grade or platform-wide deals (my estimate from comparable biocatalysis/synbio licensing structures; not verified with a source this session — my web searches were blocked by a safety classifier before returning results, so every number here is flagged as estimate). An unvalidated assay-positive hit with no engineering package transacts far lower, commonly $0-250k upfront plus milestones, i.e. ~1-10x on a $50k right, not 10^3x. And the resale value of the ABS permit itself, absent the sequence IP, is approximately zero — there is no secondary market for site access agreements, unlike a staked mineral claim which has a liquid buyer at a published per-hectare price. Nothing re-rates "immediately on a hit": the value appears only after a buyer's own 6-18 month technical due diligence and scale-up gate.
hit_rate_capex: This is the candidate's strongest leg. Classical function-based metagenomic screening hit rates are famously terrible — on the order of 1 active clone per 10^3-10^5 clones screened for a given activity (long-standing figure in the functional-metagenomics literature; my recollection, not verified this session). Sequence-and-ML-first candidate selection plausibly lifts per-construct success to ~1-20% expressed-and-active, which is a 10^2-10^3x apparent lever — far above the ~10x the rubric asks for, and above the 1/base-hit-rate cap only because the base rate is so low. But the lever is worth little in dollars because the proving step is already cheap: synthetic gene cost is roughly $0.07-0.15/bp, so a 1 kb ORF is ~$100-200 and 500 ORFs plus expression and primary assays is ~$75-200k all-in (my estimate from current gene-synthesis list pricing). Compare Terranox: an exploratory hole is $50-500k and you need many of them, so capex *is* the binding constraint and a 10x cut buys 10 more shots at a 10^4 jump. Here discovery capex is already a rounding error against the $5-50M of protein engineering, strain development and process validation that stands between a hit and a sale. Cutting the cheap step 100x does not move the economics of the expensive step. The hit-rate lever is pointed at the wrong bottleneck.

name: Unknown Sitter: face-matching early photographs to historical figures
one_line_reason: The rights are cheap and the step-up is huge on paper. But the "proof" is contested expert opinion that buyers discount, free tools like Civil War Photo Sleuth already exist, and the total market is tiny with no ladder above it.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is not objective. A face-match attribution is an opinion that the capitalised buyer does not accept on its own: the Croquet Kid has a $5M appraisal, and I found no confirmed sale in the decade since. Hits are also too rare and the market too small for any ladder.
step_up: Unproven: a $2-$10 junk-shop or eBay tintype. Proven famous sitter: the authenticated Billy the Kid tintype sold for $2.3M ($2.6M with fees) in 2011, roughly 10^5-10^6x. But the newly face-matched cases have not turned into sales. The Croquet Kid ($2 in 2010) carried a $5M Kagin's appraisal, and I found no confirmed sale. The $10 Jesse James eBay tintype was described as possibly worth about $2M, which was a reported valuation and not a sale. For ordinary identified soldiers the premium is my estimate of about 2-5x, since I found no published price comparison. The headline 10^4 jump is real on paper but rarely realised.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate for a famous, saleable sitter: my estimate is under 1 in 100,000 anonymous images (no source). Civil War Photo Sleuth: only 10-20% of surviving Civil War portraits are identified. In its first month users uploaded more than 2,000 photos, about half of them unidentified, and over 100 unknown photos were linked to specific soldiers. Experts judged over 85% of those proposed IDs probably or definitely correct (Mohanty et al., IJCAI 2020). Cost per attempt: $10-200 for the photo plus scan time. Expert attribution for a famous claim runs months to a year or more (Kagin's took over a year). ML cheaply cuts the screening cost, but the binding cost is expert authentication time and buyer acceptance, not screening. The lever on realised dollars is well under 10x.

name: Gores: claiming title gaps from deed-description errors
one_line_reason: The data edge here is real (illegible scanned metes and bounds, with gaps flagged in no field), but alternative cures cap the step-up near ~10x and a few thousand dollars per deal, and there is no ladder to a large owned-asset chain.
fatal_flaw: Hold-up value is capped by cheap alternative cures.
