Proven by a pilot only: animal health licences pay an undisclosed upfront plus milestones. For example, Oasmia/Abbott had up to $21.5M in milestones that were mostly back-loaded and tied to development and sales. My estimate for a pilot-proven asset is $1-5M of realisable value, so roughly 10-50x, not 100-1000x. Whole-company exits after approval, which is far beyond the pilot: Aratana sold for $234-245M and Kindred Bio for ~$440M, both after hundreds of millions spent over 7-10 years. That is weak compared with the money raised.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: no published success rate exists for veterinary pilots. My estimate is that 20-40% of open-label canine oncology pilots show a response signal worth pursuing, partly because these pilots are open-label and not randomised. At that base rate the ML lever is capped at about 2.5-5x, not 10x. Cost per attempt is ~$0.3-1M (candidate's figure; I consider it plausible), but approval adds ~$22.5M over 6+ years (Animal Health Institute via Veterinary Practice News). Some industry sources put it as high as $100M (Anivive). ML does nothing to cut that downstream cost, and that cost is most of the capital.

name: SubsetRx: rescuing failed trials via responder subgroups
one_line_reason: Cheap distressed rights and a strong ladder, but the proving step that buyers accept is a prospective trial, not ML discovery, and the step-up is about 10x with a low confirmation rate. It fails C1 the same way geothermal in coal mines does.
fatal_flaw: A retrospective subgroup found by searching many hypotheses in a failed trial is not accepted proof by regulators or acquirers. The value-creating proving step is a prospective confirmatory trial costing tens of millions, so discovery is a minority of the work in the only rung that has a buyer, and the step-up is about 10x, not 10^4x. Lantern Pharma has pursued this exact thesis since 2019 without a market re-rating.
step_up: Unproven: failed or wind-down assets clear at about $0.1-4M (Humanigen's whole estate went on a $2M stalking-horse credit bid in 2024; Transdel sold to Cardium for $4M). Proven, if prospectively confirmed: licensing deals of $10-50M upfront are possible (my estimate). After a retrospective subgroup only, buyers pay a heavy discount; I'd estimate $2-10M, or 2-5x. Even the candidate's own optimistic case of 10-50x is 2-3 orders of magnitude below the 10^4 benchmark. Lantern Pharma, which has run exactly this 'rescue' thesis since 2019, has a small-cap valuation of roughly $50M (estimate, from memory), so the market has not re-rated rescued assets.
hit_rate_capex: Base rate: post-hoc subgroups from failed trials rarely hold up when tested prospectively. Examples: the E5 sepsis subgroup failed its second Phase 3; Götte et al. 2017 show that subgroups selected for the most extreme effect overestimate it; Dyson 2021 found a BRCA1 subgroup with HR 0.59 against 0.97 overall but framed it as hypothesis-generating only. I'd estimate 5-15% of rescue subgroups confirm. Cost per attempt: $0.5-2M for the retrospective step, but $20-100M+ for the confirmatory trial that actually creates value (estimate). ML can cheaply generate many candidate subgroups, but it does nothing to cut the confirmatory trial cost, so the capex drop on the step that matters is far below 10x. ML also makes the multiplicity and false-positive problem worse.

name: Isolate Rights / Strain Vault: dormant university and USDA microbial isolates for crop biologicals
one_line_reason: Fails like the geothermal-in-coal-mines example: picking the tube is easy with legible public genomes, while field proving, formulation and manufacturing are the expensive bespoke work. The strains are free rather than bought cheaply, and incumbents such as Ginkgo/AgBiome and Lavie/ICL already do the ML mining.
fatal_flaw: The proving step that buyers pay for is multi-season field efficacy plus formulation and manufacturing, not a single greenhouse assay, and it is the hard bespoke part. Underneath that, the strains are free and the genomes are already legible, so there is no cheap illegible right to buy and no information edge over Ginkgo/AgBiome, Lavie Bio/ICL and Pivot Bio, who already do ML-first strain mining at scale. Lavie Bio, the closest analogue (an AI biologicals discovery company), sold its whole platform for $15.25M.
step_up: Unproven: an ARS NRRL Open Collection strain costs $0. The NRRL site says strains are free apart from postage, capped at 24 per lab per year. University TTO licences are an estimated $1-50k. Proven, the best public comparable is the Corteva-Lavie Bio exclusive biofungicide licence, a $5M advance in two instalments plus milestones and royalties (2023). That came after Lavie's AI discovery plus greenhouse and field work, not after a single greenhouse assay. The whole Lavie Bio platform (microbial bank, programmes, products, team) sold to ICL for $15.25M in 2025, plus $3.5M for the MicroBoost AI engine. Certis licensed the patented Szeged strain B. mojavensis R3B without disclosed terms. A greenhouse-only hit realistically goes from ~$30-50k all-in to an estimated $0.1-1M option value, about 3-20x. The 10^3x figure needs a field-validated asset, which costs $1-5M+ to get to (my estimate).
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is low. In Ginkgo's own Bacillus biofungicide funnel, 4,171 strains gave 136 (about 3%) with significant disease control and 3 (about 0.07%, roughly 1 in 1,400) strong foliar or root-rot leads. Globachem tested more than 100 UHasselt strains and took 2 into a licence pending greenhouse trials (about 2%). Cost per greenhouse or in vitro attempt is an estimated $10-50k each, including fermentation. ML pre-filtering on genomes (antiSMASH, Bt toxin homology) could plausibly raise the first-pass hit rate from 3% to 15-30%, a 5-10x lever on greenhouse spend. But greenhouse-to-field attrition, which is roughly 70-90% of greenhouse hits failing in the field by industry consensus (my estimate), is mostly about colonisation, formulation and environment, not genome features, so ML barely touches the expensive step.

name: Shelved Germplasm / Germplasm Trait Finder: licensing shelved public breeding lines
one_line_reason: This fails on the right. Public germplasm is free to everyone through NPGS and GRIN or licensed non-exclusively for $100-500, the trait outcome is often already in legible registration and GRIN fields, and the step-up is roughly 10-100x at best, not 10^3.
fatal_flaw: There is no exclusive, cheaply buyable right. Registered public germplasm must be deposited in NPGS and is freely distributed through GRIN to anyone, including the seed majors. They can therefore screen the same line themselves without paying for the step-up. Secondary flaws: the trait outcome is usually already written in the registration abstract or GRIN descriptors, and the proving step is a slow, bespoke biological season rather than a trivial physical step.
step_up: Unproven: public germplasm moves at nominal prices. UW-Madison charges a $100 transfer fee per released inbred and $500 per breeding population for private companies. Iowa State charges $500 per inbred for research and test-crossing, then $500 plus per-MVK royalties for commercialisation. NCSU charges about $200 per tomato line for a non-exclusive breeding licence. Proven: I found no disclosed price for a single trait-donor line. The disclosed deals are bundled programmes: DuPont Pioneer sold its alfalfa programme plus facilities to S&W for up to $49M, and Americot paid $6.8M for the NexGen brand plus DPL germplasm. Public FHB wheat cultivars (Maryland, Georgia going to AGS and UniSouth) are licensed for royalties, not lump sums in the millions. My estimate for a proven donor is $50k-500k upfront or a royalty stream, so roughly 10-100x on a $500-5k entry. The candidate's $0.5-10M figure is unsupported.
hit_rate_capex: The candidate claims a base hit rate under 2%. That is unverified and is my estimate as well. Most lines registered for a trait already carry that trait, but finding a hidden, unscreened resistance to a new pathogen in old lines is rare, plausibly 1-5%. Cost per proving attempt is $10-80k (the candidate's figure; my estimate agrees for a multi-location trial or disease nursery plus KASP). A ~10x capex cut is possible in principle. But public programmes already screen at scale for free: USDA-ARS is screening germplasm and commercial varieties for tar spot, and Michigan State's NIFA Great Lakes Tar Spot Initiative is screening diverse maize germplasm. That removes much of the room for an ML lever.

name: Orphan Cultivar: unreleased selections of retiring private breeders
one_line_reason: The long-tail royalties and the ladder are real, but the proving step is slow, costly biological field trialling, the very inversion the coal-mine geothermal counter-example rules out. ML over notebooks cannot shortcut the phenotyping.
fatal_flaw: Proving is not trivial or abstracted. It means 8-20 years of physical, multi-site field trials (Agroscope: 15-20 years, 1 in 30,000 seedlings). The step-up arrives slowly through royalties, not at the moment of a hit. Discovery is a small share of the rung, and leftover selections are adversely selected rejects.
step_up: Unproven: a seedling or selection with records, roughly $0-5k (my estimate; I found no market comps for orphan selections). Proven tail: Cosmic Crisp (WA 38) earned WSU more than $8M in one fiscal year, inside $19.4M of total WSU royalties in FY25. Its terms were $1 per tree plus a 4.75% royalty per box. Honeycrisp was about $1 per tree. So a top hit is 10^3-10^4x on paper. But the value is not realised at proof. It comes years later, as trees are planted and fruit is sold, and it depends on a club manager's marketing spend (Cosmic Crisp had a $10.1M marketing budget). Most licensed cultivars earn little. I found no upfront fees for licensing an advanced selection.
hit_rate_capex: Base rates: Agroscope reports 1 in about 30,000 seedlings becomes a variety. Zaiger trials about 700 selections a year and commercialises about 7 (about 1% at the advanced-selection stage). Cost per proving attempt: a multi-site trial of one selection over 3-10 years costs about $20-100k (my estimate), plus the propagation and land you must own. ML that ranks notebook text cannot replace genotype-by-environment field data. Public breeders already use genomic selection (RosBREED). Realistic lever: maybe 2-3x at the selection-to-trial stage, not 10x, because the outcome needs new phenotypes that no archive contains.

name: Sleeper Hunter / Old Master Sleepers: misattributed Old Masters at regional auctions
one_line_reason: This looks like Terranox at a glance, but rights are bought in competitive open auctions, so the step-up gets competed away at the hammer. The proof is gated by subjective expert opinion rather than a cheap physical test, and the market and ladder are too small.
fatal_flaw: The unproven right is sold in an open, globally broadcast auction where sleeper-hunting dealers and online bidders already bid hits up to near-proven value (the $500-800 Rembrandt hammered at $870k). The proving gate is subjective expert acceptance, and ML cannot make it cheaper or abstract it away. So the 10^4 step-up goes to the seller, not to the buyer, and the total market is too small for a ladder.
step_up: The headline cases are huge. Salvator Mundi was bought for about $1,175 in 2005 and sold for $450m in 2017 (about 10^5). A Rembrandt at Nye & Co (New Jersey, 2015) was estimated at $500-800. But the realised step-up from what an informed buyer actually pays is much smaller, because the hammer price already captures most of the value. The Nye Rembrandt hammered at $870k against that $500-800 estimate. An Adam's Dublin sleeper was estimated at EUR 800 and sold for EUR 120k. A Banbury 'Italian Old Master' (2025) made GBP 685k hammer after a bidding battle. Sotheby's 'Let the Little Children Come Unto Me' made $1.7m in 2014 as an anonymous Netherlandish work, then $10.59m in 2026 as Rembrandt (about 6x). So the step-up the buyer captures is about 3-20x. The 10^3-10^4 jump mostly goes to the uninformed seller. My score of 3 gives some credit for the rare true sleeper that nobody bids up.
hit_rate_capex: This is my estimate; I found no published hit rate. Probably well under 1-2% of 'circle of' or unattributed lots are autograph works. Each proving attempt costs the purchase price ($500 to $30k+), plus $5-20k of technical analysis, plus 1-5 years of scholarly lobbying. ML triage could cut wasted purchases and technical analysis several-fold, so the capex lever is real but capped. The bigger constraint is that competitors see the same lots. Art Recognition's own figure is more than 500 authentications, and the 2024 Germann sale was the first work authenticated by AI alone. Even so, dealers such as Van Haeften say they 'would not under any circumstances' accept an AI attribution. ML does not lower the cost of the real gate.

name: Reverter Capital: possibility-of-reverter rights and orphan strips
one_line_reason: The data really is illegible and the rights can be bought, but statutes extinguish most old reverters. Proving one is an adversarial quiet-title suit that ML does not make cheaper. A hit yields a nuisance-value release (roughly 10-100x) rather than 10^3x. There is no capitalised eager buyer and no real ladder.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is contested litigation on a shrinking, statute-extinguished asset class. Marketable Title Acts and reverter-duration statutes (California 30 years, Ohio, Kentucky draft and Illinois 40 years, Oklahoma 30, Minnesota MTA, which voided exactly this heir-quitclaim play in Wichelman v. Messner) kill most old reverters. Some states bar assigning them at all. The survivors require heir tracing plus a quiet-title fight with an unwilling occupant, so proving costs are dominated by legal work that ML does not cheapen.
step_up: Unproven: quitclaim from heirs at an assumed $200-2,000 (candidate's figure, unverified; I found no published price data). Proven: no market price exists. The value is a negotiated release or a share of the sale proceeds, and the occupant (school district, church, trail) resists. Comparable: the UK Oxfordshire claim was worth GBP 1.2m but the heirs ultimately lost at the Supreme Court. Trails Act railroad-reversion takings paid about $49m in a single year across roughly 8,000 pending claims (2013 report), which my estimate puts at low thousands to tens of thousands of dollars per parcel owner. So the realistic step-up is my estimate of 10-100x on the rare clean hit (a $1k quitclaim turning into a $10k-100k release), not 10^3-10^4. Also, the 'proven' value is capped by the occupant's cost to litigate or insure over the cloud, so buyers pay nuisance value, not the land value.
hit_rate_capex: I found no published base rate; these are my estimates. Of conditional grants found, most are already dead by statute. California Civ. Code 885.020/885.030 abolishes possibilities of reverter and expires powers of termination 30 years after recording unless a preservation notice is filed. Ohio 5301.49 and the Kentucky HB 256 draft use 40 years. Oklahoma uses 30. Minnesota's MTA barred the heirs' reverter claim in Wichelman v. Messner after they had bought quitclaims, which is exactly this business model failing in court. Florida (21 years, unverified) and Illinois (40-year Reverter Act) add more limits. The common-law rule in some states (e.g. Illinois) is that reverters are inheritable but not transferable inter vivos, so the right cannot even be bought. My estimate: under 5% of found grants are both live and assignable, and a fraction of those win. Cost per proving attempt (my estimate): heir tracing $2-10k, plus quiet title $10-50k+ if contested, plus 1-3 years. ML only reduces the search cost, which is the small part. Litigation cost per attempt does not fall, so the capex lever is well under 10x.

name: Orphan Railroad Fee Strips: defunct-railroad parcel quitclaims
one_line_reason: The data is illegible, but the step-up only becomes real after per-parcel litigation against adjoiners who usually win by reversion. Discovery is not 80% of the rung, and the ML lever on total capex is about 2-3x.
fatal_flaw: Proving is litigation, not discovery. Most railroad strips were easements or grants limited to railroad use. Those revert to adjoiners by law, so the quitclaim the company buys is usually worthless, as in the SC CSX $104k quitclaim, the Kansas ruling and the Indiana Penn Central settlement. Even fee hits need contested quiet-title actions per parcel against neighbors who have the legal presumption, so ML does not drive the cost that binds.
step_up: Unproven: a bulk quitclaim at a nominal price. My estimate is $1k-$100k per railroad estate. For comparison, a private buyer paid CSX $104,000 for a quitclaim on a 1.19-mile segment (sclawyersweekly). Proven: a fee strip is worth roughly the adjoining land per acre, about $5k-$500k/acre (estimate), or a holdout premium when it blocks a data-center or homebuilder site. Per parcel, the gain from a near-zero allocated cost can be 100-1000x on a rare blocking hit. Typical strips are narrow remnants, with value in the low thousands of dollars, so the realistic gain is 10-100x after legal cost. That same CSX quitclaim was worth $0: the court held the railroad owned only an easement, so fee title went to the adjoiners.
hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is low. Most railroad corridors were acquired as easements or as grants limited to railroad use ("so long as used for railroad purposes"). Those revert to adjoiners on abandonment, so the quitclaim conveys nothing (Kansas Supreme Court; SC CSX case; Washington Milwaukee Road split; the Indiana Firestone class settlement gave abandoned Penn Central land to adjoiners in 51 counties). Estimate: 1-5% of parcels are fee-owned and unconveyed with real value, which matches the candidate's own figure. Cost per proving attempt is dominated by quiet title, about $5k-$30k per parcel and 6-24 months contested (estimate). Desk research is only about $100-$500 per parcel. ML cuts desk-screening cost, but desk screening is not the binding cost. The lever on total capex is perhaps 2-3x, not 10x.

name: SiteSeed: entitled build-to-suit tower sites
one_line_reason: Good ladder and cheap options, but entitlement is mostly approved and the step-up depends on private carrier tenancy, not on discovery in public data, so this is not a Terranox frame.
fatal_flaw: The value step comes from an anchor carrier tenant, which is driven by private carrier RF plans and search rings, not from entitlement. Entitlement itself succeeds most of the time (about 70-85%, estimate) under federal shot-clock and substantial-evidence rules. So ML on public zoning data attacks a step that is neither the main failure point nor the source of value. That caps the lever at about 1.3x, and a permit-only flip lands near breakeven on total spend.
step_up: Unproven: a 2-3 yr ground-lease option at about $500-2,000 (candidate's figure, plausible). Entitled with no tenant: speculative sites trade thinly. My estimate is $10-50k, plus reimbursement of entitlement costs, because the buyer still has to put $150-300k (my estimate) into building the tower and needs a tenant. Entitled with an anchor carrier lease: tower companies value towers at about 15-25x tower cash flow. A single-tenant tower at about $20-30k/yr of rent is worth roughly $300k-600k (estimate, consistent with the candidate's $250k-1M+ range), but that value belongs to the tenant lease, not the permit. On total cost per proven site (about $40-60k), entitlement alone gives about 0.5-1x. With a tenant it is about 5-10x. The 10^3x figure on the option ignores the entitlement spend. Score 2.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate for entitlement is high, not low. Telecommunications Act Section 332(c)(7) requires any denial to rest on substantial written evidence, and FCC shot-clock rules (150 days for a new tower) push localities to approve. My estimate is that 70-85% of properly sited tower applications are eventually approved, often with conditions or stealth designs. Cost per attempt is about $30-60k (candidate's figure; consistent with industry site-acquisition fees, my estimate). The lever is capped at 1/0.75, about 1.3x, nowhere near 10x. The low-hit-rate step is getting a carrier to commit, and public data cannot predict that well. I could not verify these figures because the web search budget for this turn was already used up, so all numbers are estimates from prior knowledge.

name: Hidden Lots: antiquated-subdivision legal-lot discovery
one_line_reason: The data is illegible and the outcome is unsummarised, which is real. But discovery is not 80% of the sellable rung: entitlement dominates. The step-up on a whole parcel is about 1.1-3x, not 10^3. And each shot costs a full $1-5M parcel.
fatal_flaw: A Certificate of Compliance proves a legal lot, not a buildable one. In the high-value coastal markets that drive the step-up, the real value step is bespoke entitlement (Coastal permits, CEQA, water and septic). That is harder than discovery, which is exactly the coal-mine geothermal failure mode. On top of that, the right can only be acquired by buying the whole parcel at full market price, which kills the cheap-shot economics.
step_up: The quoted 10^3x 'on option' is an artifact of a small option premium. It is not an asset step-up, and the owner has to sign the option, which tells them what you found. On a whole-parcel purchase at market, the realistic uplift is the value of the extra lot minus discounts for entitlement risk, carry and legal cost. If the extra lot is buildable and entitled, that is roughly 1.3-3x the parcel price. As a bare CoC without entitlement, it is likely 1.1-1.5x. These are my estimates. I could not verify any comps this turn because the shared web search budget was already used up (0 of 5 searches ran).
hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt (my estimates, not verified): title chain and abstract $1-5k; boundary/ALTA survey $5-20k; land-use attorney $10-50k; county CoC application fee about $2-10k. Total about $20-80k and 6-24 months per parcel. ML could raise the hit rate of the desk screen. But the expensive failures happen after discovery: merger findings, conditional CoC terms, and refused CDPs or permits. ML cannot predict those well from deeds. So the capex lever is maybe 2-3x, not 10x. Base hit rate is unknown. After Gardner v. County of Sonoma (2003, Cal. Supreme Court: pre-1893 antiquated maps do not by themselves create legal lots), a large share of the old-plat candidates simply fail (my recollection of case law, not re-verified this turn).

name: Floodway Flip / Floodway Lot Revival: LiDAR-driven FEMA map revisions
one_line_reason: Not excluded but weak (11/25). The ML-findable case (SFHA-to-X) is a ~1.2-2x step-up that a free elevation lookup mostly solves, and the 20-200x floodway case is dominated by engineering, politics and development rather than discovery. These scores come from prior knowledge, because the shared search budget ran out before any search ran.
fatal_flaw: The big step-up is in the floodway-to-buildable case, and there the proving step is not mostly discovery. It needs a hydraulic no-rise re-model, community concurrence, entitlement and site development, much as the bespoke geothermal plant dominated the coal-mine case. The rung where discovery does dominate (an SFHA-to-X LOMA) only yields about 1.2-2x. A DEM-vs-BFE lookup already captures it, the outcomes sit in legible LOMC fields, and the base hit rate is probably already high. So ML has little lever.
step_up: No sourced numbers: the shared web search budget ran out before any query ran. Estimates from prior knowledge: SFHA-to-X removal adds about 10-50% to land value, so roughly 1.2-2x. The SFHA discount has narrowed under Risk Rating 2.0, and lenders and buyers increasingly use First Street-style risk scores whatever the FEMA zone says. Floodway land in growth metros may trade at about $1-5k/acre against $50-300k/acre for entitled residential land (estimate). But most of that gap is entitlement plus development cost, not the map change, so the step-up that comes purely from proving is probably 2-10x.
hit_rate_capex: Estimates, unverified (no searches ran). LOMA cost: no FEMA review fee, plus a surveyor's elevation certificate at about $500-2,000. LOMR-F: FEMA fee in the hundreds of dollars plus survey. Physical-change LOMR or floodway revision: FEMA fee of several thousand dollars plus $20-100k+ of engineering, and 6-18 months. My recollection is that most LOMAs FEMA receives are approved, because applicants pre-screen with elevation data. If so, the base hit rate for pre-screened attempts is already high, perhaps 50%+, and the most ML can cut capex is about 2x, not 10x. For floodway removals the hit rate is low, but the cost is set by the hydraulics and the politics, not by discovery.

name: Coastal Vested Rights: frozen California coastal lots
one_line_reason: The step-up is real (~10-50x) and the right can be bought, but proving costs $150k-1M+ and takes 2-5 years of political and legal process that ML does not shorten. Base hit rates are not low, much of the outcome is already in LCP/ESHA/water-moratorium fields, and the ladder ends at a regional luxury homebuilder.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is discretionary, multi-year, bespoke entitlement and litigation against the Coastal Commission, plus hard physical constraints (water, septic, slope, fire access). It is not a cheap, quasi-mechanical test like an exploratory drill, so discovery is a minority of the work. Base hit rates on screened lots are already moderate, so ML cannot cut capex 10x. This is the same structural failure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
step_up: These are my estimates; the web search budget was used up and no live search ran. Substandard or ESHA-constrained lots in places like Malibu's El Nido/Big Rock, Montara, Big Sur and Sea Ranch change hands at roughly $20-150k. Comparable lots with a permit or an approved CDP sell at roughly $1-4M in Malibu and $300k-1.5M elsewhere on the coast. That gives about 10-50x on a hit, and up to ~100x at best. The anchor case is Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council (1992), where buildable beachfront lots were valued around $975k. Entitlement costs of $150k-1M+ eat into the multiple, so the net step-up is closer to 5-20x.
hit_rate_capex: My estimates, not sourced. Each proving attempt costs about $150k-1M+ in consultants, studies, legal fees and appeals, and takes 2-5 years, not the 1-2 years the pitch assumes. On lots screened by an experienced entitlement attorney, the base hit rate is plausibly 30-60%. The Commission usually allows some economically viable use to avoid takings liability (for example, approving reduced-footprint homes in ESHA). The cases that fail do so mainly for physical reasons: no water meter, septic infeasible, slope, fire access. ML cannot change any of those. With base hit rates that high, the lever is capped at about 2-3x, not 10x, and ML does nothing to the dominant cost, which is the entitlement process.

name: Ghost Offsets / OffsetBank: unclaimed emission reduction credits from shut-down sources
one_line_reason: Clean paperwork-only frame with real capitalised buyers, but valuable shutdown tonnage is already legible and broker-canvassed, the base hit rate is not low (lever ~3x), and the step-up is mostly 10-100x on small sources, so it is a solid niche, not a Terranox analogue.
fatal_flaw: There is no purchase discount where the value sits. The outcome (who banked) is already in legible public registries, and brokers already canvass large shutdowns. The only cheap rights are small, low-tonnage, short-window sources, so the hit-rate lever is capped near 3x and the opportunity is a niche origination business, not a 10^4 discovery engine.
step_up: These are my own estimates. All web searches failed because the shared search budget was used up, so no number here was checked live. Price unproven: $0-25k for an assignment or option, as stated in the candidate. Price proven: a typical small to mid shutdown (a boiler, kiln or small turbine) yields maybe 5-50 tpy of NOx or VOC. At SJV NOx of ~$10-20k/t (the candidate's 2025-26 figure, from memory of the district's annual ERC report; some trades run higher) that is ~$50k-$1M. In Houston-Galveston-Brazoria and SCAQMD, scarce VOC/NOx sometimes reaches $100k-300k per ton. Return on capital deployed is ~10-100x, with rare outliers near 1000x. The right is not near-zero in the owner's eyes when the owner knows ERCs exist. The step from 'expiring and unclaimed' to 'certified' is genuinely large, but only for the minority of sources that slip through.
hit_rate_capex: Unverified estimate: the base hit rate is the candidate's 20-40% for moving from 'shutdown identified' to 'credit certified', mostly lost to baseline or surplus disqualification and missed deadlines. Cost per attempt is about $10-50k (my estimate) for consultant baseline work, legal assignment, the district filing fee and any stack-test reconstruction. That makes 1/base hit rate only ~2.5-5x. ML raising the hit rate cannot cut capex 10x. The proving step is not expensive or mostly failing. It is cheap paperwork that mostly succeeds when the source is eligible.

name: Chapter 7 Abandoned Causes of Action
one_line_reason: The sellers are informed trustees with contingency counsel, so the claims they sell cheaply are the rejected residue. Litigation is not an abstracted physical step. The step-up is about 10-100x and arrives years later, not as an immediate 10^4 revaluation.
fatal_flaw: Adverse selection by an informed fiduciary. The Chapter 7 trustee has a legal duty to maximise the estate, is paid a percentage of recoveries, and can hire contingency counsel at zero estate cost. Any claim with real expected value gets pursued, not sold for $1-10k. What reaches nominal-price sale or abandonment is the residue the expert already rejected, and the sales are open to overbid, with the defendant as the natural bidder. Value is realised only through years of litigation, not at the moment of proving.
step_up: My estimate, no source verified: a claim bought for $1-10k that turns out good might be worth $100k-1M as a funded or contingency-backed claim, roughly 20-300x on paper. Commercial funders such as Burford and Omni typically want claims with damages in the high seven or eight figures and fund rather than buy outright. Most Chapter 7 claims are small individual or small-business claims, so the realisable step-up is lower and comes years later, discounted by funder share (often 20-40% of proceeds, estimated). That puts it at about 10-100x. It is not 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is the candidate's own 1-3% (my estimate and unverified). Each proving attempt costs very little: ML triage is near-free, plus about $5-25k for a merits and damages memo (estimate). Today's capex is not large and mostly failing in the way a $100k-1M exploratory drill is, so a 10x capex cut buys little. The lever cap of 1/hit rate (about 30-100x) exists in theory. In practice the binding constraint is deal flow from trustees, not the cost of evaluating.

name: Restitution Claim Matcher / Provenance Claims: looted-art restitution
one_line_reason: This is a legal-collections business dressed as discovery: matching is the easy part, heirship and litigation are the bespoke hard part, the step-up is about 10-100x on the company's share, and the market is shrinking with no ladder.
fatal_flaw: The work after discovery (multi-generation heirship proof, then years of contested negotiation or litigation against reluctant possessors under limitations, laches and good-faith-purchaser defences) dominates the effort and the failure rate. Discovery is nowhere near 80% of the rung. The pool is also finite and shrinking, and the work is already partly matched by free or nonprofit bodies (HCPO, the Commission for Looted Art in Europe, the Lost Art Foundation, the Art Loss Register).
step_up: The unproven right costs a few thousand dollars per assignment, or more typically a contingency share of about 20-40% of recovery (that range is the practice of heir-hunting and restitution firms such as Mondex, from memory, not verified this run). A proven claim on a mid-market work pays roughly $50k-$5M as a settlement or sale split; outliers like the Klimt Adele Bloch-Bauer I were sold for $135M after restitution. Measured on the company's cash outlay (about $5-20k of research and genealogy per claim, my estimate) against its share of a typical settlement (about $100k-$500k), the step-up is about 10-100x. 10^3x happens only on rare blockbusters. Most claims end in a split with the possessor (Washington Principles "just and fair solutions"), and that shrinks the payout further.
hit_rate_capex: I could not verify this: the shared search budget was used up before this agent ran, so every number is an estimate from prior knowledge. Cost per proving attempt (provenance match plus heirship file): about $5-50k. Base hit rate from candidate match to recovery: I estimate 5-15%. The main reason claims fail is not finding the work. It is legal defences (statute of limitations or laches outside the US HEAR Act window, "forced sale" disputes, good-faith purchaser laws in Switzerland and other civil-law countries) and getting heirs to cooperate. ML speeds up the matching but leaves those failure modes untouched, so I estimate the real capex lever at about 2-3x, not 10x.

name: Black Box Publishing / Catalog / Claimant: orphan compositions behind unmatched royalties
one_line_reason: This is a cheap, crowded matching problem: the MLC and PROs already surface unmatched status, the long-tail payouts are small, and the realistic step-up is about 2-20x rather than 10^3+, so it fails C2, C3 and C4 even though a buyer exists.
fatal_flaw: The outcome is already legible: the MLC, SoundExchange and the PROs publish searchable unmatched and unclaimed status, and the MLC and admin companies are already matching. On top of that, the per-work dollars in the long tail are tiny, so a hit yields roughly 2-20x on a small purchase, not 10^3-10^4. The hard cost is title and heir clearance, which ML does not solve.
step_up: From memory, not newly searched: small catalogs sell for about 5-12x NPS on Royalty Exchange-type marketplaces, and large catalogs for about 12-20x. Suppose a share bought for $500-10k is actually unclaimed and the pool has, say, $200-2k of accrued money (my estimate for one long-tail work). After the claim you collect that money and the share sells for maybe 6-10x its ongoing annual NPS. Real step-up on the purchase price: about 2-20x, nowhere near 10^3. The reason is that the long tail of unmatched money is spread over millions of works, so very few are worth much. Under the MMA, unclaimed money is eventually paid out by market share, and the date keeps getting extended. A hit is income you can claim. It does not move an asset from about $1 to $10k.
hit_rate_capex: From memory: in Feb 2021 the MLC received about $424M of historical unmatched mechanical royalties from DSPs, and since then it has reported match rates above 90% by dollar value. The money left over is spread thin. The proving attempt is cheap: a database lookup plus a claim filing costs maybe $50-500 per work, and the legal title work costs maybe $1-5k per estate (estimates). So the proving step is neither expensive nor mostly failing in a way that ML would improve 10x. Discovery capex is low already, so the 1/base-hit-rate lever is small. The cost that matters is title and heir clearance, which ML does not cut. Web search budget was exhausted, so no new sources were added.

name: Reversion Rights Partners: out-of-print book reversions
one_line_reason: The hit depends on producer taste found through pitching, and an option pays only a few times its cost, so there is no expensive, mostly-failing proving step with a 10^3x payoff for ML to make cheaper.
fatal_flaw: The 'hit' is a buyer's taste decision found by pitching, not a hidden fact proven by a cheap test. On top of that, options pay only about 1-10% of purchase price, so the step-up at proof is about 2-5x rather than 10^3-10^4. Modern ebook and POD 'in print' definitions also shrink the pool of titles that can be reverted.
step_up: My estimates (web search budget was exhausted, so no live sourcing). Unproven right: $1-10k to fund a reversion plus a co-ownership share. Option sale on a midlist or backlist novel: usually $1k-$25k, about 1-10% of the purchase price. Purchase price if the project is made: about $50k-$500k for midlist, more for a known IP. Backlist audio rights: about $1-5k advances. So an option, the 'proof' event, is about 1-5x the cost. The 10-100x claimed in the pitch only arrives at a purchase-price exercise, which is rare and comes years later. No 10^3-10^4 jump happens straight away.
hit_rate_capex: My estimates from industry folklore, not sourced this run. Commonly cited: under 10% of optioned books (often given as 1 in 10 to 1 in 20) get made. The share of reverted backlist titles that ever get optioned is probably in the low single-digit percent. Each attempt is cheap, though (legal letters plus pitching, about $1-10k), so the expensive proving step that ML could make 10x cheaper does not exist. Predicting adaptation demand is a taste problem with a weak signal. ML might lift option rates a little, but it cannot cut a large capex because there is no large capex.

name: SEP Essentiality Prover (cellular, Wi-Fi, codec, JEDEC, industrial standards; incl. university SEPs)
one_line_reason: This is a reasonable patent-arbitrage niche but not a Terranox analogue. The step-up is about 5-30x, not 10^4. Proving does not convert straight into cash: value only arrives through litigation or slow pool payouts. Incumbents (IPlytics, Acacia, InterDigital) already mine this data, and the ladder tops out at an InterDigital-sized licensing company.
fatal_flaw: The step-up is only about 10x and it is not realised at certification. The value comes from years of royalty distributions or costly FRAND enforcement on a 20-year asset that is shrinking. Meanwhile, well-funded aggregators already run ML claim-to-spec screening at the same auctions, and the 8-36% base rate caps the hit-rate lever at about 3-10x.
step_up: Estimates from prior knowledge; no live search was possible. Secondary-market patents typically trade at ~$50-250k per asset (Richardson Oliver Law Group market reports have put average ask prices around $100-200k and falling). Undeclared or unverified telecom families from distressed or university sellers might go for ~$10-50k each in bulk. A family certified essential and placed in a pool might be worth ~$100k-1M NPV. That figure depends on remaining life, how many jurisdictions it covers and how pool shares are split; Avanci 4G/5G vehicle royalties of ~$20-32 per car are shared across thousands of families. That makes the realistic step-up ~5-30x, with rare outliers at ~100x. It is far from 10^3-10^4, and it is not immediate: cash arrives over years of distributions.
hit_rate_capex: Base essentiality rate of declared families: about 8-36% across studies (Goodman & Myers 2005 put 3G at ~21%; later LTE/5G studies by Fairfield, Cyber Creative Institute and others fall in the ~15-40% range). Using the candidate's own figure, the ML lever is capped at ~3-10x, and in practice lower, because ML alignment pre-screens are already used. Cost per proving attempt: ~$5-30k per family per evaluator (candidate figure; Avanci/Sisvel-style evaluations commonly run ~$10-20k). Cheap ML pre-screening already exists (IPlytics/LexisNexis, Patentcloud SEP OmniLytics, Unified Patents, Amplified), so the costly human evaluation is already the confirmation step, not the search step.

name: Function-Category Arbitrage: US/EU devices into Japan STM reimbursement
one_line_reason: This is regulatory arbitrage with a roughly 10-50x step-up (estimated), a high base approval rate, outcomes already published in MHLW price tables, and incumbent distributors who already do the same in-licensing. It fails the 95-5 discovery frame.
fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck and the proving step rarely fails. Function-category mapping is largely a predicate lookup, and its answer is published in legible MHLW price tables. Clearing regulatory and QMS steps and winning commercial uptake is most of the work, and approval of a cleared device into a B category succeeds at a high base rate (estimated). So ML cannot cut capex by anything like 10x. The capitalised buyers (Japan Lifeline, Century Medical) already run this exact in-licensing playbook, so they compete with the company rather than pay it a step-up.
step_up: Unproven right: exclusive Japan option, $20-100k (from the candidate, unverified). Proven right: a Japan-approved device with a B-category price, licensed or sold to a distributor. My estimate is $0.5-5M upfront plus a supply margin, depending on category size. That gives roughly 10-50x, not 10^3. Japan also cuts reimbursement prices every two years and applies foreign-average-price adjustments, so the step-up shrinks over time. All numbers are estimates; I found no sourced deal prices.
hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt is $100-300k (from the candidate). In my estimate, $0.3-1M is more realistic for Class III/IV once QMS audits and MAH costs are included. The base hit rate is HIGH, not low. A device with FDA/CE clearance that maps onto an existing B category is usually approved, because Japan accepts foreign clinical data for most such devices, and its category is predictable from the predicate. Failures come mainly from commercial non-uptake, not failed proving. With a hit rate of perhaps 50-80%, the ML lever is capped at about 1.25-2x, nowhere near 10x. This is an estimate: the search budget ran out before any search could run, so I could not source a PMDA approval-rate figure.

name: Dead-Fabless Mask-Set Revival
one_line_reason: This is the geothermal-mine pattern. Discovery is the easy, half-readable part, the physical revival is the hard part, and an established authorized-aftermarket player is both the only buyer and a competitor.
fatal_flaw: Reviving the part (getting a foundry and process match, validating wafers, requalifying) is much harder and costlier than finding which dead lines have demand. That demand signal is already largely readable in DIBBS, GIDEP and vendor obsolescence databases, which incumbents like Rochester mine while also competing for the same estates.
step_up: My estimate, with no sources found: the IP and wafer bank costs $0-100k from an estate. If it has real sole-source defense or rail demand, the revival rights might sell or license for $0.5-5M, which is about 10-100x. That gain mostly comes after revival and requalification, not right after a data "hit". A bundle that has not been validated would probably sell to Rochester or Lansdale for only about 1-5x what you paid, because they are the natural buyers and their team already does this valuation. The 50-1000x in the candidate pitch is not backed by any source.
hit_rate_capex: I have no sourced numbers because the searches did not run. Estimates: most dead fabless lines have no captive installed base, so maybe 5-15% are worth reviving. Checking demand on paper costs little (analyst time, a few $k). Validating wafers or masks plus requalification costs about $100k-$1M+ per line. ML only speeds up the cheap paper step, so the expensive step is untouched and the lever is about 2-3x on total capex, not 10x.

name: EastWest Rights / PMDA Bridge: ex-Asia rights to drugs approved only in Japan, China or Korea
one_line_reason: This is drug development dressed as discovery. Proving value takes a trial, not a cheap drill, and both the outcome fields and the sellers are already legible and competitive.
fatal_flaw: The FDA minutes create no step-up that a buyer pays for. The value-creating proving step is a US-acceptable clinical trial costing $5-150M with ordinary drug-development hit rates. So discovery is a small share of the rung, ML does not touch the dominant cost, and the field is already crowded and legible. MediciNova has run this exact model since 2004 with no approval.
step_up: The unproven right costs about $0.5-10M upfront (candidate's figure). It is not near-zero, and the Chinese assets in this space now command $50M-$1.25B upfronts (Pfizer paid 3SBio $1.25B upfront in 2025). A buyer pays for clean data that FDA will accept, not for minutes. FDA minutes that agree a bridging plan might lift the asset's value 2-5x (my estimate). The candidate's own figure is about 20-100x, and that holds only after a successful bridging or pivotal trial, not at the minutes. There is no public market for 'minutes-stage' Asian assets. Comparator: MediciNova (est. ~2000) has used this exact model since in-licensing ibudilast from Kyorin in 2004. More than 20 years later it has no US approval and a market cap of roughly $100M (my recollection).
hit_rate_capex: Base rate: of drugs approved first in Japan, about 70% (80% for Japanese companies) are never approved by the FDA or EMA (Japanese Journal of Health Economics and Policy analysis). The pool of candidates is large, but most of them are me-too or local-standard-of-care drugs. Cost per proving attempt: about $0.5-2M to get minutes, but the step that actually creates value (a bridging or pivotal trial) costs $5-150M per attempt (estimate). ML only cuts the cheap triage part, which is already cheap: a BD analyst plus translators costs perhaps $50-200k per asset. So ML cannot cut total capex 10x. Most of the capex is trial cost, and ML does not touch it.

name: Survivor Genetics / Wild Elite Tree: resistant survivor trees in blight-killed stands
one_line_reason: Low hit rates are real, but proof is slow and biological rather than instant, survivors in clonal crops usually have nothing new to patent, imagery is legible and already used by public breeders, and per-tree royalties of about $1 give at most a 10-100x step-up after years.
fatal_flaw: Proving a survivor takes years of biological testing (a 34-year field record for the best Florida example), not a quick discrete event. Survivors in clonal orchards are usually not genetically distinct, so there is nothing new to patent and the owner is not a seller who cannot read the data. Public breeding programmes already scout these same survivors for free.
step_up: Unproven: a survivor tree has roughly $0-1k of option value (candidate's figure; no market exists). Proven: no per-tree citrus royalty rates are published. My estimate is the typical woody-plant patent royalty of about $0.50-2 per tree. One large Florida order was 300,000 HLB-tolerant trees (FreshPlaza), which at that rate is about $0.15-0.6M. A good variety might earn about $1-5M over the patent life, received 5-10+ years later. Italy only allows Leccino and FS-17 (CNR-patented) for replanting, which caps demand for new olive selections until regulators accept them. Discounted for time and risk, the realistic gain on a ~$1-5k right is roughly 10-100x, not an immediate 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: The base rate is low. Penn State found 13 of 1,762 ash trees still alive in 2019, about 0.7%. The 2021 Frontiers study of Puglia olives found 30 paucisymptomatic trees, and 23 of them clustered genetically with Leccino/FS17, so most were already known resistant cultivars rather than new ones. USFS lingering-ash crosses gave 15-40% of progeny with better defence. Cost per candidate is about $2-20k (candidate's estimate, plausible) over 1-5 years. In theory ML could cut capex 10x. In practice, imagery cannot separate genetic resistance from microsite, rootstock, chance escape or treatment history, so better triage gives perhaps 2-3x (my estimate).

name: Bone Rights / Deep Time Rights: private-land vertebrate fossil leases
one_line_reason: The step-up is spectacular, but this is a lottery rather than a rung. Value is only realised after costly excavation and prep, landowners are savvy and take 50/50 splits, the ML lever is limited by erosion, and the whole end market is a few hundred million dollars.
fatal_flaw: The market is tiny and lumpy (a few eight-figure skeletons a year), and landowners already know the value and take about 50%. Bones turn up where erosion exposes them, not hidden under data the way uranium is. Excavation and prep come before any value can be realised. ML can make prospecting somewhat cheaper, but not by 10x, and even then there is no ladder to a large company.
step_up: Unproven: the ranch where Gus the T. rex was found sold for about $6M for 6,537 acres, about $900/acre (Fay Ranches / Hall and Hall listing, my arithmetic). A lease costs around $2-20k per section (the candidate's own figure; I found no published lease rates). Proven: Gus hammered at $43M and sold for about $50M in July 2026; Apex (stegosaurus) $44.6M in 2024; Big John (triceratops) about $7.7M in 2021; Trey (triceratops) estimated at $4.5-5.5M in 2026. So a hit takes a $2-20k lease to a $1-50M sale, nominally 10^2-10^4. But that value only shows up after excavation, prep and sale, not on discovery. The landowner usually takes about 50% (Larson's 50-50 split, Gus proceeds split with Licking). Typical commercial specimens are mostly worth $0.1-2M, not $40M.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: auction-grade, mostly complete skeletons are very rare. My estimate is a handful a year across the whole Hell Creek, Morrison and Judith River region, despite decades of work by commercial and academic crews. Fragments are found all the time. Cost per attempt: a field season of prospecting costs about $50-200k (my estimate), which is cheap. Successful digs go on to cost $100k-1M+ for excavation and prep. The ML lever is limited: bones are mostly found where they erode out each year, and walking crews already cover the known badlands. Drone ML bone-spotting can raise coverage per dollar, perhaps 2-3x (my estimate), but it will not cut capex 10x. The main constraint is how fast erosion exposes new bone, not where to look.

name: Die Hunter: unattributed coin and stamp varieties
one_line_reason: The frame passes on paper: discovery dominates and proving is a cheap mailing. But the step-up is usually 1-5x, proving costs only $10-60, the references are legible, cherrypickers and AI apps already compete, and the market is too small to climb.
fatal_flaw: The pool of mispriced rare varieties is tiny and finite, and both the buyers and the step-up are thin. Most hits are worth 1-5x on items that cost tens of dollars, and the variety references are fully legible to human cherrypickers and to AI ID apps already on the market. It is a capped hobby arbitrage with no 10^3 step-up and no ladder, and proving is already cheap, so ML has no 10x capex lever.
step_up: This is my estimate, not sourced data. A typical attributed hit is worth 1-5x the common-type price. Some low-population VAMs sell for no premium at all, even in an attributed holder (CU forum). Only famous varieties give 100-1000x, for example an 1882-O/S early die state in XF sold for "a couple thousand dollars" against a common Morgan at about $40-60, roughly 40x (CU forum). Famous doubled dies like the 1955 or 1969-S DDO reach 100-1000x+, but they are well known and seldom sold unattributed. The weighted median hit is around 2-10x, nowhere near 10^3.
hit_rate_capex: The proving step is neither expensive nor mostly failing. PCGS variety attribution is an add-on of roughly $18-24 per coin (forum-cited, likely dated) on top of grading. PCGS charges $10 if the coin does not qualify (PCGS variety FAQ). The Philatelic Foundation charges 5.5% of submitted value, with a $27 minimum for US stamps and $35 for foreign (PF FAQ). The cost is in search labour and the purchase price, not in proving. ML speeds up screening, but it does not cut proving capex 10x, because you submit only what you already believe is a hit. My estimate is that the base hit rate on submitted coins is already high (>50%) for experienced cherrypickers.

name: Reversion Rights Co: 1875-Act and easement-only rail corridors
one_line_reason: Discovery is cheap, has a high base hit rate, and is already done by rail-trail takings lawyers, while the hard part (holdout-prone assembly) is not abstracted. The real step-up is about 1-10x, not 10^3.
fatal_flaw: The value is already priced and owned by others. Owners' reversionary claims are worth tens of thousands of dollars per parcel in takings litigation that contingency law firms already pursue using the same title analysis. Railbanking keeps many corridors from reverting at all. Assembling continuity across hundreds of owners with holdout risk is the real work, not discovery. And the named buyers co-locate on active rail and highway right of way, paying only about $8.5k per mile for easements, rather than paying a large premium for assembled abandoned corridors.
step_up: The pitch assumes options at $100-1,000 per parcel. But real reversionary claims are already priced far higher in takings litigation. Nickel Plate Trail paid $7.6M to 168 owners (about $45k each, my arithmetic). Covington GA paid $1.5M to 47 owners (about $32k each). Haggart v. US paid about $140M for about 25 miles of BNSF corridor. Informed owners will not sell for $100-1,000. On the buy side, the only developer number found is SOO Green offering about $8,550 per mile for easements, which is a few thousand dollars per parcel. Realistic step-up on an informed option price is about 1-10x, not 100-1000x. 100x or more only happens if owners are uninformed, and contingency-fee plaintiff firms keep informing them.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is high, not low. Brandt (2014) held that 1875 Act rights of way are easements, and many state-law grants are easements too. Plaintiff firms win a large share of rail-trail cases on easement findings. My estimate is that 50-80% of parcels on 1875-Act or condemned corridors are easement-only. Proving cost is paper title work: about $500-2,000 per parcel for an abstract or title opinion, and maybe $100k-500k per corridor (my estimates). With a high base rate and cheap proving, the ML lever is capped at roughly 1.3-2x, not 10x.

name: StrandRescue: dark fibre bought out of bankruptcies and failed municipal networks
one_line_reason: This is distressed-asset arbitrage among sophisticated bidders, with a ~3-10x price gap and a high base hit rate. There is no frame in which discovery is 80%+ of the work and no 10^3 jump on a hit.
fatal_flaw: The asset's existence and value are not hidden. Fibre is mostly real (high base hit rate, so little ML lever). Distressed lots are sold in competitive 363 auctions or municipal RFPs that the end buyers attend directly. And the gap between the distressed and proven price is about 3-10x, not 10^3-10^4. Confirming and transferring the asset (permits, pole consent, splice repair, operations) is as hard as finding it, which is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure.
step_up: From recalled precedents, not sourced this session: iProvo cost about $39M to build and went to Google Fiber for $1 in 2013 (it carried bond debt). Lake County MN built on about $66M of RUS loan money and sold for about $13M in 2016 (~0.2x of cost). Burlington Telecom sold to Schurz for about $30.8M in 2017. In the 2001-03 telecom bust (360networks, Global Crossing, etc.) assets cleared at 5-20 cents on the dollar. Proven or fair value is roughly 1-5x the distressed price, call it 3-10x at best. In the bust cases the gain came from the market recovering over years, not from an immediate proving event. Nothing close to 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate of 'is the fibre real and usable' is high, my estimate 70-90%. Fibre that is in the ground or on poles mostly exists and mostly works; the uncertainty is about condition, assignability and demand, not existence. With a hit rate that high, the lever (capped at 1/base rate) is about 1.1-1.4x, not 10x. Each proving attempt costs $1-3k/mile for OTDR (candidate's figure) plus legal diligence. Each 'shot' is a whole lot bought at auction ($100k to $10M+), not a cheap drill.

name: Zombie Spectrum / Rebanded: licences in bands about to be repurposed
one_line_reason: The step-up is real but modest (about 5-100x) and binary on regulators. ML forecasts rather than proves, the data is mostly legible, and Anterix and incentive-auction speculators already play this game.
fatal_flaw: The 'proof' is an FCC rulemaking outside the company's control, not a discovery. ML cannot raise its base rate, and the FCC deliberately strips windfalls from speculative post-NPRM acquirers with freezes and 'comparable facilities' relocation. Licence liveness is also already a legible ULS status field, with automatic termination on discontinuance.
step_up: From memory, not verified this run (search budget was used up): Anterix (pdvWireless) bought Sprint's 900 MHz narrowband licences for about $90M in 2014. After the FCC's May 2020 realignment order it leased 3x3 MHz broadband to Ameren (about $47M), Xcel (about $80M), Evergy (about $30M) and LCRA (about $30M). That is roughly a 3-10x gain on purchase price, before Anterix paid narrowband incumbents to relocate or retune. The best precedent was the 2017 broadcast incentive auction: speculators such as LocusPoint and NRJ bought UHF stations for single-digit to tens of $M and some received $100M+ in the reverse auction, about 10-100x. My estimate of a typical hit is 5-100x, not 10^3-10^4. The FCC usually gives incumbents 'comparable facilities' relocation rather than a windfall, so many zombie licences realise about 1x.
hit_rate_capex: My estimate, unverified: the FCC finishes only about 1-3 band-repurposing proceedings a year (examples: 900 MHz 2020, 3.7 GHz C-band 2020, 2.5 GHz EBS 2019, 4.9 GHz band manager 2024, 600 MHz incentive auction). In most of them small legacy incumbents got relocation or nothing (4.9 GHz went to a FirstNet band manager; incumbents got no upside). Buying a licence is cheap, about $1k-$100k each, so the cost per attempt is already low. The expense is time (years) and binary regulatory risk, not discovery spend. ML cannot raise the chance that the FCC acts, and it adds little to forecasting, because docket trajectory is read closely by the trade press, law firms (Wiley, Keller and Heckman) and spectrum brokers. The 10x capex lever does not apply.

name: ResidualUnits: unused density in legacy Florida DRIs and PUDs
one_line_reason: The buyer and the ladder are real, but the step-up is 2-10x not 10^3, the remaining-units outcome is already in legible monitoring reports, and proving is a cheap title/zoning check, so the Terranox 95/5 discovery asymmetry is absent.
fatal_flaw: Florida residual units are neither a cheap stand-alone right nor hidden. They run with the land or the master developer's covenants and appear in mandatory DRI monitoring reports and county buildout tracking. The realistic step-up is 2-10x, and proving is a cheap legal desk check rather than an expensive mostly-failing shot, so ML has no 10x capex lever.
step_up: My estimate (searches were blocked; no sourced figures): exurban Florida raw or ag land trades at roughly $10-50k/acre. Entitled land at 4-8 units/acre that builders pay $15-60k per entitled unit for comes to roughly $60-300k/acre, a 3-10x step-up. Finished lots run $80-150k but need development capex. The near-zero starting price exists only when a defunct entity holds a pure allocation with clean transferability, which is rare. The typical case is 2-10x, nowhere near 10^3-10^4. The candidate's own 10-100x claim is at the optimistic end.
hit_rate_capex: No sourced numbers (search budget exhausted). My estimate: proving costs a title/land-use attorney review plus a county zoning verification letter, about $5-25k and a few weeks per tract. That is a cheap desk exercise, not an expensive physical attempt that mostly fails. Once a tract is identified, the base hit rate of the verification step is probably moderate (30-60%, my estimate). So the 1/hit-rate cap on the ML lever is only about 2-3x, not 10x. Most of the risk lies in title, negotiation and lapse, not in discovery.

name: AccessProof / Second Egress: proving legal access to landlocked or stranded parcels
one_line_reason: The data and the right-buying mechanics fit, but proving access is slow, contested legal work that ML can't speed up. The step-up is only ~2-10x, the buyers are small and scattered, and there is no meaningful ladder above.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is adversarial litigation or county approval, which costs tens of thousands of dollars and takes years. It is the bespoke hard part, like building the geothermal plant in the counter-example, while discovery is the easy part. And a win only lifts value about 2-10x on small parcels. ML speeds up research, but neither the bottleneck nor the step-up gets near 10^3.
step_up: No live searches ran because the shared per-turn search budget was used up, so every figure here is my estimate from general appraisal knowledge. Appraisal practice usually values landlocked land at about 10-50% of comparable accessible land, a 50-90% discount. Proving access therefore yields about 2-10x: a $200/acre rural parcel might reach $1,000-2,000/acre. A $10k fire-zone lot might reach $50-150k as buildable, up to ~10-15x at the best. The candidate's own ~5-50x is optimistic at the top. Nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
