There are about 7,000 rare diseases and only a few hundred have active programs, but registries exist mostly where interest is already high. Each attempt costs only $25-250k plus curation, so the step is not expensive and the ML lever is at most 4-10x on paper. Sponsor arrival is also largely readable from public sources: ClinicalTrials.gov, FDA orphan designations, and preclinical and academic pipelines. A simple pipeline lookup gets most of the way there, so the real ML gain over that is small.

name: CRL Salvage: drugs rejected only on fixable CMC or inspection grounds
one_line_reason: This is a variant of the already-weak stranded-drug-rescue idea. CRL text is now public and legible, the expensive step is manufacturing remediation that already succeeds at a high rate (so the ML lever is about 1.4x), and the step-up is about 10-100x, gated behind 12-24 months and $5-20M per asset.
fatal_flaw: The regulator writes the answer: published CRLs state the deficiency category in plain text, so discovery is not illegible and ML adds almost nothing. And the proving step (CDMO tech transfer, validation, stability, inspection) is the expensive bespoke physical work, not discovery. The cost sits in the fix, not the find.
step_up: Estimate, not sourced (no search budget left): an abandoned CRL asset in a 363 bankruptcy sale or from a wind-down typically goes for low single-digit $M (the candidate's $0.5-5M range is plausible). An approved specialty or orphan NDA sells to specialty pharma or royalty buyers for $50-500M, depending on sales. That is about 10-100x on purchase price. After adding the $5-20M+ fix cost, the multiple on total invested is about 5-30x, and it arrives only on approval, not immediately on a single cheap test.
hit_rate_capex: From memory, not verified this turn: FDA's own analysis of CRLs from 2008-2013 (Lurie et al., BMJ 2015) found about half cited manufacturing/facility issues, and resubmissions that only had to fix quality problems were approved at high rates. My estimate is that well-chosen CMC-only resubmissions succeed about 60-80% of the time. So the proving step does not mostly fail. The low hit rate (~10-15% of CRLs are fixable and buyable) is in screening, which is cheap desk work. The lever is capped near 1/0.7, about 1.4x, on the expensive step. Cost per proving attempt is about $5-20M (candidate's figure, consistent with my CDMO tech-transfer estimates).

name: Shortline Rx / Dormant ANDA Revival: approved generics bought ahead of shortages
one_line_reason: A real business model, already run by ANI/Novitium. Value is created by manufacturing and regulatory work, not discovery, step-ups are about 5-50x and temporary, and the shortage outcome is already in public lists, so it fails the Terranox frame.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is execution, not discovery. Turning a dormant ANDA into supply needs scarce sterile CDMO capacity, tech transfer, stability data and PAS approval (about $1-5M and 12-24 months), and ML does not shrink any of that. The shortage signal is also already written into the public FDA and ASHP shortage lists. Incumbents such as ANI/Novitium already run the dormant-ANDA revival play. So no rung exists where discovery is 80%+ of the work.
step_up: Estimates, not verified: the web search budget ran out before any search returned. A dormant ANDA sells for roughly $10k-500k (the candidate's own figure, consistent with broker deals I know of). A revived, marketed ANDA for a shortage molecule might sell for or earn $1-10M. That is about 5-50x in typical cases. About 100x or more is possible only for deep sterile-injectable shortages, and those spikes are temporary, since competitors return within 1-3 years. Research I recall (not re-checked) found shortage price rises in the tens of percent on average, with rare grey-market cases at 10-80x. Most shortage volume is sold under GPO contracts (Vizient, Premier), which cap price. Score 2.
hit_rate_capex: Estimates, not verified. A proving attempt costs about $1-3M plus 12-24 months: exhibit batches, stability, PAS and API qualification (candidate's figure; I would put it at up to $5M for sterile products). The hit rate at the forecasting stage is moderate rather than very low. Shortages are persistent and clustered: about 100-300 active shortages a year, concentrated in sterile injectables, so a simple rule like 'sole-source injectable plus a recent warning letter or import alert at the maker' probably already catches a large share. The cost of a failed attempt comes mainly from execution (CDMO, inspection, API supply), and ML forecasting does not touch that. Best case the lever is about 2-3x, nowhere near 10x.

name: Breakthrough Shelf: TTO device IP pushed to Breakthrough Designation
one_line_reason: The base hit rate is already about 55-60% (lever under 2x), designation alone does not produce a large step-up in what buyers will pay, and the prototype work needed before filing makes this a build business, not a discovery business.
fatal_flaw: Breakthrough Device Designation is granted about 55-60% of the time and is not the main value event. That caps the ML hit-rate lever at under 2x, and buyers pay little for designation without clinical data. Before even applying you must build a prototype and generate bench data, so the physical step dominates and the rung is not 80%+ discovery.
step_up: Unproven: exclusive option about $5-25k (the candidate's figure; consistent with typical TTO option fees of roughly $5-50k, my estimate). Proven: no public price for a BDD-only asset, since acquirers price on clinical data, 510(k)/De Novo/PMA clearance and reimbursement. My estimate is that a designated, preclinical, single-patent asset licenses or sells for about $0.1-1M, sometimes more if TCET/NTAP reimbursement looks likely. Against the full cost basis (option + prototype + BDD request, about $100-500k), that is about 1-5x on capital. Against the option fee alone it is 10-100x. Both are far below the 10^4 jump in Terranox. Not verified: the web search budget ran out before I could pull deal comps.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: FDA's Breakthrough Devices Program statistics show about 55-60% of decided requests granted, and more than 1,000 designations through 2024 (from memory of FDA's public program stats page; I could not re-check this session). The ML lever is capped at 1/0.55, about 1.8x, so the required ~10x cut in discovery capex is impossible. Cost per attempt: the request itself is cheap, about $30-100k in regulatory consulting with a 60-day decision (candidate's figure, plausible). The real cost is the prototype and bench evidence: about $100k-1M+ per device (my estimate).

name: Orphan Data Comp: FIFRA data-compensation rights from defunct registrants
one_line_reason: This is a niche legal claims-buying play. The proving step is expensive arbitration, the supply is cut off by the 15-year window, and reliance is already semi-legible, so it fails the discovery-is-95% frame.
fatal_flaw: The 15-year compensability window collides with the age of defunct registrants' data. Most orphaned studies are already out of the window, and those still in it usually passed to an acquirer. On top of that, the proving step is costly contested arbitration, not cheap discovery, and reliance is already listed in the data matrices and offer-to-pay letters.
step_up: Unproven right, per the candidate: $5-20k (not verified). Proven value, my estimate: compensation is a share of the original study cost, and FIFRA guideline studies cost about $0.1M to $10M each. A typical recovery on a compensable package might be $50k to a few $M, before arbitration fees and legal costs of roughly $100k-$1M (estimate). So the net multiple is about 10-100x on a hit, not 10^3. It is also capped by study cost, and by the 15-year compensability window counted from original submission.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate (the share of defunct-registrant studies that are still inside the 15-year window and were relied on by a solvent follow-on registrant) is unknown. My estimate is low, under 10%, mostly because of the window. The cost of a proving attempt is mostly legal (arbitration plus experts, estimated at $100k+). ML only lowers the screening cost, which is the cheap part, so it does not cut the expensive arbitration capex 10x.

name: Revenant Actives: EU-withdrawn crop protection actives revived as new US AIs
one_line_reason: Finding the right withdrawn active is cheap and easy next to the $10-30M+ US registration spend that creates the value, and the sellers are the people who wrote the data.
fatal_flaw: The value step-up needs the $10-30M+ regulatory data package, not the discovery step, so discovery is a small share of every sellable rung. On top of that, the dossier owners are the sophisticated originators, who already know the data and why they dropped the molecule, so there is no cheap illegible right to buy.
step_up: Unproven: $50-500k per dossier (candidate's figure, not verified). After greenhouse efficacy plus a gap analysis, the asset is still unregistered and off-patent, and it is missing most of the data a US filing needs. My estimate is that an option or license on that package fetches about $0.5-3M, a 3-10x step-up. The 100-1000x figure ($10-100M+) only shows up after the $10-30M+ registration spend, so the step-up depends on capex and does not arrive immediately on a hit. For reference, AgbioInvestor/Phillips McDougall put the full cost of discovering and developing a new AI at about $300M over about 12 years (2019 study, from memory). The 10-year FIFRA exclusive-use data protection covers only the NEW data the company pays to generate, not the molecule itself.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: no figure found. My estimate is that 10-30% of shortlisted EU-withdrawn actives would show useful efficacy against resistant weeds or pests. These molecules were originally commercial products, so efficacy is often already known, which keeps the hit rate high and leaves ML little room. The ML lever is capped at 1/hit rate, so about 3-10x, and only on the cheap part ($50-200k per greenhouse or small-plot attempt). The expensive, failure-prone part is the tox and ecotox package, which ML cannot shrink 10x. The 1-in-160,000 screening rate for new chemistry (Phillips McDougall, from memory) applies to novel discovery, not to reviving known actives.

name: VoucherWorks / VoucherForge: foreign-approved tropical-disease drugs turned into US PRVs
one_line_reason: The buyer and the payout are real ($100-160M vouchers), but the law now requires a new sponsor-run trial. That makes this regulatory and clinical execution, not discovery, in a tiny universe with legible data that informed players already work.
fatal_flaw: FDARA 2017 requires new clinical investigations essential to approval, sponsored by the applicant, and bars trial data submitted in India, Brazil, Thailand or PIC/S countries before 2007. That kills the core idea of "foreign dossier plus a little new work". The proving step becomes a real trial whose cost and risk ML does not reduce, and it sits in a small, well-mined universe that MDGH, DNDi and big pharma already work.
step_up: Unproven right: $0.2-2M (the candidate's figure; I found no market data). Proven: voucher sales of $103M (Valneva, 2024), $150-160M (Zevra, Abeona, Bavarian Nordic, 2025), with historical tropical vouchers at $125M (Impavido, 2014) and $290M (Vaxchora, 2016). That is roughly 50-500x on the right. But all-in proving cost is $15-40M (my estimate, because a new essential trial is now mandatory), so the step-up on deployed capital is about 4-10x. Score 3.
hit_rate_capex: I found no published hit rate for this. For a drug already approved abroad with good efficacy data, I estimate the base success rate of the NDA/trial at 30-60%, so the ML lever is capped at about 2-3x, not 10x. Cost per attempt: $5-25M (candidate's figure); I estimate $15-40M with a new essential trial and the time it takes. The expensive failures come from trial cost and CMC/inspections, which ML does not cut. Only about 10 tropical vouchers were awarded from 2009 to 2019 (PMC table).

name: Ex-US Rare Pediatric Drug to US PRV Arbitrage
one_line_reason: The PRV price is real and liquid ($150-205M in 2025-26), but finding candidates is an easy, legible join that incumbents already do, and the expensive slow work is regulatory and clinical, where ML gives no leverage.
fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. The candidate set is a small, legible join of the EMA/PMDA approval registers against the Orange Book, and established players already work it (Eton, Zevra, Leadiant, Recordati). 85%+ of cost and risk sits in the bespoke clinical, CMC and NDA step ($10-40M, 2-4 years). That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode, made worse by a PRV program that sunsets in Sept 2029.
step_up: Unproven right: US rights to a foreign-approved orphan drug at roughly $1-5M upfront plus milestones and royalties (the candidate's figure and my estimate; no public comparable found). Proven right: a rare pediatric PRV sells for $150-205M. Recent sales: Zevra $150M (net $148.3M, Apr 2025), Abeona $155M, Bavarian Nordic $160M (tropical-disease voucher), Rocket $180M (Jun 2026), Jazz $200M (Jan 2026), Ultragenyx $203M. On top of that comes the US franchise. On the rights alone that is about 40-200x. All-in, with $10-40M of proving cost plus a 2-4 year carry, it is about 4-15x, and that is the number that counts.
hit_rate_capex: I found no public base hit rate. My estimate: once a drug already has EMA/PMDA approval with clinical efficacy data, FDA approval odds are high (about 50-80%), because the hard scientific risk is already gone. That caps the ML lever at roughly 1.3-2x, not 10x. The cost per proving attempt is $10-40M (my estimate) plus 2-4 years, and ML does not reduce it, because it is clinical and regulatory spend, not search spend. The real failure modes are that the drug does not qualify (FDA has previously approved the active moiety, or the disease does not meet the RPD definition of serious or life-threatening with most patients under 18) or that FDA demands a new adequate and well-controlled trial. Both can be checked cheaply by hand.

name: Hidden Sire: genomic elite-animal hunting in untested herds
one_line_reason: Testing is already cheap and routine, and the results already sit in public EPD fields, so there is no illegible edge. In under-tested breeds the test cannot prove value, and the typical step-up is about 3-10x, not 10^3.
fatal_flaw: Catch-22 on legibility. Where genomic proof is valuable and accepted (registered Angus, Holstein, Nelore), testing is already routine (75% of registered Angus calves genotyped) and the answer sits in public EPD fields that owners can read, so nothing is mispriced. Where herds are untested (commercial cattle, goats, alpaca, local breeds), animals are unregistered and reference populations are too small, so the $40 test proves nothing a capitalised buyer will pay 10^2x for. The hit is also cheap to find and to fail, so there is no expensive discovery step for ML to make cheaper.
step_up: Unproven: a commercial calf or heifer at $1.5-3k (the candidate's figure, roughly consistent with US feeder and weaned calf prices). Proven, typical case: a genomically documented seedstock bull sells for about 2-7x that. Nelore CEIP (certified superior) bulls averaged about R$10.5k (roughly $2k) at CFM's 346-bull virtual auction (comprerural). Australian Angus stud sales average $5.5-14k AUD (Stock Journal, Countryman). Proven, tail case: record bulls reach $44k-$275k AUD (The Land, 2025), and the rare bull bought by an AI stud reaches $100k-1M. That tail is maybe 1 in 1,000 or fewer of tested animals, and it depends on market uptake, not just the test. The expected step-up on a hit is about 3-10x. 10^2-10^3 is the rare outlier.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: the top 0.1-1% qualify, by the candidate's definition (1 in 100 to 1 in 1,000 at random). Cost per attempt: a $30-50 test (Neogen/Zoetis) plus buying the calf. Most of the calf's cost comes back as feeder or slaughter value, so the net cost per failed shot is only about $50-300 (my estimate). Proving is cheap and failure is cheap, so there is little capex for ML to cut by 10x. Pedigree-based pre-screening could at best raise hits about 5-20x, and the cheap test already makes testing everything rational. That is why 75% of 309,926 registered Angus calves were already genotyped in FY2025 (angus.org).

name: Fall Rights / Fall Recovery: radar-tracked fresh meteorite falls
one_line_reason: Clean physical step and surface-owner rights fit the rubric, but NASA already publishes the strewn fields, the hit-rate lever is about 2-3x, and the market is a few million dollars a year with no ladder.
fatal_flaw: The outcome is already public: NASA ARES posts radar-derived strewn fields for every detected fall, so the ML edge is mostly racing other hunters to the field. And total annual supply (a few US falls, mostly ordinary chondrites at $5-50/g) caps the market at single-digit millions with no ladder.
step_up: Unproven right: an access or recovery agreement, usually free permission or a finder's split with the landowner. The candidate's $500-5k figure is my estimate; I found no market price. Proven: an ordinary chondrite from a fresh fall sells for about $5-50/g (my estimate). Rare types sell for much more. Aguas Zarcas (CM2) goes for about $200-300/g retail, and the total known mass is 27 kg. Winchcombe pieces sold at Christie's for about $7,400/g (1.7 g) and $2,000/g (15 g), but only 602 g was ever recovered and about 90% of it went to the UK national collection. The Maine museum offered $25k for the first 1 kg in 2023. So per parcel the value goes from about $1k to about $10k-100k, roughly 10-100x. It reaches 1000x only for rare carbonaceous or achondrite falls, which happen a few times a decade.
hit_rate_capex: A museum chair estimated that only 8-10 of the hundreds of meteorite falls each year are recovered. That counts all falls, most of which are unobserved. For radar-detected US falls, my estimate is that hunters already recover something in roughly 30-60% of cases. A search costs about $5-30k per event in travel, drones and labor (my estimate). The lever is capped near 2-3x, not 10x, because NASA's radar strewn-field predictions already exist and most misses come from terrain, vegetation and stone size, not the prediction.

name: Trails Act Corridor Interim-Use Arbitrage
one_line_reason: Taking the role is cheap, but the subsurface value belongs to reversionary landowners, discovery is a small share of the work, continuity is already legible in STB dockets, and buyers avoid trail title risk.
fatal_flaw: The trail sponsor does not own the subsurface or the utility right. In most corridors adjacent landowners hold the reversionary fee (Brandt 2014), and utility use beyond railroad or trail purposes is a new burden. That creates per-landowner takings and trespass liability, the same pattern as the fiber-on-railroad class action settlements. So the proving step is a legal title fight ML cannot win, not a discovery problem.
step_up: On a cash basis, an assumed-liability right (about $0 cost, with ongoing maintenance) becomes a recurring license fee. My estimate: long-haul fiber on rail rights of way has historically licensed at roughly $1-10/ft one-time or a few $/ft/yr, about $5k-50k/mile. HVDC corridors could pay more per mile, but buyers such as SOO Green chose active Canadian Pacific rail corridors, not trails. Because the starting cost is about zero, the cash multiple looks very large. The real multiple is limited because the sponsor holds no fee or subsurface title: the underlying fee usually belongs to adjacent landowners (Brandt v. US, 2014). Unverified; search budget ran out before I could get per-mile lease figures.
hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving step. Proving a corridor is cheap desk work (dockets, deeds, GIS), my estimate a few thousand to tens of thousands of dollars per corridor. The hit rate on finding continuous railbanked corridors is high, since NITU/CITU orders already list mileposts. The binding uncertainty is legal: easement scope and takings exposure, decided by courts and not learnable from data. So ML cannot cut capex 10x, because discovery is not the cost driver.

name: LandingRight: permitted subsea cable landing parcels
one_line_reason: Cable landings are a permitting and construction business with few, concentrated buyers and legible data. There is no rung where discovery is 80%+, and no 10^3x step-up on a cheap hit.
fatal_flaw: Proving is permitting plus construction, not discovery. The value of a landing comes from winning coastal, Corps, FCC and Team Telecom approvals and building HDD bores, manholes and backhaul; reading data adds little. Base hit rates are not low, so ML has almost no 10x capex lever. This repeats the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure.
step_up: My estimate, not sourced (the search budget was used up before I could run any query). A coastal parcel or easement option costs roughly $50k-$2M. A permitted, open-access landing station is worth a few million to the low tens of millions, realised through landing fees, colocation and backhaul contracts. That is about 3-10x on the parcel, and maybe ~10-30x on the option premium alone. It is nowhere near 10^3-10^4. The candidate's own ~10^2x looks optimistic, and the value comes from the permit and the build, not from a discovery hit.
hit_rate_capex: My estimate, not sourced (no searches were possible). The proving step is not a cheap shot that mostly fails. Cable route feasibility work is a routine consultant job: desktop study ~$50-200k, marine route survey ~$1-5M+. When a landing is pursued seriously, the base hit rate is fairly high (I'd guess 50%+); failures come from political or permit opposition, not from missing data. Lever is about 1/base hit rate, so under 2x, not 10x. ML over bathymetry and AIS anchoring data copies what route engineers (e.g. SubCom, ASN, NEC, and survey firms like Fugro) already do.

name: LiveMap: zombie tentative tract maps in California
one_line_reason: The status of a California tentative map is a legible, county-confirmable fact held by sophisticated sellers on land already priced at market. Proving is cheap and the step-up is about 2-4x, so it lacks the Terranox mix of near-zero asset, expensive failing proving step and illegible signal.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is a cheap, definitive lookup, not an expensive mostly-failing bet. Each planning department already records the tentative-map expiration date and confirms it on request. Sellers are sophisticated land holders. The pool of 'zombie' maps shrank once the 2008-2013 statutory extensions ran out (about 2016-2020). Even on a hit, already-priced raw land steps up about 2-4x, not 10^3-10^4.
step_up: I could not verify this by search (the shared web-search budget was used up). My estimate: California land with a tentative map sells for about 2-4x unentitled land, because a tentative map still needs a final map, improvement plans, bonds and current fees. The asset does not start near zero; the seller already has the land priced at raw value. The candidate's '5-20x' figure looks inflated except in rare infill cases. Realistic step-up is about 2-5x, or 10^0.5, not 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: Proving means a records reconstruction plus a written confirmation from the planning department. That costs about $2k-$20k per parcel in staff, legal or title work (my estimate), so it is cheap, not an expensive drill that usually fails. Base hit rate is unknown. The candidate pool shrinks every year. The statutory extensions (SB 1185 2008 +12mo, AB 333 2009 +24mo, AB 208 2011 +24mo, AB 116 2013 +24mo, the last for maps approved after 1 Jan 2000) together add at most about 7 years, so nearly every map from the 2000-2008 era ran out by about 2016-2020. That leaves only later relief (AB 1561 2023, an 18-month extension, recalled not verified), discretionary extensions and litigation or moratorium tolling (Gov Code 66452.6). Because the cost per attempt is small next to the land price, raising the hit rate does not cut total capex 10x.

name: TapRight: dormant utility connection entitlements in moratorium districts
one_line_reason: The step-up is real but modest (about 10-20x, estimated). The answer is mostly already in district meter registers and on title reports, the final proof is a district's discretionary approval, and the market is a niche of a few thousand lots with no path up a large ladder.
fatal_flaw: The outcome already sits in a legible public field. Districts record meter and EDU allocations against each parcel number, special assessments appear on tax bills and title reports, and in moratorium towns every party checks water status first. On top of that, the proving step is a discretionary approval by the district (often refused during a moratorium), and the market is tiny. That leaves no information gap for ML to exploit and no 10^3 step-up.
step_up: Unverified: the search budget ran out before any search returned, so these are estimates from memory. Cambria CSD (California) has had a connection moratorium since about 2001 with a waitlist. Lots without water there have reportedly traded around $15-50k, and buildable lots with water roughly $250-500k, so about 10-20x. In Bolinas (BCPUD, moratorium since 1971), water meters have reportedly sold on their own for six figures, roughly $200-400k, against lots worth much less without one. The candidate's 20-50x is plausible only at the top end. My central estimate is 10-20x, which scores 3. That is nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate only, nothing sourced. The base hit rate, meaning the share of moratorium-district vacant lots that hold an unrecognised but valid prepaid entitlement, is likely well under 1-2%. A proving attempt (records requests, a title or records researcher, legal review of 1911/1913/1915 Act rolls) costs maybe $2-10k. But the cost that matters is buying the lot, often $20-50k, and here the lot is the asset bought before proving. So ML mostly saves acquisition capital on lots that turn out to have nothing. The lever looks real on paper (1/hit rate is above 50x), but the hit space is tiny and limited by the supply of lots.

name: By-Right Parcels: legacy zoning that already permits data centers
one_line_reason: Discovery is cheap and the proving step is trivial, but the step-up from zoning alone is about 2-5x because power drives value, the zoning field is already legible, and buyers will not buy the zoning-only rung. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: the hard part (power) is not the part ML finds.
fatal_flaw: Zoning is not what makes data-center land valuable; power is. A parcel that permits data centers by right but has no near-term utility capacity is worth only a modest premium over agricultural or industrial land. Separately, the zoning outcome is mostly already in a legible field (the district code in GIS), so neither of the 10^3-10^4 jumps the model needs exists.
step_up: I could not verify this: the shared search budget ran out before any query ran. These are estimates from prior knowledge. Agricultural land in data-center counties sells for about $5k-15k/acre. Northern Virginia data-center land traded at about $1M-3M+/acre in 2021-2024 (Loudoun and Prince William deals). Nearly all of that premium comes from power availability and location, not zoning. Industrial-zoned parcels without power trade at about $50k-300k/acre. A zoning-only hit on an unpowered parcel is therefore plausibly 2-5x on land value (estimate). The 10^2x on option premium is leverage from the option itself, not value created.
hit_rate_capex: Not verified (no searches available). From prior knowledge: a zoning verification letter costs about $50-500 in most jurisdictions. A formal zoning-administrator determination or vested-rights determination runs about $500-5k, plus legal fees of $5k-20k. That is cheap, and it is not mostly failing on screened candidates. The expensive, mostly failing step is the power study and utility queue. An interconnection or large-load study costs $50k-500k+ and takes 1-3+ years, and ML over zoning text does not move it. ML can lift the hit rate on candidate screening, but proving capex is already low, so there is no ~10x capex lever. (Estimate.)

name: Reimburse: orphaned Texas MUD developer reimbursement claims
one_line_reason: A clever distressed-credit niche, but the outcome sits in EMMA audit footnotes, good claims are not sold at 2-10c, collection depends on future tax-base growth rather than discovery, and the true orphan supply is small.
fatal_flaw: Payment depends on a future bond issue, which only happens when new taxable value is built in the district. That is outside the claim holder's control, so collection is decided by real-estate absorption, not discovery. The amounts owed are also already disclosed in MUD audit footnotes and Official Statements on EMMA, so there is no illegible-data edge and no seller who cannot see what they hold.
step_up: Proposed purchase price is 2-10 cents, collected at par, which is 10-50x. That ratio is unverified. Searches failed (the shared web-search budget was used up), so all numbers are my estimates. Based on how the market works, a claim whose district has a live tax base and a clear path to bonds would not trade at 2-10c. It would sell for about 40-80c to the developer, the lender or the next landowner. Claims that do trade at 2-10c are cheap because the district has no tax base, the agreement has lapsed, or the claim was already assigned or released. Realistic step-up is about 2-5x on good paper, with heavy duration risk (often 5-15 years to the next bond issue). Interest accrual is capped under the agreement and TCEQ rules.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate only, no sourced figures. Validating one claim costs about $10k-50k (legal review, a reimbursement audit by the district's auditor, and engineering report reconciliation). The audit is normally done at the district's expense when bonds are sold. My guess is that 20-40% of identified orphan claims are collectible. The lever is capped at about 3-5x, not 10x. Most failures come from the legal chain and the district's capacity to issue debt, not from failing to find the claim.

name: Dormant Permit Perfection: Nevada and Utah permits near cancellation
one_line_reason: This is administrative arbitrage on a legible status field: the step-up is likely about 3-20x, not 10^3-10^4, proving is cheap and rarely fails for reasons ML can fix, and certification is capped by use that already happened. It is a niche water-brokerage business, not a Terranox-shaped rung.
fatal_flaw: Proof of beneficial use only certifies water that was already put to use by the statutory deadline. The State Engineer certifies the quantity actually used, and in over-appropriated Nevada basins any change application gets heavy scrutiny. So the step-up is not created by discovery: it is mostly a legal and administrative conversion of value the holder already partly sees. name: Lapsed Patent Revival (incl. robotics and deeptech)
one_line_reason: Cheap to buy and cheap to petition, but the revival right legally does not exist for most deliberate lapses, and intervening rights strip the value from the hits ML finds. That leaves a 3-30x legal arbitrage in a soft patent market with a low ceiling, not a 10^4 discovery rung.
fatal_flaw: The unintentional-delay standard plus intervening rights. Most maintenance-fee lapses are deliberate, so they cannot be honestly revived, and swearing otherwise invites unenforceability and inequitable-conduct challenges. For the minority that can be revived, 35 USC 41(c)(2) intervening rights shield exactly the current products ML would flag, because those makers acted during the lapse. That wipes out most of the step-up.
step_up: Unproven: a lapsed patent bought from a small inventor or the estate of a dissolved company for about $1-5k (the candidate's figure; plausible, my estimate). Proven: a charted, enforceable US patent in the brokered market. From memory, Richardson Oliver Insights put average asking prices at roughly $100-250k per asset, with only about 20-30% of listed packages selling. On paper that is about 30-100x, which scores 3. But 35 USC 41(c)(2) intervening rights protect anyone who made, bought or started using the product during the lapse, and the products ML would flag "reading on current products" are exactly those. That cuts the proven value well below a normal patent's, so I put the realistic step-up at about 3-30x and score it 2. Nothing is near 10^3-10^4 immediately on a hit.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: about 1-5% of issued patents read on a commercial product and can be licensed (my estimate, consistent with the usual figure that under 5% of patents ever earn licensing revenue). Roughly half of US patents lapse for non-payment before full term (my estimate from USPTO maintenance-fee renewal rates). Cost per attempt: an EoU chart costs about $5-20k from a firm (estimate), petition fee about $2.1k for a large entity and about 40% of that for a small entity (FY2025 schedule, from memory), plus acquisition and back fees. ML could plausibly raise the screening hit rate 5-10x and push charting cost toward the cost of a GPU run, so the lever is real but capped at about 1/0.03 ≈ 30x. The binding constraint is not the hit rate. It is the share of lapses that can honestly be called unintentional, and ML cannot raise that.

name: Mandate-Essential: patents that read on coming regulatory mandates
one_line_reason: Buying the right is cheap and the buyers exist, but the proving step is litigation rather than discovery. Essentiality to mandates is mostly illusory. Where it is real (3GPP/ETSI), it is already declared publicly. That leaves a 10-100x step-up and an NPE-sized ceiling.
fatal_flaw: Regulatory mandates are performance-based and technology-neutral, so patents do not become essential to them. Real essentiality comes only from interoperability standards, where declarations and pool lists already put the answer in a legible public field. Value is then realised only through slow, expensive licensing or litigation (more than $2M per case, with about two-thirds of IPR-challenged claims lost), not through a cheap, discrete proving step.
step_up: Unproven price is $5-30k per maintained small-entity patent (candidate's figure; it fits my recollection that the brokered secondary market prices most assets in the tens of thousands to low $100ks). A proven patent reading on a standard sells or yields roughly $100k-$1M+ per family (my estimate from memory of brokered SEP deals and pool payouts). Avanci's 4G vehicle royalty is about $20 per car, but it is split across thousands of patents. That gives about 10-100x for a typical winner. 1000x is reachable only for rare litigated outliers, and it arrives slowly, not on the day of a hit. Note: I could not verify these figures live because the shared web-search budget was used up.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: probably well under 5% of mapped patents end up licensable at a premium (my estimate). Pool essentiality checks reject many submissions. Of claims that reach a final IPR decision, about 60-70% are found unpatentable (my recollection of PTAB statistics). Cost per proving attempt is not the $5-30k purchase. It is the essentiality evaluation (about $10-20k per patent per pool evaluator, my estimate) plus litigation, which costs $2-5M+ per case through trial (my recollection of the AIPLA economic survey). ML cuts the screening cost, which was never the big cost. It does not cut the litigation and validity cost, so the realistic capex lever is about 2-3x, not 10x.

Proven by coupon: a materials patent licensed before qualification typically brings $0 to low six figures upfront plus small royalties (estimate, based on the general AUTM pattern that most licensed university patents earn under $100k). The expensive, mostly failing step is downstream (scale-up and qualification, about $1-10M+ per alloy and 3-10 years for aerospace, my estimate), and ML over old reports does not de-risk it.

name: NCI Compound Rights Desk
one_line_reason: This is stranded drug rescue with a government licensor. The data is legible and crowded, the IP is weak because the compounds' public disclosure is prior art, the proving step is bespoke biology, and the step-up is about 10x on a hit and mostly contingent milestones. fatal_flaw: There is no illegible-data edge and no defensible right. NCI-60 and PubChem are public, structured and already heavily mined by funded repurposing companies. On top of that, the proving step is bespoke wet-lab biology that buyers discount steeply, so the immediate step-up is about 10x, not 10^4.

Cost per proving attempt is $50-200k (candidate's figure; consistent with contract research organization pricing for one efficacy model plus PK, my estimate). The real attrition is downstream: about 90% of drugs entering clinical trials fail (widely cited BIO/Informa figure). Proven: ECA or real-world-data licenses for a single indication are, to my knowledge, usually in the low hundreds of thousands to low millions of dollars. The proving step is neither expensive nor mostly failing today, so a 10x discovery-capex drop does not apply. Unsourced; searches were blocked.

name: Surplus Physics: mis-listed scientific instruments
one_line_reason: Rights are cheap and buyers are real, but proving and refurbishing dominate the work (the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure), the net step-up is about 10-30x, and there are only tens of lots a year with no ladder to a large company.
fatal_flaw: The physical proving and refurbishment step (freight, He-3 mixture, compressor, multi-day cooldown, repair) is costly, slow and dominates the work, while discovery is a small share. On top of that, supply is only tens of high-value lots a year, so the TAM is tiny. It is an equipment-flipping business, not a 95-5 discovery rung.
step_up: From memory, not verified (search budget was exhausted): a new dilution fridge (Bluefors or Oxford Triton) costs about $400k-$1M+. A used or refurbished working unit probably sells for about $100-400k. Untested cryostat or 'vacuum chamber' lots on GovDeals, Public Surplus or eBay usually clear somewhere from a few hundred dollars to $20k, often with key parts missing. A mis-labelled lot bought for $2-5k and resold working for $150k would be about 30-75x gross. Net of the $50-100k refurbishment, test and freight, it is about 10-30x. 1000x happens only on rare jackpot lots. UHV chambers and magnets are more like 3-10x. Realistic C2 is the 10-100x band.
hit_rate_capex: I have no sourced base rate. My estimate is that well under 1% of 'untested lab equipment' lots are high-value quantum or fusion hardware that is truly mis-described, and maybe 30-60% of those can be restored economically. Each proving attempt (pickup, freight, leak test, cooldown with He mixture) costs roughly $10-50k per large cryogenic lot, also my estimate. ML raises the share of the right lots spotted, but most of the capex is the physical test and refurbishment, which ML does not reduce. Bidding is cheap compared with testing, so the lever is capped well below 10x.

name: SpacingSlot / Roadside Rights: new billboard permit sites
one_line_reason: Qualifying a billboard site is a rules check on legible data that incumbents already run, and a bare permit is worth only about 10-100x the option before costly construction, so neither the 95/5 frame nor the 10^3+ step-up holds.
fatal_flaw: Whether a site qualifies is a deterministic rule check (spacing, zoning, caps) over mostly legible GIS and DOT inventories, and incumbents' site teams already run that check. What is left of the risk is local politics and regulatory caps, which ML cannot lever. Separately, a permit's value is small until someone pays for a real build (about $100k-400k), so the frame is not 80%+ discovery and the step-up is only about 10-100x.
step_up: All figures are my estimates; the search budget was used up before I could verify any. Unproven right: an option or ground lease at about $500-5k a year, matching the candidate's own range and typical rural billboard ground rents. Proven right: a permitted but unbuilt interstate site probably sells for about $20k-150k. The candidate's $100k-1M+ figure applies to built, leased structures, especially digital, and building one costs roughly $100k-400k of real capex. Step-up on the right itself: about 10-100x. That is far from 10^3-10^4, and the TAM per site is small.
hit_rate_capex: My estimate, not verified. Filing a permit costs roughly $100-2k plus survey and legal, so maybe $2-10k per attempt including the option. Eligibility is a deterministic rule check: commercial or industrial zoning, spacing of about 500 ft on interstates in many states, plus local caps. A good rules-based screen gets hit rates high on its own. Failures come mainly from discretionary local politics and caps, which ML over documents does not predict well. The base hit rate is not low and each attempt is not expensive, so there is no ~10x discovery-capex cut to buy. The lever is about 1.5-3x at best.

name: Pharmacy Location Rules site prospector (Australia)
one_line_reason: This fails on three counts: (1) only pharmacists can own the proven asset, (2) the step-up is about 10-50x, not 10^4, and (3) approval rates are high and the distance rules are legible, so there is little ML hit-rate lever.
fatal_flaw: Australian law limits pharmacy ownership to pharmacists, and Section 90 approvals must be held by pharmacists. So the company cannot own the proven asset and keep the step-up itself. On top of that, approval is not where the value is realised; a fit-out and a trading business are. The base approval rate is high, so ML gives almost no hit-rate lever.
step_up: Unproven: a lease option, probably about A$5-50k in option fees and holding cost (estimate). Proven: an approved site before it trades may sell for low hundreds of thousands of AUD (estimate). An established pharmacy sells for roughly 25-40% of turnover, about A$1-4M (industry rule of thumb, unverified this run). Most of that value comes only after build-out and trading. The immediate step-up on approval alone is about 10-50x on the option cost, not 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: well-prepared ACPA applications are mostly approved, my estimate about 60-80%. That caps the lever at roughly 1.3-1.7x, not 10x. Cost per attempt: surveyor about A$5-15k, consultant or legal work about A$20-60k, plus the application fee (all estimates; I could not verify them because the search budget was used up). The failure mode is not finding a site. It is rule technicalities and objections from nearby pharmacies, which ML over past decisions only partly helps with.

name: Shovel-Ready Berths: permitted-but-stalled marine terminal sites
one_line_reason: Permit status is already legible, owners know what they hold, the step-up is only about 2-5x, and building the terminal dwarfs the discovery work, so discovery is never 80% of any sellable rung.
fatal_flaw: There is no illegible discovery problem. Permit validity and expiration are legible fields the owner already knows, so you cannot buy at raw-land prices. The value step-up is about 2-5x because the bespoke terminal build (dredging, quay, FERC) dominates the work. That is the same pattern as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
step_up: My estimate is 2-5x, not 10-50x. Deepwater-access industrial land already trades at a waterfront premium (very roughly $100k-$1M/acre depending on port, estimate). The permits save a buyer about 2-5 years and a few million dollars of permitting cost. That is a real premium but not orders of magnitude. Reference points from memory, not verified this run: Tradepoint Atlantic bought the Sparrows Point site (about 3,100 acres) for roughly $110M as raw brownfield. Stalled LNG projects that changed hands (e.g. Magnolia LNG, Commonwealth-type sales) were priced mostly on FERC authorizations and offtake, not on USACE permits. I could not run any web search (the shared budget was used up), so these numbers are unsourced estimates.
hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing physical proving step. 'Proving' means pulling the permit file and a title/lease review, roughly $10k-$50k of legal and survey work per site (estimate). Whether a permit is valid is close to certain once you read the permit document. So the base hit rate of proving is high, and ML has no 10x capex lever to pull. The real uncertainty is buyer demand. The offshore-wind port pipeline shrank sharply after 2025 federal actions against offshore wind, and ammonia/e-fuel export projects are mostly pre-FID. Both are market risk, not discovery risk.

name: SlagBank / FlueDust: smelter and roaster residues re-read for Ge, In, Ga, Te, Sb, Bi, Co, Re
one_line_reason: The ML read of RI/FS tables is a genuine gap, but sampling is cheap, enrichment is predictable from feed history, and value is gated by recovery chemistry and Superfund liability, not by finding the pile.
fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the hard part. For trace Ge/In/Ga in glassy smelter slag, the binding constraint is metallurgical recovery plus CERCLA liability transfer. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode: the bespoke physical and legal step dominates, so there is no frame where discovery is 80%+.
step_up: The unproven right is $0-50k per the candidate, and is often negative because the piles are carried as liabilities. A proven pile is worth what a secondary-feed smelter pays: payables are usually a fraction of contained metal, with penalties for As/Pb/Cd plus freight. My estimate is a step-up from near-zero to perhaps $0.5-5M per mid-size pile on a hit. That reads as large in multiple terms only because the base is about zero. On a value-per-tonne basis the multiple versus remediation cost is about 3-10x at best. Many hits will still net out negative after the cleanup obligation. Estimate only; my web search budget ran out, so none of these numbers are verified.
hit_rate_capex: Proving is cheap. Grab/trench sampling plus ICP-MS full-suite costs roughly $5-50k per site (candidate figure; estimate), and recovery testwork is about $50-150k. The base hit rate for 'contains elevated Ge/In/Ga' is probably not low at Zn/Pb smelters, because these metals concentrate predictably by feed type (sphalerite gives Ge/In/Ga; Cu gives Te/Se/Re; Pb gives Sb/Bi). Domain metallurgists can predict that without ML. So the ML lever on discovery capex is under 2-3x, and capex is not the bottleneck anyway. Unverified: search budget exhausted.

name: Breeze Signal: ML bloodstock pinhooking
one_line_reason: Fails the Terranox test: training a horse is the bespoke plant, not the drill. Discovery is under 50% of the rung, outcomes are already legible, sellers are sophisticated, and the market is small.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is physical and costly, not abstracted. Every horse costs about $30-60k a year to raise and train, with injury and death risk, whatever ML picks. Most failures come from unobservable soundness and temperament, not from things ML could see in the data. The outcomes (breeze times, race results, black type) are already legible public fields that efficient, sophisticated auction buyers price, and EQB-style analytics firms already mine the illegible video and biometric signals.
step_up: These are estimates from memory, not sourced this run. A typical good pinhook returns about 1.5-5x, for example a $30k yearling resold for $75-150k at a 2-year-old in-training sale such as OBS March or Arqana. A $5-30k horse that becomes a Grade 1 winner and colt stallion prospect can be worth $5M-$30M+, which is 10^2-10^3x. But that happens about 0.1-0.5% of the time and takes 2-3 years. The step-up is also not immediate. The 10^3 step needs years of racing, not a single cheap test, so the expected step-up on the cheap proving step (the breeze) is only about 3x.
hit_rate_capex: These are estimates from memory, not sourced this run. Commonly cited industry figures put stakes winners at about 3% of North American foals, and graded stakes winners under 1%. Industry folklore holds that roughly half of pinhooks lose money once costs are counted. The cost of one proving attempt is the purchase ($5-30k) plus preparation and training to a breeze or race. My estimate for that is $30-60k per horse per year in the US (training fees about $100-150 a day, plus vet, farrier and insurance). Total is about $50-150k a shot. The base hit rate is low, but the lever is mostly unavailable. Most failures come from soundness, temperament and injury after purchase, which video and pedigree cannot predict. So ML cannot cut the cost per shot about 10x; my guess is 1.5-2x on selection at best. Training cost is fixed per horse whatever the model says.

name: Cohort Strains: exclusive isolate rights over banked human microbiome cohorts
one_line_reason: Total 8/25: the ML call may be right but you cannot own it - strains are re-isolable by anyone, the data is a tidy labelled matrix thousands of papers have already mined, culturing is the hard part rather than the trivial part, and the preclinical microbiome buy side that would pay the step-up has collapsed.
fatal_flaw: The asset is not excludable. A bacterial strain is not a mineral title: anyone can re-isolate a conspecific strain from any donor or buy the type strain from a culture collection, so the "exclusive isolate right" purchased from a biobank fences nothing, and no step-up can be captured even if the ML call is correct. Compounding it, the physical step is harder than the find (>70% of gut species have never been cultured) and the public data is already fully legible with the outcome label in a metadata field - the exact condition the rubric says kills the edge.
step_up: Claimed $50-250k -> $20-200M (10^2-10^3x). Real comparables do not support it, and the sector repriced to near zero. Evelo paid Mayo Clinic US$12,500 for a single Prevotella melaninogenica strain (Evelo 10-K exhibit, Mayo agreement), i.e. raw strain material is a four-figure item, not a scarce right. Preclinical LBP upfronts: Takeda/Finch $10M (2017); OptiBiotix's L. plantarum cholesterol strain licence was a "six figure payment" on signing. Exit economics: Seres sold VOWST - an FDA-APPROVED product with revenue - to Nestle Health Science in 2024 on undisclosed terms sized to clear ~$110M of Oaktree debt, and Nestle later bought out remaining sales milestones for $25M total ($12.5M on 2026-07-01 and 2026-10-01). Kaleido shut down (2023), Evelo failed its primary endpoint and its board resigned, 4D pharma went into administration. So the honest step-up on a culture+mouse hit is roughly $100k -> low single-digit millions in a good case (~10-30x), and it is not immediate: it is realised over years and only if the clinic cooperates. Scored 2-3; I give 2 because the "immediate on a hit" condition fails outright. (My estimate, anchored on the deals above.)
hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt (my estimate from CRO price lists and standard practice): targeted anaerobic isolation + whole-genome confirmation ~$30-150k per strain; one mouse efficacy study at a CRO ~$150-500k including colonisation/germ-free or gnotobiotic housing, which is the dominant cost. So ~$200-650k per attempt, in the candidate's stated range. The problem is the direction of the base rate. The nominal proving step (does the strain do something in a mouse?) has a HIGH base hit rate - the microbiome literature is saturated with positive mouse results - so 1/base-hit-rate caps the ML lever at roughly 2-3x, not 10x. The step with the genuinely low base rate is human efficacy, and ML over observational metagenomes cannot raise it, because the associations are confounded: the canonical case is that the type-2-diabetes gut signature is substantially a metformin signature, with a classifier trained on metformin-exposed T2D samples outperforming one trained on metformin-unexposed samples; a 2025 bioRxiv preprint on confounder-free microbiome phenotype models shows transit time, inflammation and BMI overriding the variance explained by colorectal-cancer case status. ML here buys more shots at a target that is partly an artefact.

name: Orphan Enzyme Estates: lapsed enzyme patent families proven against live markets
one_line_reason: The value comes from litigating against infringers, not from discovery, so this is a patent-troll model with about 10-100x upside, litigation-dominated costs and expiring assets.
fatal_flaw: The step-up is realised through enforcement, not discovery. A patent is worth money only if someone currently infringes it and cannot design around it, and proving that means litigation at a median cost of $0.6-3M per case with low win rates. That is not trivial, ML cannot drop it 10x, and expressing the enzyme in the lab adds no value. On top of that, families that truly lapsed are public domain and cannot be bought, and families that are still live but cover markets that appeared after filing have little term left.
step_up: Unproven: a dormant family at roughly $2-20k (candidate's figure; my estimate is low thousands to tens of thousands for small-owner families in a bulk deal). Proven: the median NPE suit resolves for about $0.52-0.55M in combined legal and settlement cost, with a mean of $6-7.6M skewed by a few large cases (RPX NPE cost studies, 2013). On the asking side, Ocean Tomo's average ask per patent was about $150-180k in 2020-21, and 2006-08 live auctions averaged $116k-$622k per lot sold, with about half of lots unsold. A realistic hit is therefore about 10-100x, not 10^3. The $1-50M exit needs a major's flagship process to sit squarely inside the claim, which is rare and is exactly what majors' freedom-to-operate teams already check.
hit_rate_capex: The proving step the candidate names, expressing and assaying, costs about $1-10k per sequence (my estimate for gene synthesis plus expression and assay) and succeeds often, so it is not the bottleneck and ML has little to lever. The real proving step is enforcement. Median litigation cost is about $0.6M through claim construction and $1M through trial for $1-10M at risk, and $1.5M / $3M for $10-25M at risk (AIPLA 2025, as reported by IPWatchdog). Patentee win rates at trial are commonly cited around 25-35% (my estimate from general patent-litigation statistics). ML cannot drop that cost 10x. Legal fees, inter partes review challenges and design-arounds dominate. The lever is capped near 1-2x.

name: Phage Rights: exclusive phage isolates for crop bacterial disease
one_line_reason: Scores 8/25: real vertical ladder and genuinely non-summarised outcome data, but the proving step is cheap rather than expensive (no 10x capex lever), strain-level host-range ML has <40% precision in published benchmarks, and the "right" is unownable because phages are isolable de novo for a few hundred dollars, so there is no $1/ha-to-$10,000/ha asset to hold.
fatal_flaw: No excludable right: the asset is infinitely substitutable. A new lytic phage against any of these pathogens can be isolated fresh from the environment for a few hundred dollars in days, and deposited phages are distributed non-exclusively, so there is nothing scarce to buy cheaply from an owner who cannot read the data — and the value-creating step is the multi-million-dollar field-efficacy and FIFRA registration package, not discovery.
step_up: Claimed $5-30k to $10-100M (10^3-10^4x) is unsupported by any observable transaction. Price of the unproven right: public culture collections distribute deposited phages for roughly $100-500 per isolate (DSMZ/ATCC-type catalogue pricing; my estimate within that range), and exclusive commercial licences on an already-public deposit are generally not available at all because deposits under Budapest-Treaty/open-collection terms are distributed non-exclusively. Price of the proven right: no disclosed comparables exist. The closest real datapoints found are the Phagelux acquisition of OmniLytics (AgriPhage, the only EPA-registered crop phage product line in the US) with no disclosed value, and EcoPhage, formed 2019 by Bayer with the Bayer-Trendlines Ag Innovation Fund as a seed-stage vehicle rather than an acquisition. Both suggest the whole registered-product company trades at venture-seed to small-M&A scale, not $10-100M for a pre-registration cocktail. Honest estimate for a plate+greenhouse-positive cocktail with no field or regulatory data: $100k-1M in option/milestone terms, i.e. roughly 10-100x on a few thousand dollars of inputs, not 10^3-10^4x.
hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap, not expensive, which breaks the C3 lever: a host-range plating campaign against a panel of field isolates costs hundreds to a few thousand dollars, and phage hunters routinely screen dozens of candidates because screening is the cheap part. With a cost per attempt that low there is no 10x capex to cut; ML buys you nothing you could not buy with a bigger plate panel. Worse, the ML itself underperforms where it would need to work: a published benchmark of 11 host-prediction tools using 16 broad-spectrum phages found ML/DL methods are accurate mainly at species or genus level, while at strain level only moderate sensitivity (<80%) is reachable and precision is low (<40%). Receptor-binding-protein models report PR-AUC 73.6-93.8% but only on narrow, well-sampled hosts (E. coli, Salmonella, C. difficile) — not Xylella, Clavibacter or Ralstonia, where phage-host training pairs are sparse. The expensive, mostly-failing step in this business is the field trial and registration package (multi-season, multi-site, my estimate $1-5M and multi-year for a FIFRA biopesticide), and ML on phage genomes does not raise that hit rate.

name: SportScout: somatic-mutant ornamental plant hunting
one_line_reason: Fails the Terranox shape. The physical proving step (stabilisation, trials, patent) is most of the work and ML barely moves it. The signal is already legible and priced by sellers, incumbents find most sports in their own labs, and royalties of cents per plant cap the step-up well below 10^3 at the moment of a hit.
fatal_flaw: The value is not illegible and not realised on a hit. Sports are visible and already priced by the hobbyists who list them, and the listing starts the one-year patent bar. Most commercially useful sports come out of incumbents' own tissue-culture labs. Proving stability takes years of physical propagation and trials that ML cannot speed up, and the payoff is cents-per-plant royalties. That makes the step-up small, slow and owned by the licensor.
step_up: Unproven: a $20-200 plant (candidate's figure). Hobby sellers who see variegation already list it at $100s-1000s, and variegated Monstera fell to $25-50 retail once tissue culture scaled it up (plantcelltechnology blog). Proven: royalties run about $0.10-2.00 per plant over a 20-year patent (Bellingrath). Proven Winners says it is usually "a few cents" and gives 50,000 plants x $0.02 = $1,000 as its example. Assuming 50k-500k plants a year at $0.05-0.25, a typical licensed sport earns roughly $2.5k-125k a year (my estimate), paid slowly. The candidate's $100k-2M figure fits only rare hits. A realistic upfront-equivalent step-up is about 50-500x on the plant cost, before the $2-5k proving cost, and nothing is realised at the moment of a hit.
hit_rate_capex: The candidate puts the base hit rate at about 1-5% surviving reversion. No measured reversion rate was found; sellers say most tissue-culture plantlets of rare variegates revert to green. Each proving attempt costs about $2-5k for propagation and trials plus about $3k for the patent (Bellingrath), and takes 12-24+ months. ML vision can only rank what a plant looks like in a photo. Whether a sport is stable depends on the chimera's layer structure, which a listing photo cannot show, so ML barely improves the hit rate on the costly step. A 10x capex cut is implausible; my estimate is at most about 1.5-2x from better triage.

name: War Cargo Title / Cargo Ledger / Underwriter's Wreck: insurer- and government-owned sunken cargo
one_line_reason: The discovery rung isn't sellable: value only comes after hard, bespoke recovery (the coal-mine geothermal failure mode). Owners already know the cargo value and award rights by tender for a net share. And 25 years of Odyssey losses, ending in a $21M sale of its whole database, cap the upside.
fatal_flaw: The step-up is not realised at the discovery rung. A located wreck has no liquid buyer, and value comes only after bespoke, deep, legally contested recovery. On top of that, the cargo value is already known to the owners, who award rights by competitive tender and not for a cheap cash price. So there is neither an information-asymmetry purchase nor a sellable 95%-discovery rung.
step_up: There is no observed price for the unproven or the proven right. UK DfT awards contracts by competitive tender, with the salvor bearing search and recovery risk and keeping 80% of net salved value after expenses (Odyssey press release). There is no up-front purchase price, so the '$10-100k right' in the candidate is unsupported. Finding the wreck creates a contingent claim on a cargo whose value is already known, but nobody pays a quoted price for that claim. My estimate is a 3-10x option-value uplift that is illiquid. For scale: Odyssey's entire shipwreck research database and assets sold for $21M in 2015 (net book $13.5M). Total Gairsoppa monetisation was ~$80M over two years against cargo estimates of $121-260M.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate per search is unknown. One data point: the 1989 Gairsoppa search by the sole bidder failed to find the wreck, and Odyssey later found it. Cost per proving attempt is ~$0.1-3M for a survey (my estimate, consistent with the 'single-digit millions' total budget). Better positioning from ML could cut search cost, but search is the minority of total project cost. Recovery is tens of $M, so a 10x discovery-capex cut does not give 10x more shots at the full value. Industry economics are poor: of 52 annual reports from listed shipwreck-recovery firms since 1996, only 5 show a net profit, and Odyssey has ~$150M in cumulative losses (secondary magazine source, unverified).

name: Sleeper Atelier: mis-catalogued Chinese imperial ceramics and works of art
one_line_reason: Low estimates are not low purchase prices: crowd bidding already finds the sleepers, so ML has no information edge and no cheap right to buy, and the proving step is a specialist's opinion rather than a measurement.
fatal_flaw: The step-up is captured at the purchase itself: regional sales of Chinese works are bid globally online (Chinese bidders compete GBP 30-40 estimates up to GBP 63k, and CHF 500-800 up to CHF 5M). The 10^4 jump goes to the consignor, and there is no cheap, unreadable 'right' to buy before proving.
step_up: The headline cases are real: a Geneva vase estimated at CHF 500-800 made CHF 5M in 2017 (10,000x the estimate); a Keys (Aylsham) lacquer box estimated at GBP 30-40 made GBP 63,000 in 2022; ATG cites plaques estimated at GBP 30-50 that sold for GBP 7,000. In every case the step-up happened AT the regional sale, because mainland Chinese online bidders competed it up, and the gain went to the consignor, not to a buyer. The step-up a buyer can actually capture (hammer price to HK resale) is my estimate at about 1.5-5x, with occasional 10x+. The 10^3-10^4 figure is estimate to hammer, not purchase price to resale.
hit_rate_capex: I found no published price for a TL test; the candidate's ~$500 figure is plausible (my estimate: $300-700 per sample; Oxford Authentication runs about 3,000 samples a year, about 90% of them Chinese ceramics). Base hit rate (my estimate): for a typical 'decorative 20th century' lot, well under 1% is actually imperial. But the cost per attempt is mostly the purchase price, and pieces that look imperial are bid up publicly whatever their status, so ML does not cut the cost of an attempt. It only filters which lots to bid on, and there it competes against thousands of human eyes looking at the same images.

name: Unconsummated Abandonment Lines: dormant federally preempted rail corridors
one_line_reason: Preemption status is a docket lookup and isn't where the value comes from. The value comes from rehab and finding shippers, which is the geothermal-coal-mine trap. Realistic step-up is 2-10x and only comes after heavy capex.
fatal_flaw: The step-up depends on traffic and rehab capex ($250k-$1M/mi) rather than on discovery. And the 'proof' (whether a consummation notice exists, i.e. preemption) is already a legible STB docket field that the selling carrier understands. So there is no illegible-data edge and no discount from uninformed owners.
step_up: The unproven side is salvage or net liquidation value. East Penn 8.6 mi: county NSV $377,804 (about $44k/mi) vs the railroad's NLV $2.16M (about $251k/mi). Idaho 66.8 mi: NLV $1.8M (about $27k/mi). The proven side is a going-concern short line, which needs traffic: San Luis and Rio Grande, 154 mi for about $7M (about $45k/mi, rural); G&W/Rail Management, about $330k/mi; G&W/Georgia-Pacific, about $445k/mi with a 20-year service contract (per-mile figures are my calculations from deal totals). A dormant line with no traffic sells near salvage no matter how clean its preemption status is. Even the going-concern comps are only 1-10x salvage, and that comes from traffic, not legal status. I found no published rail-served land premium. The listings I saw ($50-70k/acre in Strafford, MO; about $65k/acre in Lubbock) suggest a premium in the tens of percent at most (estimate). So realistically 2-10x, and only after rehab capex is spent. The candidate's ~10-100x claim is not supported.
hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving step. Checking legal status means reading dockets plus a title search, perhaps $5-30k per segment in attorney and title work (estimate). Among segments that are actually dormant, the base rate of 'still legally in the national system' is high, because no consummation notice means authority can lapse and the line stays in the system. So ML has little hit rate to improve. The costly, failure-prone step is finding a shipper and funding rehab ($250k-$1M/mi), and ML over dockets does not touch that. Lever: about 1-2x.

name: RoofBank: rooftop and riser rights in densification hot zones
one_line_reason: The step-up depends on a carrier's private siting decision, not on discovery. Aggregators only buy easements that already have tenants, data that matters is private, and densification is moving to cheap municipal poles, so the Terranox 95/5 frame does not exist here.
fatal_flaw: The proving event (a carrier tenant signing) is decided by the carrier's private RF plan and capex budget, not by discovery from public data. There is no capitalised buyer for an untenanted easement. The rung therefore has no sellable output until a third party decides to use the site, and carriers can substitute any nearby roof or a municipal pole.
step_up: My estimate, not checked against sources (search budget used up). Unproven: $5-20k upfront for a 20-30 yr easement with no tenant, per the candidate. Proven: one carrier rooftop lease at roughly $1,500-3,000/month (industry folklore range) is $18-36k/yr. Aggregators buy that at roughly 10-20x annual rent (my estimate), so about $180-700k. That is ~10-40x on a hit, but only after a tenant signs, which can take years. It is not instant like a drill core. In expectation (hit rate times value) the uplift is much smaller.
hit_rate_capex: My estimate. Base rate that a speculative rooftop easement gets a carrier tenant within 5 years is very low, likely under 5%. Carriers pick sites from their own RF search rings, they have many interchangeable rooftops to choose from, and macro or rooftop builds have slowed. Examples: T-Mobile decommissioning ~35k Sprint sites, AT&T and Verizon cutting capex in 2024-25, and EchoStar/DISH exiting its own network in 2025 (general knowledge, unverified this run). Cost per attempt is $5-20k plus legal/RF, roughly $10-30k. In theory a low hit rate gives a big lever. In practice ML cannot raise it much, because the deciding variable is the carrier's private RF plan and budget. The carrier already knows that answer and outsiders do not. The lever is mostly fictional.

name: Holdout: site-based incumbents inside future overlay auctions
one_line_reason: This is regulatory arbitrage on legible public dockets with cost-based compensation, not a discovery-dominated rung. Low step-up, no ML hit-rate lever, and the outcome is already in structured fields.
fatal_flaw: The step-up comes from FCC policy, not from discovery. The FCC compensates site-based incumbents at relocation cost under formulas published in legible dockets, and freezes assignments once a band is identified. So there is no hidden signal for ML to find, and no reliable 10^3x jump.
step_up: From memory, not verified (search budget exhausted). Normal FCC relocation law (Emerging Technologies, AWS-1 and 2 GHz microwave cost-sharing) pays incumbents comparable facilities or their actual relocation costs. That is roughly 1x, not a windfall. The windfall cases are the exception: 39 GHz Auction 103 incentive relinquishment (2019-20), Straight Path's 39/28 GHz licences sold to Verizon for about $3.1B in 2017 after being acquired cheaply, and the C-band Auction 107 accelerated relocation payments of $9.7B to the satellite operators (SES about $4B, Intelsat about $4.9B). Those went to large satellite and mmWave holders, not to small site-based fixed links. Realistic step-up for a small site-based licence: 1-10x (my estimate). It is 10-100x only in rare Straight-Path-like setups, which the FCC now closes off with filing and assignment freezes and pro-rata MHz-pop formulas.
hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive proving step that usually fails. Licences are cheap (my estimate: a few thousand to low hundreds of thousands of dollars per site-based licence). A 'hit' comes from FCC policy, not from a better prediction. Base rate that a given band gets an overlay auction with incentive payments: maybe 10-30% within 5 years for bands already in an NPRM (my estimate). Bands named in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act / upper C-band 3.98-4.2 GHz proceeding are already public knowledge. The FCC usually freezes new applications and assignments once a band is identified, so the window to buy before it is legible is narrow. ML cannot raise this hit rate much, because the outcome is set by politics and lobbying, not hidden in data. The lever is well under 10x.

name: VestedRights: tax-deed parcels with grandfathered entitlements
one_line_reason: Proving is cheap paperwork, the typical step-up is about 10x not 10^3, rights on neglected parcels usually lapse by law, and billboard and permit status is already in legible registries, so this is a weak entitlement-arbitrage niche, not a Terranox analogue.
fatal_flaw: The neglect that makes these parcels cheap is the same thing that legally kills the right. Abandonment and discontinuance clauses (typically 6-12 months), approval expiry dates and billboard permit lapse rules mean that most rights on tax-deed or neglected parcels have already expired. Where a right does survive, the answer is usually in a legible registry (DOT billboard permit status) or a cheap zoning verification letter, so ML gives no lasting edge.
step_up: My estimates, not from sources (the search budget was used up before I could check): a typical tax-deed lot clears at about $2k-20k. If it truly carries a vested approval, a transferable sewer allocation in a moratorium market (tap or capacity fees often $10k-50k per unit in capped markets), or a valid nonconforming billboard site (ground-lease buyout values often $50k-500k for good sites, from industry knowledge, not verified this run), resale is maybe $20k-200k. That is usually 3-30x and rarely 100x+. The 10^3-10^4 claim needs a near-zero parcel with a big right attached, and that is extremely rare. Typical step-up is about 10x.
hit_rate_capex: I could not check either number this run because the search budget was used up. Cost per proving attempt is cheap: a zoning verification letter is about $100-500 and a records request plus attorney review about $1-5k (my estimate). Because proving is already cheap, there is little capex for ML to cut ten-fold. The base hit rate is very low (my estimate is under 1% of tax-deed parcels carry a valid, transferable legacy right). The main cause is law, not search difficulty: most ordinances end nonconforming-use rights after 6-12 months of discontinuance, plat and site-plan approvals usually expire after 1-5 years, and billboard permits typically lapse when the structure is removed or neglected. ML raises recall in the search, but the cost being saved is screening time, not drilling-scale capex.

name: Remnant: surplus DOT and government remnant parcels as assemblage keystones
one_line_reason: This is holdout arbitrage, not discovery. The step-up is about 2-10x on small dollars, the signal is mostly legible public filings, adjoiners get first offer, and ML adds little over a filter on planning agendas. Numbers are estimates because the search budget was used up.
fatal_flaw: A remnant becomes a keystone only after a developer has publicly started assembling. By then the answer is already in a legible public field (rezoning or site-plan filings) that incumbents and the adjoiner can read. The adjoiner's priority rights and appraisal-based pricing take most of the premium. And the value comes from a holdout negotiation that buyers can design around, not from discovery.
step_up: Estimate only; both searches were refused because the shared search budget was used up. Remnants usually sell at an appraised standalone value of nominal to low-five-figure amounts. Sale at fair market value is broadly required for federally funded right of way (23 CFR 710.403, from memory). A keystone in an active assemblage can fetch a holdout premium of maybe 2-10x appraised value. In rare cases it is 10-100x on tiny, near-zero-value strips, but the dollar amounts are small. A 10^3-10^4 jump is not plausible, because any appraiser or adjoiner already sees part of the plottage value.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate only. The proving attempt is buying a remnant: about $5k-$100k plus closing and holding costs, and each one has to be bought. The base hit rate for a remnant becoming a real keystone in a deal that closes is maybe 1-5% if bought blind. But public planning filings show where the assemblages are, so a simple rules-based filter, not ML, gets most of the lift. Each miss is not a sunk cost like a dry drill hole: you still own a resellable remnant at about cost. That means the cost of failing is low, so the ML lever is small.

name: HeirShare: lost mutual ditch company shares
one_line_reason: This is title-clearing arbitrage on an already-priced asset whose holders the issuer tracks through assessments: there is no 10^3 proving step-up, ML has little to lever, and the orphan pool is thin.
fatal_flaw: Proving title does not create value. A ditch share is already priced in a liquid, legible local market, and mutual ditch companies track holders through annual assessments, forfeiting and reselling delinquent shares. So genuinely orphaned, unclaimed shares are rare. The only margin is underpaying uninformed heirs, which is small, legally fragile, and hard to scale.
step_up: The share's market value does not change when title is proven. A proven NPIC, C-BT or similar share trades at a known, published price (the candidate cites C-BT at ~$85k/AF in 2025; I could not verify this because the search budget ran out). The 'step-up' only exists against cash paid to uninformed heirs: $500-10k paid for an asset worth roughly $30-100k is about 3-100x, most likely ~5-20x once heirs are told the asset exists, which a valid quitclaim effectively requires. This is information arbitrage on a fully priced asset, not 1 -> 10^4 value creation. My estimate, unsourced.
hit_rate_capex: Proving is cheap per attempt: a few hundred to a few thousand dollars of records research. A quiet title runs maybe $5-25k in legal fees if contested (estimate). The base hit rate is not low because of hard discovery. The constraint is that true orphans are scarce. So ML has little to multiply: lever well under 10x. All numbers are estimates; no web searches ran (shared budget used up).

name: Gravel Pit Storage Rights
one_line_reason: This has the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: building the lined storage and litigating the decree outweigh finding the pair. The outcome is already shown in legible CDSS status fields, the net step-up is only about 3-10x, and the hit rate is already high, so ML has no 10x capex lever.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is construction plus water-court litigation, not discovery. The slurry wall (about $2-6k/AF) and the change-of-right case are most of the work and cost. Discovery is trivial because pits and decree statuses are already public in structured databases, and incumbent aggregate companies already capture the lined-storage step-up. On top of that, the anti-speculation doctrine and the risk of losing priority make the 'pair an old decree with a new pit' trick legally fragile.
step_up: My estimates, from memory; no web searches ran because the shared budget was used up. Unlined mined-out pit land sells for about $5-15k/acre. Lined storage holds about 30-60 AF/acre and Front Range utilities pay roughly $10-40k/AF of capacity, so about $0.5-2M/acre. That is about 50-150x gross. But the liner costs about $2-6k/AF (about $100-300k/acre), and legal and engineering add more, so the net multiple on capital deployed is about 3-10x. The step-up is also not immediate: it arrives only after construction, the leak test, and a water-court decree, which takes years.
hit_rate_capex: My estimate: the proving step does not mostly fail. A competently built slurry wall passes the SEO leak test in most cases (I estimate more than 70% on the first test, with remediation available after a failure). Water court outcomes for change cases are also mostly favorable, just slow. Each attempt costs millions in construction (for example, 1,000 AF at $2-6k/AF is $2-6M) plus about $0.2-1M in legal fees, and that cost is mostly fixed by geometry. ML cannot cut it 10x. Since the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, it is at most about 1.5x.

name: Ridgeline Storage: closed-loop pumped hydro site origination
one_line_reason: Building is the hard part and site discovery is a commodity: NREL already ranks the sites publicly, permits are free and first-come, and value appears only after years of licensing. It fails the 95-5 frame.
fatal_flaw: No rung exists where discovery is 80%+ of the work. NREL has already published ranked closed-loop sites, the key right (the FERC preliminary permit) is free first-come, and PSH value is made by a 5-10 year licensing, financing and civil build process. So ML site-finding moves neither the hit rate nor the price. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
step_up: My estimate (no live search was possible): a rangeland option costs roughly $50-500/acre-equivalent, and a preliminary permit costs almost nothing. An early-stage permitted PSH package with a desktop screen trades at nominal value, often a development fee or earn-out. Licensed, shovel-ready projects might fetch roughly $10-50/kW, which is $10-50M for 1 GW, but only after many years and tens of millions in development spend.
