Immediate step-up on a 'hit' at the preliminary permit stage: about 3-10x at best, because nothing is de-risked. The candidate's own estimate is 10-100x over 5-10 years.
hit_rate_capex: Base rate from my background knowledge, not verified this session: FERC has issued hundreds of PSH preliminary permits (tens of GW to over 90 GW pending at any time). Only a handful of US PSH projects have been licensed since about 2014: Gordon Butte, Swan Lake, Eagle Mountain, and Goldendale more recently. Even fewer have been built, so permit-to-construction is likely under 5%. But failures come mostly from cost, financing, offtake and transmission, not bad geology, so ML site ranking does little for the hit rate. A preliminary permit costs almost nothing to file. The expensive attempt is licensing ($10-50M+, estimate), and ML does not cut that 10x.

name: Upgrade Credit Recovery: stranded network-upgrade refund and transmission-credit claims
one_line_reason: This is collecting a capped receivable with a known face value, not discovering hidden value. Real-world step-up is probably 3-10x after pricing, the obligor already keeps the legible record, and there is no ladder to a large company.
fatal_flaw: The repayment rights belong to projects that reached commercial operation, and those projects are owned by live plant owners. Orphaned estates mostly hold claims that are worthless or already settled by formula. The value is capped at a face amount that the obligor already computes and tracks, so this is discounted debt collection with no 10^3-10^4 step-up.
step_up: The candidate says 1-5% of face goes to 100% of face, which is 20-100x on paper. I could not verify any real trade prices because the web search budget was used up before my first search ran, so every number here is my estimate. Under the FERC pro forma LGIA (Order 2003, Art. 11.4), repayment of funded network upgrades through cash or transmission credits is tied to the generating facility reaching commercial operation, and runs over up to 20 years with interest. A dissolved developer whose project never reached COD usually has no refund stream at all, only a refund of unspent security when it withdraws, which the RTO or transmission owner computes and pays out routinely. Where a stream does exist, it belongs to whoever holds the LGIA, and that is normally the operating plant owner, not an estate that can't read its own files. Once you price in probability and the discount for 20-year payment timing, I expect the real step-up per hit to be about 3-10x (an estimate). It is a discount on a known face value, not a 10^3-10^4 jump.
hit_rate_capex: I have no sourced base hit rate; the search budget was used up. My estimate is that most orphaned claims are worth nothing, because the projects withdrew before COD and their security was already refunded or forfeited under tariff formulas. The cost of each proving attempt is mostly legal and document review: roughly $5k-$50k per claim to parse the agreements, plus the time spent negotiating acknowledgement with the transmission owner (also an estimate). ML can cheapen the document parsing, but the binding cost is legal: getting transmission owner acknowledgement or consent to assignment, and possibly litigating at FERC. ML does not cut that 10x. The lever is small.

name: QF Attribute Title / Uncaptured Legacy RECs
one_line_reason: This is really a legal and administrative REC-aggregation business with low-value existing-tier RECs and a ~2-3x maximum ML lever, not a discovery-dominated rung.
fatal_flaw: Old QFs mostly qualify only for low-price 'existing' REC tiers (~$1-15/MWh, my estimate), the gap shows up in structured registries and is filled by existing brokers, and state law has often already given REC ownership to one side. That leaves no illegible-data edge, no 10^3 step-up and no low-hit-rate shot for ML to improve.
step_up: My estimate, not sourced, since searching was blocked. Pre-1997/1998 hydro, biomass, waste-to-energy (WTE) and landfill gas (LFG) plants mostly qualify only for the 'existing' tiers: MA Class II or WTE, CT Class II, PJM Tier 2, at roughly $1-15/MWh. They mostly do not qualify for MA/CT Class I (~$30-40/MWh, alternative compliance payment (ACP) around $40), because of vintage cutoffs. Worked example: a 5 MW hydro at 50% capacity factor makes ~22,000 MWh/yr. At ~$5-10/MWh that is $110-220k/yr, worth maybe $0.5-1.5M NPV. Against a near-zero bought claim that is maybe 5-30x on the contracted price. That is not a 10^3 jump, and part of the value goes back to the QF owner through the revenue share.
hit_rate_capex: My estimate, unsourced. The proving step is a legal and registration process, not a mostly-failing probabilistic shot. Cost is ~$25-150k in legal opinion, PUC filing and metering per facility. Once a real contract-silent QF is identified, the hit rate is fairly high (maybe 30-60%). The main risk is utility litigation under state law that gives RECs to the utility; many states settled this after American Ref-Fuel (FERC 2003) and the Wheelabrator Lisbon v. CT DPUC 2d Cir. 2008 decision, some of them for the utility. With a base hit rate of ~0.3-0.6, the ML lever is capped at ~2-3x, nowhere near 10x.

name: Foam Bank: CFC-11 in pre-1993 building and cold-storage insulation
one_line_reason: Finding a CFC-foam building is easy and cheap. Monetising it means physically recovering and destroying the foam for low-priced, possibly ineligible offsets, so no discovery-dominated rung exists and there is no 10^3x hit.
fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Proving is cheap and usually succeeds, so the ML lever is under about 2x. The value appears only after costly physical recovery, transport and certified destruction (the coal-mine-geothermal failure mode), and building insulation foam is likely not eligible under the CARB/WA compliance ODS protocol, leaving thin voluntary prices.
step_up: Unproven: the foam is waste with a disposal cost, roughly -$1 to -$5/m2 (my estimate). Proven, my estimate: 30-40 kg/m3 polyurethane, about 10 cm thick, about 3-4 kg of foam per m2, and roughly 5-8% residual CFC-11 after decades of off-gassing. That leaves about 0.15-0.3 kg of CFC-11 per m2. At GWP 4,750 (AR4) that is about 0.7-1.4 tCO2e per m2. At ODS offset prices of roughly $5-15/t voluntary and about $15-25/t for CARB compliance (from memory of 2023-2025 ranges, not verified this session), gross value is about $5-30/m2 before recovery and destruction costs, which take a large share of it. A cold-storage warehouse of about 10,000 m2 of panel would gross about $50k-300k. Going from negative to positive makes the multiple look unbounded, but the realised gain is about 10x in absolute terms, and nothing is gained at the moment of a hit, only after destruction.
hit_rate_capex: Proving is cheap: a core sample plus GC lab analysis costs roughly $100-500 per building (my estimate). The base hit rate is high for the target set. For cold storage and commercial roofs insulated with PUR/PIR before about 1993, the chance of CFC-11 is likely 40-70% (my estimate; CFC-11 was the dominant PUR blowing agent until the Montreal Protocol phase-out in 1993-96). Since the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, ML can improve the hit rate by about 1.5-2.5x at most. A cheap test that mostly succeeds already leaves little discovery capex to cut. No searches could be run (the shared search budget was exhausted), so these numbers are not verified.

name: Superfund Forensics: CERCLA cost-recovery claim assignments
one_line_reason: Discovery is a small slice of the value of a CERCLA claim. Value depends on incurred cleanup costs, polluter solvency and slow litigation, so the step-up is about 3-10x over years, not an instant 10^4x.
fatal_flaw: The claim's value is set by response costs actually incurred and by litigation, not by discovery. Naming the polluter does not turn the asset into money. Someone still has to pay for cleanup and spend years in court, and the polluter has to be a solvent successor that still exists. The physical steps are much harder than finding the PRP, the same failure as geothermal in coal mines. On top of that, Phase I research (EDR/LightBox) and EPA PRP searches already make most of the attribution readable.
step_up: Estimate, unsourced (the search budget was used up before any search ran). An assigned claim with no known PRP is worth close to $0. Once a solvent PRP is named, a funded claim is still worth only what the court is likely to award times the recovery rate, minus fees: roughly 20-50% of incurred costs. It also takes 3-8 years and needs the costs to be spent first. If you buy at 5-15% of face and the claim is funded or settles for 30-60% of face, the step-up is about 3-10x and arrives slowly, not 10^3-10^4x right away. The candidate's own "$0 to $1-20M" counts an unknown PRP as $0, but most of that value comes from cleanup spending, not from discovery.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate, no source. A manual PRP search or historical forensics study (EPA contractor PRP searches, consultants working from aerials and Sanborn maps) costs roughly $20k-$150k per site. My guess is it names a viable, solvent PRP at maybe 20-40% of orphan sites; the rest are dead or dissolved companies, and §107 needs a successor that still exists and has money. ML could cut the cost per attempt a lot. But the lever is capped at about 3-5x (1/base hit rate), and the binding limit is whether the polluter is still solvent, which imagery cannot fix.

name: Zombie Vertical Software Rescue: dead-vendor installed bases in government and utilities
one_line_reason: This fails the core test: finding the installed base is cheap and partly handed over with the asset, while servicing and re-contracting is most of the work. The step-up is about 6-18x over months, not 10^3x on a hit, and Harris/Constellation already work this space.
fatal_flaw: The value comes from servicing and re-contracting old government software, not from discovering it. Finding agencies still running a dead vendor's software is cheap and largely given away by the vendor's own customer list. Turning them into paid maintenance needs agency consent and new procurement, plus a real support operation. Buyers like Harris pay 1-3x for proven ARR only, and they already work this niche. So there is no discrete rung where discovery is 80%+ and a hit immediately gives a 10^3x step-up.
step_up: Unproven: code and IP rights from a defunct vendor or bankruptcy trustee at $10-100k (the candidate's figure; plausible for asset sales out of liquidation). Proven: Constellation/Harris-style buyers pay roughly 1-3x recurring revenue for small VMS books (from my memory of Mark Leonard letters and roll-up commentary; I could not verify it this run). Example (my estimate): $50k for IP; 20 agencies at $15k/yr maintenance gives $300k ARR, which sells for about $300-900k. That is about 6-18x, and it only happens after months of contracting and support, not right away on a 'hit'. It is nowhere near the 10^3-10^4 jump.
hit_rate_capex: The proving attempt is cheap today: a records request, a phone call to the IT department, or a search of the agency's check register for the vendor name. That costs maybe $100-1,000 per agency (estimate). The real cost is converting and servicing each agency, which ML does not touch. Base hit rate is unclear but not the bottleneck. Many installs of a dead vendor's software are already known to the bankruptcy trustee or former employees through the old customer list, so the hit rate given a good lead is high. ML's lever on discovery capex is small, maybe 2x at best, not 10x. No sourced numbers: the web search budget ran out this run.

name: Dormant App Installed-Base Acquisition
one_line_reason: This is a coal-mine-geothermal case: picking the app is easy and legible, while rebooting it is bespoke operating work that sells at earnings multiples, not as a discovery step-up.
fatal_flaw: Proving is operating, not discovery. The value comes from months of engineering, growth and monetisation work that is then priced at 2.5-4x earnings, and the selection signal (installs, ratings, decay) is already in legible app-intelligence fields that every app flipper uses. There is no immediate 10^3 step-up and no illegible-data edge.
step_up: No searches could be run: the shared WebSearch budget for this turn was already used up, so every figure here is my estimate from prior knowledge. Dormant apps with no revenue usually sell on Flippa or Acquire.com for about $500-$10k, and the candidate itself assumes $1-10k. A revived app is priced on earnings, at roughly 2.5-4x annual profit (my recollection of the range Flippa and Acquire.com publish). For a typical win, say $3-5k MRR revived from a $3-5k purchase, that means a sale price of about $100-200k. That is about 20-50x on the purchase price but only about 5-15x once you count engineering and marketing spend. It is not an immediate step-up on a hit like a drill core: the value has to be earned over 6-12 months of revenue history before a buyer will pay.
hit_rate_capex: Estimates only, no searches. Each proving attempt costs about $1-10k for the purchase plus $10-50k of engineering and marketing. I estimate 10-20% of revived dormant apps reach meaningful sellable revenue. The users of an abandoned app have mostly uninstalled it, an update only reaches devices that still have it installed, and push tokens and consent are fragile. So the lever is capped at about 5-10x. ML only helps pick which apps to buy, while most of the cost sits in engineering and growth work that ML does not shrink 10x, so discovery capex falls by maybe 2x.

name: US rights to foreign heritage food brands with diaspora pull
one_line_reason: This is an import-distribution business in disguise. Discovery is about 25% of the rung, the proven asset is a revocable licence worth about 0.5-1.5x revenue, the demand signal is already legible, and the ML lever is capped around 3-5x by a 20-40% base hit rate.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is mostly physical distribution, not discovery. FDA/FSVP compliance, labels, freight, inventory capital and grocer slotting make up most of the work and capital, and that fixed cost does not fall with ML. On top of that, the "proven" asset is a revocable licence that the foreign parent can reclaim or reprice at renewal. That moves the step-up to the licensor, and the demand signal is already legible in commercial bill-of-lading tools and Amazon ranks.
step_up: My estimate, not sourced. The unproven right costs about $0-50k: royalty-only (typical food royalties around 3-8%) plus a small upfront. A proven US licence with $1-3M of revenue might sell for 0.5-1.5x revenue, so $0.5-4M. That is roughly 10-100x on the upfront. But it is not an immediate step-up on a hit. Value builds slowly with sell-through, and the cost basis also includes $50-150k per container of inventory and launch spend. Counted against total capital at risk, the step-up is roughly 3-30x. The parent can also refuse to renew or can buy back at a low price, so the value sits mostly with the licensor.
hit_rate_capex: Both numbers are my estimates; I found no sourced figures. Base hit rate: roughly 20-40% of diaspora-brand container tests reach repeat velocity. Diaspora pull is easy to see in advance (grey imports and Amazon reseller listings already exist), so the base rate is not tiny. Cost per proving attempt: about $50-150k (one 40ft container of product at $20-60k, freight and duty, FDA/FSVP and labelling setup, broker and slotting or promo spend, sales labour). With a base hit rate of 20-40%, ML can improve hit rate by at most about 2.5-5x, well short of 10x, and it does nothing to the fixed physical cost of each attempt.

name: CatalystShelf: pruned catalyst and porous-material patent families for new uses
one_line_reason: Patent data is fully legible and already mined, the bought family does not capture the new-use value, and buyers pay only after expensive pilot scale-up, so no rung exists where discovery is 80% or more.
fatal_flaw: The step-up does not attach to the right you buy, and the physical step is not trivial. A new use of an old material is protected by a new method-of-use patent and your own data, which needs no purchase of the pruned family. And buyers pay for pilot-scale proof costing millions, not for a $40k lab test. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure: building and scaling the material is far harder than finding it.
step_up: Unproven: the candidate assumes $5-50k per pruned family (not verified; web search budget was exhausted). Pruned families can also simply lapse into the public domain for $0. Proven: catalyst and sorbent licences are usually bundled with know-how and paid as running royalties or $1-10M+ upfront (my estimate). A lab test alone does not earn that. A realistic price for "family plus one lab result" might be $100k-1M. That is about 10-100x, and only on the rare hit.
hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt is $20-60k per the candidate (plausible for a contract-lab fixed-bed or isotherm run; my estimate, not verified). That is already cheap, so dropping it 10x saves little. The expensive, mostly failing step is pilot scale-up ($1-10M+; my estimate), and ML on patent example tables does not touch it. Base hit rate of a repurposed material beating the state of the art at the target: perhaps 1-5% (estimate). There is also heavy existing computational screening: CoRE MOF and hypothetical-zeolite databases, and academic and national-lab high-throughput work. So ML adds little over the screening that already happens.

name: Orphaned Consented Cohorts: bankruptcy biobank roll-up
one_line_reason: Bankruptcy biobank sales are public, competitive auctions that the end buyers already bid in, and consent and privacy limits erode the right. The step-up is about 3-5x, not 10^3, and ML has little hit rate to improve.
fatal_flaw: The asset is neither hidden nor cheap. Orphaned cohorts are sold in public, competitive 363 auctions where the eventual pharma buyers bid directly (23andMe went for about $20 per participant, vs. about $60-75 per consented participant in the GSK deal, a step-up of about 3-5x). Consent and genetic-privacy law can also destroy or shrink the right after purchase through deletions, re-consent requirements and attorney-general objections. There is no illegible signal that ML can extract and incumbents miss.
step_up: The facts below are from memory up to mid-2025, not from new searches in this run. 23andMe went through Chapter 11 in 2025. Regeneron bid about $256M, and TTAM (Wojcicki) won at about $305M for roughly 15M customers. That is about $20 per participant, not cents. On the proven side, GSK paid $300M in 2018 for a 4-year exclusive drug-discovery deal when 23andMe had about 5M customers, about 80% of them consented. That is roughly $60-75 per consented participant over the term. GSK extended for $50M in 2022. So unproven is about $20 per participant and proven is about $60-100 per participant, a step-up of about 3-5x. Smaller CRO or DTC collections may sell for less, but they are also worth less to pharma because they lack scale, phenotypes and recontact. The candidate's claim of ~100-1000x is not supported.
hit_rate_capex: Proving is computational and cheap. Low-pass sequencing or imputation costs about $20-50 per sample (my estimate), and burden tests are close to free. That makes the proving cost about $0.5M-5M per cohort (estimate), against purchase prices that range from $1M to $300M. The purchase dominates capex, not the proving. There is also no clear binary low hit rate, because most consented cohorts have some licensing value. ML has little hit rate to raise, and the lever is likely under 2x.

name: Closed-Hospital Tissue Archive Rescue
one_line_reason: Each block's subtype is already in its pathology report. The work is custody, de-identification and consent logistics rather than discovery, there is no low-hit-rate step for ML to improve, and established brokers already resell remnant FFPE.
fatal_flaw: There is nothing to discover. The answer for each block (its diagnosis and subtype) is already written in that block's own pathology report and LIS code. The real work is physical, legal and consent logistics for PHI-linked tissue, which is the coal-mine-geothermal failure pattern. Established biobank brokers like Discovery Life Sciences already aggregate remnant FFPE at scale.
step_up: Unproven: blocks sitting in storage under a 10-year CAP retention duty are worth about $0, or less, because storage costs money (CAP retention rule is from memory, not searched). Proven: commercial biospecimen vendors list remnant FFPE blocks at roughly $150-600 each. Rare subtypes or cases with outcome annotation can reach about $1-3k (my estimate from memory of vendor quotes; no search possible). A single sale of a good case can be 30-100x the cost of handling it. But the value is per unit and is earned through processing and selling, not revalued on a hit. Only a small fraction of any archive is ever sold. Blended across the archive, the step-up is about 10-100x.
hit_rate_capex: The proving step does not mostly fail. Every hospital archive holds thousands of cancer cases. Rare subtypes are a known few percent, and you can find them by reading the pathology reports. Scanning at $5-10 a slide plus about $10-30 a block to retrieve and recut (estimate) is a processing cost, not an exploration bet with a 1-5% hit rate. ML adds little: ML triage would replace a text search of reports that already exist. The 1/base-hit-rate cap is about 2-5x at most, and the real lever is less than that.

name: Material Threat Voucher Hunter: medical countermeasures
one_line_reason: This fails the frame test the same way the geothermal-in-coal-mines idea does: the candidate list is small, public and legible, and the value is created by an expensive, bespoke BLA and GMP effort that ML cannot shrink. The government-capped ladder also limits how big the company can get.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is a $30-150M+ manufacturing and regulatory build (GMP, animal-rule pivotals, human safety), not a cheap abstracted drill. The work is in finishing the package, not finding the asset. On top of that, the outcome is legible in Drugs@FDA, clinicaltrials.gov and USAspending, and the voucher's eligibility may have sunset (565A, Oct 2023).
step_up: Unproven right: $0.1-2M as the candidate states it (my estimate; no sourced comps). Proven right: a priority review voucher has historically sold for roughly $80-160M (SIGA's TPOXX material-threat voucher sold for about $80M in 2020; rare pediatric vouchers sold for about $100-158M in 2023-2025, from memory, not re-verified this run). Add any SNS procurement on top (TPOXX contracts were around $600M over years). So the right goes up about 50-150x on approval, but only after the $10-100M+ proving spend. All-in, that is about 2-8x. The voucher's existence is also a sunset risk: the material-threat voucher under FD&C 565A covered approvals before Oct 1, 2023 unless PAHPA reauthorized it. I could not confirm reauthorization status as of Oct 2026.
hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: the candidate's $10-30M is optimistic. My estimate is $30-150M once you add GMP re-manufacture, pivotal animal studies and a human safety cohort; BARDA-funded animal-rule programs have typically consumed $100M+. Base hit rate: only about 15-20 products have been approved under the Animal Rule since 2002 (from memory). Shelved late-stage programs usually failed for a known scientific, manufacturing or funding reason. My estimate is a 20-40% approval rate from a near-complete package. ML cannot change that much: failure comes from the biology and the manufacturing, not from picking the wrong candidate. And with only tens of candidates, the lever is capped at about 1/0.3, or 3x, and in practice is close to 1x.

name: DMF Orphan Rescue: pairing dormant API DMFs with abandoned 505(b)(2)s
one_line_reason: Pharma's version of geothermal-in-coal-mines: finding the stalled DMF/NDA pair is easy and already in FDA spreadsheets, while rebuilding the supply chain and getting CMC approval is the real, multi-million-dollar, multi-year work. The step-up is roughly 3-10x and competitors already run this.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is CMC and manufacturing execution (tech transfer, stability, FDA supplement review, inspection), not discovery, and the data that would locate targets is already legible in FDA status fields (DMF Active/Inactive, Orange Book discontinued and exclusivity). There is no frame where discovery is 80%+ and no ML hit-rate lever. Incumbents like ANI and Eton already do this deal type.
step_up: The candidate claims ~10-30x and I could not verify any of it, because the web search budget was used up before a single search ran. My estimate: discontinued or never-launched small NDAs change hands for roughly $0.5-5M; a relaunched niche 505(b)(2) with 3-year exclusivity sells or is valued at roughly $10-50M in Eton/Azurity-type deals. Adding $1-5M+ of CMC spend puts the realised step-up on total cost at about 3-10x. That is not 10^3 and not immediate: the value only arrives after FDA approval of the supplement and a launch, 12-24 months later.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate, no source (search budget exhausted). Each proving attempt costs $1-5M+ (tech transfer, batches, stability, PAS filing fee, consultants) and takes 12-24 months. The base failure mode is not a low hit rate on a hidden signal. It is execution risk (CMC deficiencies, complete response letters, a failed inspection) and commercial risk (a small market, or a generic arriving after the 3-year exclusivity ends). ML matching fee lapses to tentative approvals does nothing to lower tech-transfer or stability costs, so the capex lever is close to 1x, not 10x.

name: DormantDossier / UK REACH Dossier Bank: orphaned REACH data ownership
one_line_reason: The asset is a regulated, cost-capped, time-decaying data right whose demand is legible from public lists, so there is no 10^3 step-up and no real discovery lever.
fatal_flaw: REACH data sharing is regulated, so the step-up cannot exist. Art. 27 and Implementing Reg 2016/9 force cost-based, pro-rata pricing. ECHA can grant permission to refer when talks fail. Data older than 12 years can be cited free (Art. 25(3)). And Defra's ATRm aims to remove the UK REACH data demand this plan relies on. An orphaned dossier cannot be repriced from €10k to a monopoly LoA.
step_up: From memory, not verified this run because the search budget was used up: the candidate assumes title costs €5-20k and an LoA sells for £20-200k. But REACH Art. 27 and Reg 2016/9 require 'fair, transparent and non-discriminatory' cost sharing, which means a pro-rata share of the actual study cost plus a capped admin fee. If talks fail, ECHA can grant 'permission to refer' (Art. 27(6)/30(3)). Under Art. 25(3), anyone may cite study summaries submitted 12 or more years ago for free, and most 2010/2013 dossiers are already past that line. So the LoA price is capped by regulation, not by what the market will pay. My estimate of a realistic step-up is about 2-10x on a portfolio that has to be split across many co-registrants, with no 10^3 jump.
hit_rate_capex: There is no proving step that is expensive and mostly fails. 'Proving' is title diligence (roughly €5-30k of legal work per substance, my estimate) plus finding buyers. ECHA's dissemination portal publishes which substances are registered at which tonnage bands, so buyers can already be identified. My estimate of the base hit rate is that buyers exist for maybe 20-40% of acquired dossiers. That caps any ML lever at about 3-5x, and title risk, not discovery, is what decides each deal.

name: Registro Bank: dormant Brazilian pesticide registrations
one_line_reason: Legible registry, sophisticated sellers, a step-up of about 3-10x shrinking under the 2023 law, and no low-hit-rate proving step: brokerage, not Terranox-style discovery.
fatal_flaw: The asset and its status are already written in a legible public registry (AGROFIT/DOU), and the holders know what they own. So nothing is hidden for ML to find, the step-up is only about 3-10x and capped by the cost of a fresh registration, and Law 14.785/2023's roughly 2-year target erodes the queue premium the thesis depends on. This is regulatory arbitrage and brokerage, not discovery.
step_up: From the candidate's own framing, the purchase price is $100-300k and the resale is perhaps $0.5-1.5M. That is roughly 3-10x, on my estimate (unverified; my search budget was used up before any search ran). The ceiling is set by the cost of a fresh registration: dossier, studies and fees, which I estimate at about $0.5-2M, plus the time value of the queue. Law 14.785/2023 sets about 2 years as the statutory target for a decision, which shrinks the queue premium over time. Nothing here goes from near zero to 10^3x. The asset already has a known floor price.
hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive proving step that mostly fails. The 'proving step' is a legal and commercial check plus a signed transfer. My estimate is a hit rate of 30-60% for deals that close once a dormant registro is found and its holder is willing. Cost per attempt is legal diligence of roughly $10-50k (my estimate). A low-hit-rate step where ML would cut capex 10x does not exist. The lever is capped at about 2-3x.

name: QPL Revival: dormant Qualified Products List slots
one_line_reason: The buyer is real but the frame fails. Discovery is a simple lookup in ASSIST QPL, while making and qualifying the product is most of the work. Requalification usually passes, so ML has little to raise. The step-up is roughly 3-10x and comes from operations, not a 10^3x jump on a hit.
fatal_flaw: There is no illegible discovery problem. The ASSIST QPL source counts and DLA notices already say which slots are thin, and the value is realised through mil-spec manufacturing and qualification operations, not through finding something. This is a known PE and TransDigm roll-up play run by informed buyers and informed sellers.
step_up: Estimate only; no deal data was retrieved. A distressed or exiting small mil-spec component maker probably sells for about 0.3-1x revenue, or 3-6x EBITDA. Qualified niche defense component lines go to strategic buyers (Amphenol, TE, TransDigm, HEICO, Arcline-backed platforms) for about 2-5x revenue, or 10-20x EBITDA. On a successful requalification that is roughly a 3-10x step-up. The candidate's claimed 10-50x would only hold if the slot were bought for near zero, which is unlikely when the seller has revenue and inventory. The jump does not come from a proving event like a drill hit. It is earned by restarting production and winning DIBBS awards over quarters to years.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate only; no lab quotes were retrieved. A qualification test lot under a MIL-PRF connector or component spec probably costs $50k-$500k at a contract lab, plus several months of a running compliant line and an audit. If the product is built to the spec's drawings and processes, base pass rates are high, probably 70-90% after one or two iterations, because the spec tells you exactly what to build. At that pass rate the ceiling on any hit-rate lever is 1/0.8, about 1.25x, nowhere near 10x. Little of the cost is a gamble that ML could make cheaper; the cost is production capex and compliance work.

name: Co-op Contract Rollup
one_line_reason: This is a PE roll-up with ML-assisted lead generation, not a discovery play. Value comes from selling and delivering product (about 2-5x through multiple arbitrage and growth), the award itself is non-exclusive and near-worthless, and incumbents already mine the minutes and budgets data.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is sales and fulfilment execution, not discovery. The co-op award is non-exclusive, effectively not assignable, re-bid every few years and close to worthless on its own. Value comes only from selling and delivering product, at operating-business multiples. There is no rung where discovery is 80% or more of the work, no step-up of 10^3 or more, and the demand-signal data is already mined by Starbridge, GovSpend and GovWin.
step_up: No live searches ran (the shared per-turn search budget was used up), so every number here is my estimate from general knowledge. Lower-middle-market vendors with under $1M EBITDA usually sell for about 3-5x EBITDA. Bigger platforms that public-sector PE buys trade at about 8-12x EBITDA. That is roughly 2-3x of multiple arbitrage, plus whatever revenue growth the operator adds. Taking a $0.5M-revenue vendor to $5M of contract revenue is about 10x revenue, but that growth is paid for with sales spend and working capital, not unlocked by one discovery event. The award on its own is worth close to nothing, because it is non-exclusive. Sourcewell, OMNIA and TIPS award several vendors per category, and the award is usually not assignable without the cooperative's consent. So there is no step from $1 to $10,000 at a single moment. The pitched "10-50x" looks inflated; about 2-5x on capital is more realistic.
hit_rate_capex: These are my estimates, not sourced. Many awarded co-op vendors book little or nothing through their contract; I would guess a large share sit near zero. But the cost per attempt here is the cost of buying a company (about $0.5-5M) plus 1-3 years of sales effort, not a cheap drill. ML can make outreach better, but the base rate is limited by product fit, price and incumbent relationships, not by not knowing who needs what. A plausible gain is 1.5-2x sales efficiency, not 10x lower capex.

name: Orphan STC Bank: reviving dead supplemental type certificates
one_line_reason: Discovery is a small share of the work. The STC eligibility data is already legible in FAA DRS. Reviving an STC is mostly engineering and production work, so there is no 10^3x step-up on a match and no 10x hit-rate lever.
fatal_flaw: The value is in the private engineering data package and in production and continued-airworthiness capability, not in the public certificate. Any buyer can also design a new STC for a capped cost. So the ML discovery step is cheap, legible and not the bottleneck, and the certificate does not jump in value on a match.
step_up: My estimate, unverified because the search budget ran out: dormant STCs from defunct holders change hands for roughly $5k-$50k, which matches the candidate's own figure. Live STCs with demand and a complete data package sell as product-line deals, usually $100k to a few $M for niche GA or avionics STCs. Large freighter-conversion STC programs are worth tens of $M or more, but those are not orphaned and their value comes from the conversion capability, not the certificate. That gives a realistic step-up of about 3-30x on hits, not 100-1000x. A step-up only comes once the data package and production capability have been rebuilt, not the moment a match is found.
hit_rate_capex: My estimate, with no sourced figure: the "proving" step is ML matching plus a desk check that the data package is complete. That costs roughly $1k-10k per candidate. There is no expensive, mostly-failing physical test like an exploratory drill. The step that is expensive and fails a lot is rebuilding the package and getting it re-approved, roughly $100k-$1M+ per STC, and ML does not reduce that cost. A cheap screen can't produce a 10x capex reduction, because the screen was never the bottleneck.

name: Slot Futures
one_line_reason: The buyer and the headline price are real (about $75M for a Heathrow pair), but the right is allocated free and only to airlines, and it is proven only by flying for a season under use-it-or-lose-it. Discovery is a tiny share of the work and ML gives no capex lever.
fatal_flaw: Only an air carrier can hold slots, and a slot becomes valuable only after a full season flown at 80% use. The proving step is running an airline, not a cheap, abstracted drill. The outcome (the airport's coordination level) is also already published in the IATA WSG list.
step_up: Unproven: slots at Level 1/2 airports, and new-entrant slots at Level 3 airports, are allocated free under EU Reg 95/93 and IATA WSG. Proven: Heathrow daily slot pairs have sold for about $60-75M (from memory: Oman Air paid about $75M to Air France-KLM in 2016; similar prices since). Gatwick and other congested pairs sell for roughly $1-15M (my estimate). So the paper step-up is very large, on the order of >=10^3x over a near-zero cost basis. But the cost basis is not near zero. It includes a full season of operating losses on the route, which I estimate at $5-30M per daily pair. Net that out and the real step-up is about 1-10x, and only at the very few airports that become Heathrow-like.
hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate on predicting Level 3 designation is fairly high and not where the money is. Designations creep up slowly and are flagged years ahead in master plans, capacity studies and the published WSG list, so ML gives little lift; the lever is capped near 1/base rate, maybe 2-3x (my estimate). The cost of a proving attempt is a season of flying, roughly $5-30M per slot series per airport (my estimate, not sourced). ML does not reduce that cost.

name: Bankruptcy-Estate EV Pack Arbitrage
one_line_reason: Fails the Terranox test: the physical repack/certification step dominates, the hit rate is high and testing cheap so ML has no lever, the step-up is about 2-5x rather than 10^4, and informed liquidators and buyers already price these lots.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is cheap, passes most of the time, and gives a direct answer (a BMS/SOH readout), so ML adds almost nothing. The step-up is only about 2-5x and is capped by falling new LFP prices. Most of the work is physical hazmat handling and repackaging, not discovery.
step_up: About 2-5x at best (my estimate). Unproven lots sell for roughly -$5 to +$15/kWh. LFP has a net disposal cost of about $1-4/kg, and NMC is worth a little for its black mass. Certified second-life packs sell for about $40-100/kWh. That ceiling is being squeezed by new LFP stationary cells at about $50-60/kWh and new containerised BESS at about $100-150/kWh (2025 figures). These numbers are from memory, not checked this run. The candidate's own ~3-10x figure is optimistic. Nowhere near 10^3.
hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is high, not low. Most fleet packs from failed OEMs are young, at roughly 80-95% state of health (SOH), so about 60-80% of a lot is usable (my estimate). Each proving attempt is cheap: a BMS readout or a capacity and impedance test costs about $100-1,000 per pack (my estimate). Formal UL 1974 evaluation costs more, but it is paid once per pack design, not per pack. With a 1/base-hit-rate cap of about 1.3-1.7x, ML cannot cut capex 10x.

name: Relocation Credit Bank: billboard cap-and-replace credits
one_line_reason: The physical step is trivial and there is a capitalised buyer. But the proving step is a cheap legal filing on rights that usually lapse by statute, the outcome sits in legible permit registries, the step-up is ~10-30x at best, and the buyer is a sophisticated oligopoly that already does this.
fatal_flaw: The 'forgotten' rights mostly do not legally exist. Nonconforming sign rights end by statute after discontinuance or abandonment. Live permits already show in legible DOT and city permit status fields. Credits are often tied to the removing operator and cannot be transferred. The only buyers are three majors who already run in-house acquisition and credit-banking teams. So there is no illegible-data edge and no 10^3 step-up.
step_up: Candidate claims ~10-100x ($1-20k forgotten claim to a credit a major would pay for). Estimate only, since no search ran: in big metros a digital-conversion credit or a permitted static location might be worth ~$50k-$500k to a major. A truly dead permit is worth ~$0 because it is legally extinguished, not undervalued. Realistic step-up on the rare hit: ~10-30x, not 10^3. No sourced price for an unproven versus proven credit was found.
hit_rate_capex: Unsourced estimates. Cost per proving attempt is low: ~$2-20k of land-use attorney time plus a filing fee. The base hit rate on 'forgotten' credits is probably low (<10%), because most nonconforming-sign statutes end the right after 6-24 months of discontinuance or abandonment. ML could help triage, but with each attempt already cheap, a 10x capex cut saves little in absolute dollars. The lever is weak.

name: Dormant home health and hospice CON agencies
one_line_reason: This is a regulatory and operational CHOW business with outcomes already listed in public CMS and state status fields. Its step-up is only about 1.5-4x, and the dormancy that would make shells cheap is what voids the right.
fatal_flaw: Dormancy destroys the right. CMS deactivates Medicare billing after 12 months with no claims, the 36-month rule blocks quick flips of home health and hospice enrollments, and many state CONs lapse if unused. So a truly dormant agency has little transferable value. An agency that is still active is listed in legible CMS and state fields and priced by brokers. There is neither a 10^3 step-up nor an ML discovery edge.
step_up: My estimate is about 1.5-4x, not 10^3. In CON states the license is already priced as scarce. The candidate says shells cost $50-300k. Agencies sold to consolidators with real census are valued on EBITDA (roughly 5-12x for home health and hospice, from memory of broker reports by firms like VERTESS and Mertz Taggart). A pure shell with no census sells for a license premium, which I estimate at a few hundred thousand to about $1M in high-barrier CON states. The asset is never near zero: sellers know what a CON is worth, and the candidate's own 10-30x figure looks too high.
hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving attempt. The CHOW either clears or doesn't on a known checklist, which I estimate at more than 70% when the right is still valid. Cost per attempt is legal and consulting fees plus carrying the agency, roughly $50-150k (my estimate). The lever (1/base hit rate) is therefore at most about 1.5x. ML has nothing to raise.

name: Register-Ready: historic tax credit eligibility
one_line_reason: Fails the Terranox test like geothermal-in-coal-mines: the rehab is the work and the source of the credit, eligibility proving is cheap and high-hit-rate and often already a legible SHPO field, and the step-up is under 2x.
fatal_flaw: The HTC is a percentage of rehab spend, not a property of the building, so the value is created by the bespoke physical rehab rather than by discovering eligibility. Proving eligibility is cheap, usually succeeds, and is often already recorded in SHPO inventory fields, so the step-up is about 1.2-2x and ML has no hit-rate lever.
step_up: Candidate's own figure is about 1.2-2x on acquisition price. My estimate, with no fresh source because the search budget was used up: the credit is roughly 20% of rehab spend (plus 10-25% state credits in about 35 states), and its present value after syndication pricing (about $0.85-0.95 per credit dollar) goes mostly to whoever does the rehab. A buyer will pay a premium on the land and shell only up to part of that value. For example, a $1M shell with $5M of QREs carries about $1M of federal credit, with NPV around $0.8M. If the developer captures half of that, the shell goes from $1M to about $1.4M. That is roughly 1.4x, not 10^3-10^4x.
hit_rate_capex: Proving cost, my estimate: a Part 1 for a building inside an already listed district is about $2k-10k of consultant time. An individual National Register nomination is about $5k-25k and takes 6-18 months through the SHPO and state review board. Base hit rate is high, not low: buildings that are candidates for Part 1 are pre-screened with the SHPO, and I believe NPS approves the large majority of Part 1s (estimate over 85-90%, not verified this run). The proving step is cheap and usually succeeds, so ML has nothing to multiply: 1/base hit rate is about 1.1x, nowhere near 10x.

name: Tidefield: geoduck-grade private tidelands
one_line_reason: The bottleneck is permitting, not discovery. The step-up is about 3-10x (my estimate), suitability is already in legible public GIS fields, and the market is small.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is a contested, multi-year shoreline and Corps permit fight, not a discovery problem. Physical suitability is already legible in DOH, eelgrass and bathymetry layers, and growers already know where the good ground is. ML improves the cheap part, while the expensive, failing part (permits and neighbour litigation) is political. This is the same structure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
step_up: My estimates; web search budget was exhausted, so none of this is verified. Unproven private tidelands, often attached to an upland lot, sell or are assessed for very little, roughly $1k-$20k per acre. Growers usually do not buy the land. They lease it, paying the owner a royalty of about 10-20% of harvest or a flat rent. Farmed geoduck grosses roughly $100k-$300k+ per acre over a 5-7 year cycle. So a permitted, leasable parcel is worth roughly $20k-$60k per acre to the owner on a royalty NPV basis. That is about 3-10x over unproven value, not 10^3-10^4. Neighbour litigation can wipe out the uplift.
hit_rate_capex: My estimates, unverified. The proving cost per attempt is about $10-30k for cores and eelgrass delineation, as the candidate says. Add permitting and legal costs of $50k-$300k+ and 1-5 years where a permit is contested; Pierce and Thurston county geoduck SSDPs have repeatedly gone to appeal. The physical suitability hit rate on pre-screened parcels is probably already high, about 30-60%, because substrate, elevation and DOH classification are easy to screen. The low-success part is political or permit risk, and ML cannot raise that. The lever is capped at about 2-3x, not 10x.

name: Concesiona: idle Chilean salmon concessions
one_line_reason: This is regulatory arbitrage on a small, transparent universe of concessions. The outcome sits in INFA status fields, the step-up is about 3-10x, and permits rather than discovery set the value, so it fails C1, C3 and C4.
fatal_flaw: A concession's value comes from regulation and politics (permits, density allowances, ECMPO, the moratorium), not from discovery. Its biological viability is already written into public legible fields (INFA aerobic/anaerobic status, ACS production history) that every major already tracks, across a universe of only about a thousand sites. So there is no illegible signal for ML to extract and no 10^3 step-up.
step_up: No live data; the search budget was exhausted, so these are my estimates. An idle concession of roughly 5-10 ha in Los Lagos or Aysén trades for about US$0.3-2M. A permitted, producing concession with stocking allowance is valued at about US$2-10M in M&A, and much of that value sits in the attached production allowance, not the concession title. My estimate of the step-up is about 3-10x, and only when regulatory and ECMPO risk clears. The candidate's own 5-30x figure looks optimistic. Nothing near 10^3.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate, not sourced. The proving step costs about US$50-200k for an INFA/CPS survey plus a production-project filing, as the candidate states. It does not fail mostly for biological reasons. When it fails, the cause is permitting delay, ECMPO claims, an anaerobic INFA in a saturated ACS, or a density cap. ML cannot change those outcomes. The ML lever is roughly 1-2x, not 10x.

name: AshSeam / AshPond Critical: coal ash ponds traced to REE/Ge/Ga-rich seams
one_line_reason: Grades are widely known and high-hit-rate, and the hard part is processing, not finding. A proven ash pond is worth only a few x more than an unproven one, to a buyer who barely exists.
fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Ash REE grades are low, well-mapped and mostly above threshold already, and the value depends on unproven, capex-heavy extraction. So no capitalised buyer pays a step-up for a proven assay. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example again.
step_up: There is no observed market price for a proven ash right, so these are my estimates. Unproven: ash in place, worth roughly -$10 to -$40/t to the utility (its closure cost). Separately, well-characterised fly ash that can be harvested sells to cement at about $30-60/t (estimate; there is a fly-ash shortage). Proven REE-grade ash: total REE of about 300-600 ppm (Taggart et al. 2016, Duke: Appalachian average ~591 mg/kg, Illinois ~403, PRB ~337) works out to about $20-100/t of contained oxide at basket prices (estimate). Recoverable value is maybe 30-60% of that after leach yield. So a hit moves the right from roughly -$20/t to maybe +$10-40/t of net value, and only if a processor exists to take it. That is a 2-5x swing in dollars, not 10^3. The ">10^3 on a near-zero basis" in the pitch is an artefact of dividing by zero, not a price anyone pays.
hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is high, not low. Most Appalachian and Illinois Basin ash already beats DOE's 300 ppm REE screening threshold (Taggart et al. 2016, from memory), and you can largely predict it from basin and seam using COALQUAL alone. Cost per proving attempt is $20-300k per pond (the candidate's figure; my estimate is $20-80k for coring plus ICP-MS, with leach tests at the high end). That is cheap next to the processing capex, which is likely $100M+ per plant (estimate). If the hit rate is about 50-70%, the ML lever is capped at about 1.5-2x, nowhere near 10x. Ge and Ga hits are rarer in US coals, so the lever there is bigger, but the deposits are also much smaller. Note: the search budget ran out before any search returned, so the numbers here come from memory of published literature, not fresh searches.

name: RadiumRescue: legacy Ra-226 as Ac-225 feedstock
one_line_reason: The value is made in licensed recovery and purification, not in discovery. The holdings are already legible in licence records and collected free by government programmes, and the finite gram-scale pool does not support a compounding Terranox-style rung.
fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Legacy radium is already recorded in licence files and is actively collected for free by OSRP/SCATR and the IAEA initiative. The value comes from licensed recovery chemistry and purification, which are hard, bespoke physical steps (the coal-mine-geothermal pattern). And the total feedstock pool is tiny and finite.
step_up: Unproven: zero or negative basis. Holders pay for disposal; my estimate is $10k-$50k+ per source for licensed disposal, and OSRP/CRCPD SCATR pick up for free or subsidised. Proven: a few mg of purified Ra-226 target material. Producers do value it highly, but I could not verify a price (search budget exhausted). My estimate is low thousands to tens of thousands of dollars per mg once purified, and much less as raw sealed sources that still need recovery chemistry. Going from a negative basis to positive is a large multiple on paper. But most of that value is created by the recovery and purification work, not by discovery, so I scored it 3.
hit_rate_capex: I could not verify numbers; web search was unavailable (the shared budget was used up) and all figures below are my estimates. Finding licensed radium is not a low-hit-rate step. Holders are licensees whose possession is already recorded. Base hit rate per inspected record is probably high (>30%, estimate). Cost per attempt is a records review plus a site visit and a gamma survey, likely $1k-$10k (estimate). Because 1/base hit rate is small, ML can cut capex by about 2-3x at most, not 10x. The expensive failure mode is chemistry and regulation, and ML does not touch that.

name: Stranded Enriched Isotopes
one_line_reason: Cheap assay, owners who already know what they have, GMP buyers who refuse material without documented history, and gram-scale finite supply: there is no 10^3x hidden step-up and no 10x hit-rate lever.
fatal_flaw: The supply is finite and small, owners know what they hold (labelled vials with NIDC certificates, often DOE-leased), and the high-value buyers need GMP provenance that recovered vials cannot provide. Discovery is neither hard nor where the value sits. The real constraints are title, chain of custody and quantity, and ML does not move those.
step_up: Estimates; no source pulled because the web search budget was used up. Proven enriched material at list price: Ni-64 roughly $20-50k/g; Yb-176 (high enrichment) roughly $10-30k/g; Ca-48 roughly $100-250k/g; Mo-100 roughly $1-3k/g; Ge-76 roughly $50-100/g at kg scale. The unproven vial is not really near zero, though. Most of this material came from DOE/NIDC with a certificate of analysis and a label, and the institution holding it knows what it is or can find out cheaply. Ungraded material sold for non-GMP research would likely fetch 20-50% of list. So the real step-up is about 3-10x over what a knowing owner would accept, not 10^3x. A 10^2-10^3x step only appears for vials that are truly unidentified and that the owner would otherwise pay to dispose of, which is a rare subset.
hit_rate_capex: Estimates; not verified by search. One proving attempt (outsourced ICP-MS or MC-ICP-MS isotope ratio) costs about $100-1,000 per sample, while the material is worth $10k+ per gram. The proving step is cheap, not expensive and mostly failing. Most of the cost is outreach and acquisition (legal and EHS transfer, shipping hazmat or controlled items), and ML does not shrink that. The base hit rate on vials you actually locate is probably high (they mostly turn out to be the isotope the label says). So the lever, capped at 1/hit-rate, is about 1-2x, not 10x.

name: Restart Option Co: shut reactors in early decommissioning
one_line_reason: This fails the same way geothermal-in-coal-mines does: finding the 3 restartable reactors is trivial and already done by incumbents, and restarting them takes $1.5-2B of physical and licensing work, so there is no 95%-discovery rung to win.
fatal_flaw: No illegible-discovery frame exists. The candidate set is about 3-5 plants, already identified and mostly captured by Holtec, Constellation and NextEra. Restartability is written into NRC decommissioning filings (component removal status). The real proving step is a $1.5-2B licensing and refurbishment effort, not a records analysis. ML adds no hit-rate lever and buys no right at a discount.
step_up: From memory, because no searches were available: Holtec bought Palisades in 2022 for a nominal price, with the plant valued near zero or negative once the roughly $550M decommissioning trust was netted against liabilities. Restarting it took about $2B, backed by a $1.52B DOE loan plus state and USDA money. Crane/TMI-1 cost Constellation about $1.6B to restart, backed by Microsoft's 20-year PPA and a roughly $1B DOE loan (2025). Duane Arnold is being restarted by NextEra with a Google PPA (announced Oct 2025, target around 2029). A restarted ~800 MWe unit with a hyperscaler PPA is plausibly worth $2-5B in equity value (estimate). Going from about $0 net to billions is a large multiple on paper (more than 100x), but only after $1.5-2B of physical capex. The step-up is not immediate when a record review comes back positive.
hit_rate_capex: From memory and estimates; the search budget was exhausted. There are about 3 viable candidates (Palisades, Crane, Duane Arnold) and all three are already taken by Holtec, Constellation and NextEra. Nearly every other shut US unit (Indian Point, Pilgrim, Vermont Yankee, Oyster Creek, SONGS, Fort Calhoun, Kewaunee, Zion, Crystal River) is in active DECON. Their reactor vessels and internals are segmented, or their licenses are effectively surrendered, so the remaining hit rate is near 0. A proving attempt (engineering condition assessment plus NRC pre-application) costs perhaps $5-30M (estimate). No large population of mostly-failing shots exists for ML to improve, so the lever is about 1x.

name: Starter Rights: phage-resistant wild fermentation microbes
one_line_reason: Cheap rights and an oligopoly buyer exist. But the buyer can manufacture phage resistance itself, buys strains in bulk for tens of thousands of euros each at most, and wet-lab work plus technological-fit validation dominate the rung, so the step-up is about 10x, not 10^4.
fatal_flaw: Phage resistance is not a scarce trait you have to find. Incumbents routinely create it from their own strains by selecting BIMs and CRISPR-immunising them with phage (Danisco/IFF's own invention), and they buy whole strain collections for well under ~EUR 24k per strain (Valio: EUR 73M for 3,000+ cultures plus a plant). So a proven wild strain gets no 10^3-10^4 step-up and the discovery lever is small.
step_up: The claimed $5k right to a $5-50M licence is not supported by any public deal. Real benchmark: Chr. Hansen paid EUR 73M for Valio's culture business in 2016. That included more than 3,000 dairy cultures, LGG probiotic IP and a manufacturing plant, so it works out to under ~EUR 24k per strain even before taking out the plant and LGG. The DIAL strain collection was also bought in bulk (price not disclosed). No disclosed licence for a single phage-resistant wild strain was found. My estimate for a proven, distinctive strain is $50k-$1M in one-off or royalty value, about 10-100x on a $5k right, and most proven strains would be worth less, nearer 3-10x.
hit_rate_capex: Proving cost per strain is my estimate: about $5-30k for isolation, WGS, a phage panel and bench fermentation, before scale-up. The base hit rate for the phage-resistance trait itself is not low. Incumbents create phage-resistant strains on demand: they challenge their own strains with phage and select BIMs that gain CRISPR spacers, the routine Danisco/Barrangou method, with one new spacer being the most common outcome (Deveau/Barrangou 2008, 30 BIMs analysed). So a resistant strain is not rare and has no big discovery premium. The real bottleneck is technological fit plus a novel phage-resistance mechanism, and nobody has published a base rate for that. Because resistance can be made in-house, the ML lever is well under 10x (my estimate: ~2x).

name: Orphan PVP Certificate Roll-up
one_line_reason: A patent-troll economy on a weak right: proving by genotype is already cheap, the value only shows up through costly litigation, and certificates show a ~2% premium and expire into free USDA access.
fatal_flaw: US PVP certificates are weak, time-limited rights: the breeders' exemption allows derivative breeding, US case law on essentially derived varieties is thin, and certificates expire into free public access. Majors protect valuable germplasm with utility patents and trade secrets instead. So a 'proven' certificate is a speculative lawsuit, not an asset re-priced by a capitalised buyer, and the expensive step is litigation, which ML does not shrink.
step_up: No market prices found for PVP certificates. The best data point: Cornell hedonic study puts the price premium from a PVP certificate on NY soybean seed at about 2.3% (0.7 cents/lb), which says certificates carry little standalone value. The one big US germplasm award (Pioneer v. Holden, $46.7M, 1993-94) was won on trade secret law, not PVP or essential derivation. A certificate bought for $10-100k (candidate's estimate) that turns into a rare settlement might reach 10-30x. That is a litigation lottery, not an immediate market re-pricing. Typical outcome is about 1x or less, because the clock keeps running down the 20-year term.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: unknown; my estimate is well under 1% of orphan certificates protecting germplasm a major uses in a way that infringes. The candidate's $5-20k per variety proving cost is inflated: a SNP chip genotype costs about $20-100 per sample (my estimate). Proving is already cheap, so ML has little capex to cut. The real cost is litigation, roughly $1-5M per case (my estimate), and ML does not reduce that. Lever about 1-2x, not 10x.

name: Bud-Sport Hunter: orchard mutation discovery
one_line_reason: Low score: proving and commercialising the sport dominates the work, the payoff is small and slow, the lever is weak because attempts are already cheap, the public data is too coarse and rights in club varieties go to the licensor, so it fails C1, C3 and C4.
fatal_flaw: Finding the limb is not the bottleneck. Proving it takes years of grafting, trials and nursery commercialisation, the payoff is small and slow (tens of $k to low $M per sport), and growers can already see colour sports by eye. Public imagery cannot resolve limbs, and sports in club varieties belong to the licensor.
step_up: Unproven: a $1-5k blanket fee per orchard (the candidate's figure), and the limb itself is worth about $0. Proven: no finder payment is disclosed for any sport. The ceiling benchmark is Honeycrisp, the most successful US apple ever, which earned the University of Minnesota a total of more than $8M, mostly at $1.30 per tree over its patent life (Good Fruit Grower). A typical red sport probably earns a few $10k-$100k's in royalties spread over a decade (my estimate). Per hit that is roughly 10-100x on the orchard fee, paid slowly over years, not immediately. The claimed 10^3-10^4 is not supported.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: no source found. My estimate is that most observed sports are chimeras, unstable or not better than existing strains, so perhaps 1-10% have any commercial value. Cost per attempt: grafting plus trial rows costs about $1-10k over 3 years (my estimate). Because each attempt is already cheap, a 10x hit-rate gain saves little capex. The binding constraints are time and market demand, not capex. The lever is weak.

name: Wild Hop and Crop-Relative Flavour Discovery
one_line_reason: This is a geothermal-in-coal-mines analogue. Finding the plant is easy and already done by incumbents; turning it into a commercial variety takes a decade of agronomy, the wild genotype cannot be patented, and the market is tiny.
fatal_flaw: The physical step dominates: a wild chemotype is worth little until 7-15 years of breeding and agronomic trials (Citra took 18 years from cross to release), and plants found in the wild cannot get a US plant patent, so the cheap landowner right protects nothing. On top of that the market is about $600M a year.
step_up: Unproven: collection agreement about $1-10k (candidate's estimate). There is no observable market for a "proven wild chemotype." What merchants pay for is a commercial variety. Citra reached about 12k acres and 18.4M lb in 2021, and brewers paid about $16/lb for it. But Citra took 18 years from cross to release (1990 to 2008), and royalties are not public. A GC-MS plus pilot-brew result alone might sell as a germplasm license for roughly $20-200k (my estimate), about 10-50x. It is not an immediate 10^3-10^4 jump. The big value only arrives after 7-15 years of breeding and agronomy, which is the developer's work, not discovery.
hit_rate_capex: Proving cost is about $20-50k per candidate (candidate's estimate). GC-MS itself costs a few hundred dollars per sample. Breeding funnels discard 80-90% of seedlings in year one and keep only an elite line by year ten (Crafty Pint, The Breeder). So the failure rate is high, but the bottleneck is agronomic performance and brewer acceptance, which herbarium and imagery data cannot predict. ML could help pick where to collect a novel chemotype, but sampling is already cheap, so cutting capex 10x saves little money in absolute terms.

name: Venom Vault: peptide leads from private venomous-animal collections
one_line_reason: Fails C1 and C4: the proving step is slow, costly bespoke pharmacology (the coal-mine-geothermal failure mode), the signal lives in already-curated, target-annotated public databases that thousands of academic labs actively mine, and no exclusive right over a venom peptide can be bought from anyone, so there is no near-zero asset whose step-up the company can capture.
fatal_flaw: There is no ownable, cheaply-purchasable unproven right. A breeder cannot sell you exclusivity over a peptide sequence, published toxins are unowned, and the only ownable thing (a composition-of-matter patent on a novel analogue) exists only AFTER you have done the expensive med-chem and in vivo work. So the company cannot buy an asset for ~$0 and realise a step-up on a hit — it has to fund the whole hard, downstream, non-discovery part, where all the actual attrition lives (selectivity and PK, not finding the toxin). Discovery is roughly 10-20% of this rung, not 80%+.
step_up: Unproven side: a venom/tissue access and benefit-sharing contract with a breeder is worth roughly $1k-50k/yr (animal husbandry and sample-collection scale; my estimate — no public comparables found), and crucially is non-exclusive over the molecule: the peptide sequence is not the breeder's property. Proven side: $10-20M upfront for a validated preclinical ion-channel asset (Astellas/Chromocell $15M upfront on CC8464, >$515M biobucks). That looks like 10^2-10^3x, but the denominator is wrong — the step-up is not paid for the right, it is paid for the $0.5-2M+ of synthesis/panel/in vivo work plus 2-4 years of med-chem, and the historical analogue deals for pure venom libraries were small screening-access deals with undisclosed, modest upfronts (Xenome/MedImmune 2009, >2,000 venom-derived peptides, terms confidential). Scoring C2 as 3-10x on the right itself, because the right carries almost none of the value.
hit_rate_capex: Proving step cost: peptide synthesis $1-3k/analogue, contracted ion-channel panel ~$5-20k, mouse PK/efficacy $100-500k, so $0.5-2M per serious candidate as the candidate states (consistent with CRO list pricing; my estimate for the panel line). Base rate: venom peptide programmes that reach a licensed clinical asset are vanishingly rare — of the ~20 venom-derived drugs ever approved versus tens of thousands of characterised toxins, and of the Nav1.7 field specifically, every spider-toxin programme (GpTx-1, Pn3a, ProTx-II, Amgen/Genentech/Janssen efforts) has failed on selectivity or PK, not on discovery. So the hit rate is low, which superficially suggests a big ML lever, but the failures are NOT discovery failures — they are selectivity/PK/clinical-translation failures that ML over transcriptomes does not touch. The lever is capped by where the attrition sits, and it sits downstream. 2024 Advanced Science work on hNav1.7 spider peptides states development "has been impeded by limited selectivity," i.e. the bottleneck is engineering, not finding.

name: Hoard Lease: UK/EU farmland detecting rights ranked by LiDAR and find-spot ML
one_line_reason: Discovery-heavy and physically trivial, but the proven "asset" is a set of loose objects. They are sold mostly to museums with tight budgets out of a roughly £1M/yr reward pool, the landowner takes about 50%, the data is already legible and used by hobbyists, and there is no ladder.
fatal_flaw: There is no asset to step up and no capitalised buyer. Each hit is a one-time pull of objects from a shared, tiny pool: about £0.6-1M a year in Treasure rewards, with a £270 median find, and half goes to the landowner. Thousands of free hobbyists already search with the same LiDAR and PAS data, and heritage law and ethics constrain targeting known sites.
step_up: Unproven: a search agreement, typically free or a share of finds; the candidate's estimate is £100-1k per field. Proven, typical case: the median treasure valuation was £270 and the mean £2,671, across 241 valued cases totalling £643,683 (2016 data, Sunday Telegraph 2018). The mean is driven by rare outliers, such as the £325k Leekfrith torcs. The proceeds are also split: landowner and finder take 50:50 of any Treasure reward (Code of Practice), and the landowner owns non-Treasure finds outright in England and Wales (NCMD suggests 50/50 above £500). So the typical step-up is under 3-10x. Only a rare hoard reaches 10^2-10^3x, and that happens to a few cases a year.
hit_rate_capex: Base rate: in 2023 the public recorded 74,506 finds, of which 1,358 were Treasure cases; 2024 had 1,540, the record (PAS Annual Report 2023; British Museum). Tens of thousands of detectorists produced those, which means far below one hoard per field-season (my estimate). Cost per attempt: about £100-500 per field-day (my estimate; hobbyists do it unpaid). Attempts are already almost free, so there is no 10x discovery capex for ML to cut. ML could only shorten the search time, and the total payout pool is too small for that to matter.

name: Chassis Ledger: lost works race cars proven from period records
one_line_reason: Rare ~10x hits (Cunningham Corvette: $75k to $785k) on a finite, already-catalogued set of chassis numbers. Bespoke restoration and provenance politics dominate, so there is no 95/5 discovery frame and no 10^4 jump.
fatal_flaw: The answer is already in a legible field. Chassis/VIN numbers of works and race cars are tracked by registries, factory archives and named historians, so discovery is mostly a lookup, not ML. Meanwhile the physical step (correct restoration, authentication politics, title fights) is bespoke and expensive, and the step-up is about 10x, not 10^4. It has the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
step_up: Best documented case: the #1 1960 Briggs Cunningham Le Mans Corvette (chassis 00867S103535). Bought for $75,000 in 2012 and sold at RM Sotheby's Amelia Island for $785,500, about 10x before restoration and legal costs (Motor Authority). The Bonhams 2016 C-Type (EUR 7.2M) was a re-identification inside an already-known works car, so it was not a near-zero start. Typical step-up is about 3-10x on a running car worth $30-150k. It reaches 10-100x only for a bare chassis that proves out, which is rarer still. Nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is very low: probably well under 1 in 100 'unknown history' cars of the right marque are actually works or famous-race chassis (my estimate). The universe is tiny, a few thousand works chassis across all marques. Most of them are already located, and their numbers are tracked by registries and historians: Massini reportedly knows the histories of 20,000+ Enzo-era Ferraris, and Cunningham historian Lawrence Berman kept the Corvette's VIN on file for years. Each proving attempt costs the purchase of the car itself ($30-150k), not a cheap drill. So ML cannot cut capex much. You still have to own each car to test it, and the screen for 'is this number a known works number' is a lookup, not ML. The lever is far below 10x on capex. In practice it is a lookup-table edge, which is the same failure as the earlier grid-queue candidate.

name: Successor Shares / Certificate Chain: old certificates that still convert
one_line_reason: Inside the rung, discovery is most of the work. But buying the paper does not transfer the shares, fee caps keep most of the step-up from the buyer, and the lineage answer already sits in purpose-built obsolete-securities manuals sold for about $50, so neither the ML edge nor the step-up comes through.
fatal_flaw: The right cannot be bought. Owning a physical certificate does not confer the shares without the registered owner's endorsement and a medallion guarantee, escheated value goes to owners or heirs, and buying assignments from heirs is statutorily capped at 10-20% finder fees. The outcome is also already sold as a $49.95 lookup by the Fisher/Smythe successor service.
step_up: Unproven: collector paper at about $5-50 (the candidate's figure; cancelled scripophily typically sells for $5-50). Proven: whatever the successor shares are worth, which on the rare hits is likely $100s-$10,000s (my estimate), so up to roughly 100-1000x per hit. But most collector-market certificates are cancelled (punched or stamped) and redeem for $0. Expected value across the pool is about 2-10x at best (my estimate). No source gives a distribution of redemption values.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is about 1-3%, which is the candidate's own unsourced estimate; I found no published figure. Cost per proving attempt is already tiny: Scripophily.com / RM Smythe's Old Company Research Service traces lineage for $49.95 per company (earlier $39.95, no charge if nothing is found). Replacement or transfer via Computershare costs about $50 plus a 2% surety bond (Ford and Marathon FAQs). ML can cut a cost that is already about $50, so the capex lever is small in absolute dollars. There are no expensive failing shots like a $500k drill hole.

name: LatencyLine: low-latency microwave geodesic waypoints
one_line_reason: This fails the frame test. Discovery is a minority of the work, a single waypoint is not a sellable asset, the outcome is already legible in FCC ULS, the buyers are a few in-house HFT teams, and the hyperscaler demand is not real.
fatal_flaw: A waypoint has no standalone value. Value only appears when a complete end-to-end path is assembled and operated, which makes this a bespoke network build, not a discovery problem. On top of that, every existing path is already published in FCC ULS, and the handful of buyers do this routing in-house.
step_up: No live numbers: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran (0 of 5 searches returned), so all figures are from memory or estimates. A commercial tower-space or rooftop lease runs about $1-3k per month per antenna position (industry norm, estimate). The proven-path value sits at the network level, not the waypoint level. Spread Networks spent about $300M on Chicago-NJ fiber (2010) and was sold to Zayo in 2017 for about $127M (reported, from memory). Microwave networks reportedly cost tens of millions per route. Per waypoint, a key choke-point site might get a 3-10x premium over a normal tower lease, and only if it is truly unique and on the geodesic. That is nowhere near 10^3. The ~10^2-10^3x claim in the pitch is not supported.
hit_rate_capex: The proving step is LOS and path engineering: desktop analysis with Pathloss or similar tools on lidar/DSM data, then a path survey costing about $5-20k per hop (estimate). Success is high once a candidate site exists, plausibly over 50% (estimate). That caps the ML lever at about 2x, not 10x. The expensive failures come from landlord holdouts, zoning denials and frequency conflicts, and ML does not fix those.

name: Dirtwave: AM tower-farm land arbitrage
one_line_reason: This is ordinary real-estate entitlement arbitrage with data that is easy to read. The work is in getting the land rezoned, not in finding it, so ML adds little and owners already know what the land is worth.
fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Tower land is legible in assessor and FCC records, and both owners and brokers already price it. The step-up comes from rezoning and moving the signal, which are bespoke, political, multi-year and the same for everyone. That makes it a geothermal-in-coal-mines case: execution, not finding, holds the value, so ML has no 10x lever.
step_up: From memory, not verified this run (search budget exhausted): Cumulus sold the roughly 75-acre WMAL tower site in Bethesda to Toll Brothers for about $74.1M, around $1M per acre. In that case the owner, a large group, captured the value itself. Small AM stations trade for about $50k-$500k (my estimate from typical small-market AM sales). But a seller who owns fee land usually prices it, or a broker values the real estate separately. The realistic step-up from the station price to the price of entitled land is about 3-30x, and most of it comes from the rezoning, not from discovery. On the cost basis of the land alone the step-up is often only 2-5x, because the seller knows the land is worth more than the radio business.
hit_rate_capex: I found no measured base hit rate; these are my estimates. Screening is cheap: ML or GIS joins of FCC antenna records to county parcels cost a few thousand dollars per region. The expensive, mostly-failing step is entitlement, at roughly $100k-$1M+ per attempt in legal, engineering, FCC work and carrying cost over 1-4 years. Entitlement success depends on local politics, not on information, so ML barely moves the hit rate. The capex lever is maybe 1.2-1.5x, not 10x.

name: MoveIn / AM Move-In: broadcast allocation-chain solver
one_line_reason: This is legible-data spectrum arbitrage in a declining industry: incumbent engineers already run the search, Rural Radio rules block most move-ins, the step-up is about 3-20x rather than 10^4, and there is no real ladder.
fatal_flaw: The data is fully legible and 30 years of consulting engineers and brokers have already mined the combinatorial space, so ML adds little. The 2011 Rural Radio Order and the collapse in radio values cap the step-up at about 3-20x. And the costly, mostly failing step is a contested FCC proceeding that ML cannot speed up.
step_up: Estimates, not sourced; the web search budget ran out before any search returned. Unproven rural FM: $25k-300k (the candidate's own range, consistent with rural station trades). Proven rim/metro-reaching FM: perhaps $0.5M-5M in mid and large markets today, against $10M-50M+ before 2008. Historical move-ins in the 1990s and 2000s did reach about 10-100x. In the post-2011 Rural Radio regime, with metro FM values down roughly 70-90% since 2006 (my estimate), a realistic hit is about 3-20x. Also, a rim-shot signal from a Class A/C3 often reaches only the edge of a metro, and that sells at a discount to a full-market stick.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate (unsourced). The search step is cheap: a consulting-engineer allocation study costs about $5k-50k, and software like V-Soft Probe/ComStudy runs spacing studies in minutes. The expensive part is FCC and legal prosecution: about $50k-250k per contested rulemaking plus reimbursement of other stations' costs. Hit rate is not set by discovery. It is set by legal feasibility (Rural Radio presumption, last-local-service rules) and by competitors' counterproposals. Most good chains in the dense eastern US were mined out in the 1990s and 2000s. ML does not raise the success rate of the costly step (the FCC decision), so the capex lever is maybe 1.5-2x, not 10x.

name: HopGraph: FM translator relocation chains
one_line_reason: This is regulatory arbitrage on fully legible FCC data, already worked by consulting engineers and brokers, with an estimated 10-50x step-up into a declining industry and a short ladder.
fatal_flaw: The signal is not hidden. Translator facilities and grant outcomes are structured FCC LMS fields, and the routing is deterministic contour math that broadcast consulting engineers and brokers already run. So there is no ML discovery edge, and the step-up sits in a shrinking, low-capital AM radio market with FCC limits on serial hopping.
step_up: From memory, no searches ran. Rural or unbuilt translators trade around $5-30k. Translators that put a signal into a metro market traded around $100k-$500k+ in the 2016-2018 AM-revitalization windows, and some top-market ones were reported higher. That is roughly 10-50x at the peak, and less since then because AM is shrinking and many AMs already got translators in the 2016-2018 windows. Score 2: it sits nearer the low end now, and the multi-month path to proving it dilutes the jump.
hit_rate_capex: From my own knowledge; I could not verify. A proving attempt costs about $3-10k in consulting-engineer fees plus FCC filing per hop (my estimate). Whether a given chain works is mostly predictable with standard FCC contour and interference tools (the 60 dBu contour-overlap test for a minor change, plus spacing and contour-protection rules).
