Base hit rate for an engineered filing is high, maybe 50%+ (my estimate). Failures come from petitions to deny, interference complaints and FCC hop restrictions, not from failing to discover a path. ML cannot gain much when the base rate is already high: the lever is capped near 2x, not 10x.

name: Dormant MSS Spectrum Roll-up for direct-to-device
one_line_reason: Charlie Ergen already ran this play (about $2.8B to $17B over 13 years). The value comes from lobbying over fully legible public licences, so it fails C1, C3 and C4 for the same reason geothermal-in-coal-mines does.
fatal_flaw: There is nothing to discover. The few dozen MSS licences are fully legible and already watched by every strategic buyer and spectrum analyst. Value is created by winning FCC/political fights over terrestrial and D2D authority (Ligado shows this can fail even after an FCC win), not by reading illegible data. ML gives no hit-rate lever, and the step-up is about 6x over a decade (EchoStar), not 10^4.
step_up: From memory, because the shared web search budget was exhausted before any query ran. The best precedent is EchoStar, which already ran this exact play. In 2012 it bought bankrupt DBSD (~$1.4B) and TerreStar (~$1.38B), about $2.8B for 2 GHz MSS. The FCC then granted AWS-4 terrestrial rights in 2012, and SpaceX paid ~$17B in Sept 2025 (half cash, half stock) for AWS-4 plus H-block. That is roughly 6x over 13 years, with H-block and buildout capital added. Ligado (L-band) is a negative precedent: it went bankrupt in Jan 2025 after the 2020 FCC terrestrial approval was fought by DoD/GPS. AST's L-band arrangement in Ligado's bankruptcy was in the hundreds of millions, not a 10^3 jump. Realistic step-up is 3-10x, which scores 2.
hit_rate_capex: This is my estimate, not sourced, because searches were unavailable. One proving attempt is a multi-year FCC rulemaking or licence modification costing about $10-50M in legal, engineering and lobbying, plus the licence purchase (hundreds of millions to billions). Success depends on politics and incumbent opposition (Ligado lost to DoD despite winning the FCC order), not on hidden information. Only about 2-5 meaningful attempts have happened in 15 years. ML does not raise the hit rate of a political process, so the lever is about 1x.

name: Teleport Siting: ground-station-ready land plus earth station licence
one_line_reason: This is commodity site acquisition, not discovery. The hit rate is high, the data is already legible, the licence is tied to the operator and cannot be transferred, and the step-up is about 3-10x, so it fails C3 and C4 outright.
fatal_flaw: There is no rare discovery. Suitable gateway land is abundant, siting rarely fails, and the data is already structured and used routinely by incumbent RF coordinators. On top of that, the FCC licence depends on the operator's own system, so it cannot be built up in advance and sold. There is no low hit rate for ML to improve and no 10^3 step-up to capture: proving earns a 3-10x lease premium on cheap farmland.
step_up: No web searches ran (the shared search budget was used up), so every figure here is my estimate from prior knowledge. Unproven: US cropland is roughly $4-6k/acre (USDA land values, about $5.5k/acre cropland in 2024), so a 2-10 acre gateway parcel is about $10-60k. Proven: Starlink and Kuiper gateway leases are reported in local news at around $10-30k a year for a few acres. Capitalised at 8-10%, that is a lease worth about $100-400k, or roughly 3-10x the farmland value, and at most about 30x at the extreme. That is far below the candidate's claimed 30-300x. The uplift is a premium on a ground lease, not a jump from near zero.
hit_rate_capex: No searches ran, so these are estimates. Base hit rate: high. Most flat, RF-quiet rural parcels near fiber are workable, and Starlink alone has licensed roughly 100+ US gateway sites with little sign of siting failure. Cost per proving attempt: desk siting costs a few thousand dollars. A Comsearch-type frequency coordination is roughly $5-20k (estimate). The FCC earth station filing fee is a few thousand dollars (FCC fee schedule, from memory). If the hit rate is around 70-90%, the most ML could improve it is about 1.1-1.4x, not 10x. Proving is cheap and rarely fails, so there is almost no capex to cut.

name: Lazarus Orbital: salvage title to insured-loss satellites
one_line_reason: Discovery is a small slice of the work, the servicing capex dominates, the owner and insurer hold better data, and recoverability is already known. The frame fails C1 and C4.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is a physical docking or rescue mission costing tens of $M, not an information problem. The few recoverable failures are already known to the owner and insurer from private telemetry. ML over public TLE and photometry data neither cuts the dominant cost nor finds hidden value. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure: the bespoke fix is far harder than finding the right satellite.
step_up: Unproven: insurer-held salvage title to a written-off satellite. My estimate is roughly $0 to low single-digit $M; there is no public market price. Precedent from memory: AsiaSat 3 (1997, stranded in GTO, about $200M+ insured loss) was bought back by Hughes from underwriters and rescued with lunar flybys as HGS-1, under a profit-sharing deal with insurers, not a cash price. Proven: a revived GEO satellite under lease. My estimate is $10-50M/yr of capacity revenue, less after the servicing fee (MEV-1/Intelsat 901 was reported at about $13M/yr, from memory). The step-up on title is nominally over 1000x, but it only arrives after servicing capex of tens of $M. ML ranking alone gives no immediate step-up. Net multiple on all-in capital is about 1-3x.
hit_rate_capex: I could not verify any of these numbers. The web search budget was used up, so all figures are from memory or my own estimates. The failure mode of a written-off satellite is mostly already known; the open question is whether it can be fixed. Most insured losses (power, payload, deployment or anomaly failures) cannot be fixed by docking. The fixable class, wrong orbit or propulsion/fuel failures, I estimate at 10-20% of losses. Insurers and manufacturers already identify that class from their own telemetry. Cost per proving attempt is a servicer mission: MEV build and launch is reportedly $100M+ per vehicle, or $10-15M/yr per lease (estimate). ML does not cut the expensive step, so the lever is close to 1x.

name: GhostPlat / LotRecord: assembling antiquated paper subdivisions
one_line_reason: The hard part is assembly and holdout clearing, not discovery. Ownership is already in legible tax-roll fields, and the assembled step-up is roughly 1-3x per acre, not 10^3.
fatal_flaw: The rung is mostly assembly, not discovery. Turning a fragmented paper subdivision into a sellable tract is bottlenecked by holdout negotiation, quiet-title and curative work, and county vacation/replat process. ML cannot abstract that away, which is the coal-mine-geothermal counter-example. Ownership is already in legible tax-roll fields that land flippers use, and assembled per-acre value often does not exceed fragmented per-acre retail lot value, so there is no 10^3-10^4 step-up.
step_up: I could not verify these numbers this run because the shared web search budget was used up. They are estimates from prior knowledge and are unsourced. Deming NM and Rio Rancho-area paper lots trade at about $1-5k per 0.25-1 acre lot on eBay and land-flipper sites, which is roughly $2-10k/acre. Assembled raw desert acreage for solar in NM/AZ sells for about $1-10k/acre, or leases for about $300-1,000/acre/yr. Retail fragmentation means per-acre lot prices are often equal to or higher than assembled acreage prices, so the real step-up is about 1-3x, not 10-300x. Lehigh Acres and Golden Gate Estates lots (about $10-40k per quarter acre in Lehigh, $50-150k per Golden Gate tract, my estimate) are already individually buildable and priced by the retail market, so there is little assembly premium there either. The 10-300x only appears if you buy tax-deed scraps at about $50-500 and somehow realise acreage value, and that happens on single lots, not on assembled tracts.
hit_rate_capex: These are estimates only, not verified this run. There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving shot like a drill hole. The failure mode is assembly failure: one holdout or one unclearable title blocks the tract. My estimate is that assembling about 100-500 lots costs about $500k-$5M in acquisition plus legal and curative costs, plus 2-5 years. The chance of full assembly is probably 10-30%, and it is driven by human holdouts, not by information. ML can rank which subdivisions have the fewest owners or the most tax-delinquent owners. That is a lift of maybe 1.5-2x, not 10x, because the binding constraint is negotiation and legal process, not knowing who owns what.

name: TDR Mint / Flood Sending-Zone TDR Harvester
one_line_reason: TDR credits are allocated by a public formula and recorded in registries, the land is priced with the credit value in it, the step-up is about 1-3x, the proving step mostly succeeds, and buyers are scarce, so there is nothing for ML to discover.
fatal_flaw: The credit value is already set by a published formula and recorded in legible public registries, so the market prices it into the land. The step-up is about 1-3x, not 10^3-10^4. The proving step already succeeds most of the time. And buyers are few and erratic, since demand depends on policy.
step_up: From memory, not verified this run (the search budget was used up): Pinelands sending-zone land trades at roughly $1k-3k per acre (estimate). The PDC credits severed from it are worth roughly $1k-3k per acre's worth of credits (a PDC has historically sold for about $20k-40k, i.e. about $5k-10k per right, at 39 acres per PDC). So the step-up is about 1-3x, not 10^3. Montgomery County MD TDRs once sold for about $10k-15k each but are mostly illiquid now that receiving demand has collapsed (estimate). TRPA residential development rights and land coverage can sell for $100k+ per unit or $25-50 per sq ft (estimate). Sensitive Tahoe parcels that hold them are already priced on that value, or bought by the California Tahoe Conservancy and Nevada state lands at prices that include it. The market already prices the credit value into the land.
hit_rate_capex: The proving step is not expensive and rarely fails. Eligibility follows from zoning and the sending-zone maps, and the allocation follows a deterministic formula. Estimated cost per certification (title search, survey, LOI or certificate application, easement recording) is about $5k-25k, and most eligible parcels succeed, likely over 70% (estimate). The lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, so about 1.3-2x. ML cannot cut capex 10x when the base hit rate is already high.

name: Clearfield: FUDS stigma removal
one_line_reason: This is a stigma-arbitrage version of the killed brownfields idea: a small, unverified discount, an outcome already in public USACE status fields, a high base clean rate, and a regulatory bottleneck instead of a discovery bottleneck.
fatal_flaw: The step-up is roughly 1.2-3x on land that is already cheap. The answer to the hunt is already written into the public USACE FUDS GIS polygons and NDAI/Response Complete status fields, which removes both the information edge and the purchase discount. On top of that, the proving step depends on a regulator sign-off (USACE or the state) that a private buyer cannot get on demand. This repeats the powered-brownfields failure.
step_up: Unproven: rural land near a FUDS, where the candidate claims a 50-90% discount. I could not verify that claim because the search budget was used up. From what I know of the literature, stigma discounts near contaminated sites are typically 10-30%, and most FUDS acreage is cheap rural or agricultural land priced around $1-10k/acre (estimate). Proven: ordinary market value of the same parcel. That gives a realistic step-up of about 1.2-3x, or up to 10x only in rare cases of a deep discount next to a growth corridor. This is nowhere near the 10^4 step from $1/ha to $10,000/ha in the rubric. The candidate's own estimate of ~2-10x, and its own comparison to the killed powered-brownfields idea, agree.
hit_rate_capex: My estimates, not verified this run. Most land adjacent to a FUDS is in fact clean, because munitions concentrate in impact areas and the Archive Search Reports already outline them. So the base rate of a parcel turning out clean is high (likely over 70%), and since the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, ML can improve the hit rate by at most about 1.4x. Cost per proving attempt: survey roughly $200-1,500/acre for drone or ground DGM plus anomaly reacquisition (estimate), plus legal and regulatory work. The expensive part is the regulatory concurrence and liability, not finding the right parcel, so ML does not cut proving capex 10x.

name: Levee Re-Accreditation Land Bank
one_line_reason: This fails like the coal-mine geothermal counter-example: recertifying (and often fixing) a public levee is harder than finding it. The company cannot own the levee or the uplift, the step-up is only about 3-10x, and NLD and FEMA fields already summarise the outcome.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is not discovery. It is engineering, often repairs, on a public structure the company does not own, and it needs the levee sponsor to cooperate. The resulting value goes to every landowner behind the levee, and the outcome is already published in NLD and FEMA status fields. The step-up is only about 3-10x.
step_up: My estimate (no search budget left to verify): ag or industrial land in an AE zone behind a non-accredited levee might trade at roughly $3k-15k/acre. The same land shown as Zone X (protected) next to metro logistics corridors might bring $30k-150k/acre. That is about 3-10x, and much less where the land stays agricultural, since flood-zone status hardly affects farm value. Land behind levees also often trades at only a small stigma discount, because buyers already price in a likely re-accreditation or LAMP remap. This is far from the 10^3-10^4 step-up the rubric wants.
hit_rate_capex: These are estimates, not looked up. Cost per attempt: the candidate's own $0.5-3M per levee system for certification engineering and the LOMR, before any physical repairs, which often run $10M-100M+ per system. Base hit rate: I estimate that of the levees de-accredited since FEMA's Map Modernization era (about 2005-2013), only 20-40% could be recertified without capital works. So the ML lever is capped at about 2.5-5x, not 10x. Also, most of the cost is the engineering and repairs on the levee you pick, not wasted shots on wrong levees.

name: Burn-Lot Rebuild Rights
one_line_reason: Weak: rebuild rights are near-universal and already granted by emergency order, the hit rate is high so ML adds little, and the step-up is about 1.1-1.5x on the rung, with value tied up in construction, like the geothermal counter-example.
fatal_flaw: Rebuild rights are handed out wholesale by emergency order, and the money is in construction, not discovery. Emergency ordinances (state EO N-29-25 and LA Mayor EO 1) and standard nonconforming-rebuild clauses already grant like-for-like rights to nearly every burned lot, and DINS plus the county rebuild portals make that legible. ML has nothing hidden to find, the step-up on the rung is under 3x, and the real value sits in bespoke vertical construction.
step_up: From memory, not verified this run: Palisades burned lots traded at roughly $1.5-4M against pre-fire home values of about $3-5M+, and Altadena lot listings ran about $0.5-1M. A burned lot sells at land value, and land is about 60-80% of total value in these markets. A permit-ready lot might fetch about 1.1-1.5x a raw burned lot. Taking it all the way to a rebuilt home is about 2-3x on land cost, but that needs $500-1,000+/sqft of construction. On the rung itself the step-up is under 3x, so C2 = 1.
hit_rate_capex: Estimates: the proving step costs about $10-30k (the candidate's figure; permit-history pull plus expediter and plan check). The base hit rate is high: most burned lots in the Jan 2025 burn areas can rebuild like-for-like under the emergency orders, which I estimate at 80%+. With a hit rate that high the lever (capped at 1/hit rate) is about 1.2x, not 10x. ML would only help on edge cases: unpermitted additions, ADUs, hillside or coastal lots.

name: SeniorWater / Tax-Sale Mining Water: senior surface rights on tax-forfeited parcels and patented claims
one_line_reason: Proving is a multi-year adversarial water-court case, not cheap discovery. The outcome is already in HydroBase diversion records and the abandonment lists. And the HCU rule means dormant rights transfer almost no water, so the 10^2-10^3x step-up mostly does not exist.
fatal_flaw: The historic consumptive-use and anti-speculation rules. In Colorado (and in Utah and NM, with forfeiture after 5-7 years of non-use), a change case can only move the water that was historically used, quantified over a representative study period. So a dormant right, which is exactly what this strategy targets, yields close to zero transferable acre-feet even if no one formally abandoned it. The rights that do carry value have diversion records already in HydroBase and are already priced by the market.
step_up: Unproven: the parcel price, $1-20k (the candidate's figure). Proven: Front Range consumptive water sells for roughly $25-60k per acre-foot (AF), and C-BT units have traded around $70-100k per unit. These figures are from memory of 2023-24 reports; I could not check them this run. A hit worth about 20 AF of firm transferable consumptive use would be $0.5-1.2M, so about 50-500x on purchase price. But under the HCU rule, a right that has been dormant transfers almost no yield, so the true step-up on dormant rights is close to 1x. The hits that do transfer are rights with a documented diversion history, and those are already known and priced.
hit_rate_capex: My estimate: the base hit rate for a dormant senior right surviving abandonment and the HCU analysis is under 5%. Cost per proving attempt (HCU study plus water attorney plus change case) is roughly $100k-$1M+ and takes 2-7 years. That is from general knowledge of Colorado practice and was not verified this run. ML can only lower the cost of screening documents, which is a small share of that spend. The lever is well under 10x because each attempt's cost is legal and adversarial, not search.

name: Dormant Vintages: unissued credits on lapsed registered carbon projects
one_line_reason: Finding dormant projects is a registry filter. The hard part is the owner's meter data, a VVB audit and an LoA, and the price uplift is about 3-30x on credits whose value buyers are already discounting for integrity concerns.
fatal_flaw: Proving needs the owner's own monitoring data and a host-country Letter of Authorization, which ML cannot supply. The 'is it still operating' signal is already legible in registry and grid data. So there is no information gap to buy against and no step-up near 10^3.
step_up: These numbers are my estimates from prior knowledge, not checked this run because the search budget was used up. Unverified reductions on a dormant project are worth about $0-0.5/t, assuming an owner sells at all. Once verified, legacy renewable or cookstove VCUs sell for about $1-5/t. CORSIA Phase 1 eligible units with an LoA have traded around $15-25/t. That is at most about 10-50x, and only on the CORSIA path, which LoA scarcity limits, not verification. On the common path it is about 3-10x. Nothing like Terranox's $1 to $10,000/ha jump.
hit_rate_capex: These are estimates and could not be verified because search was unavailable this run. A VVB verification costs about $30-80k (the figure given with the candidate; my prior range is $15-60k). Add $5-20k for monitoring reconstruction and registry fees. The base hit rate for 'the plant kept running' is already high, perhaps 50-80% for grid-connected hydro, wind or solar, and it can be checked from public grid or generation data without ML. Failures come from missing monitoring data, a lapsed crediting period, methodology changes, or no LoA, none of which ML fixes. Because the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, it is only about 1.3-2x.

name: Deep Peat Finder: Peatland Code rights on upland grazing
one_line_reason: Peat is already mapped and priced, and restoration, not discovery, is the work. The step-up is about 2-3x with a high base hit rate, so the Terranox mechanism does not apply.
fatal_flaw: The thing to be discovered is already legibly mapped (2016 Carbon and Peatland map, LiDAR) and already priced into upland land values. On top of that, the physical restoration step, plus 30-100 years of permanence and monitoring, dominates the rung. So there is no 80%+ discovery frame, no low hit rate for ML to lever, and only about a 1.5-3x step-up.
step_up: From memory, because the search budget had run out. Upland rough grazing in Scotland or northern England sells for about £1.5-5k/ha, and is already priced up by natural-capital demand since 2021. Claimable reductions on actively eroding or drained peat come to roughly 100-400 tCO2e/ha over the project life, after the risk buffer (estimate). PIUs trade at about £15-30/t, so gross credit value is about £2-10k/ha, before restoration, validation and monitoring costs. The upside is about 1.5-3x the land price, and nowhere near 10^3. Land prices already include the carbon option: the Scottish market saw a 'natural capital premium' in 2021-23 sales.
hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is high, not low. Deep peat (Class 1/2 on the 2016 Carbon and Peatland map) and its broad condition (erosion and drainage are visible on aerial imagery and LiDAR) are already mapped. A field probe survey costs about £20-50/ha (from the candidate brief, consistent with consultant rates), and I estimate that over 50% of map-identified Class 1 sites confirm as eligible. With a hit rate that high, the ML lever is capped below about 2x, not 10x. Restoration costs about £1-3k/ha (Peatland Action range, estimate), and that dwarfs the cost of proving.

name: Species Bank: eDNA-proven endangered-species conservation credits
one_line_reason: This is a wetland-bank clone. Entitlement and endowment, not discovery, make up 80%+ of the work and set the value. Species presence is already in legible public fields, the step-up is about 2-8x net and slow, and the ladder caps out at a few-$B market.
fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Credit value comes from a bespoke, multi-year regulatory entitlement plus an endowment and a permanent easement, priced against service-area demand. Species presence is mostly already legible in CNDDB and critical habitat maps. This is the coal-mine geothermal counter-example, and the same flaw that killed wetland banks.
step_up: These are recalled from memory, because the shared web search budget was used up before this run and no searches returned results. Unproven: Central Valley or foothill rangeland at about $3-10k/acre (the candidate's figure, consistent with USDA/ASFMRA pasture values I remember). Proven: released credits at roughly $20-80k/acre for California tiger salamander or giant garter snake, and about $100-300k+/acre for vernal pool preservation in the Sacramento region (recalled Westervelt and Wildlands price ranges, not verified). Gross that is about 5-30x. Net of endowment, easement, restoration, legal costs and 3-7 years of carry, I estimate 2-8x on capital, realised slowly as credits are released and sold. It is not an immediate step-up on a hit.
hit_rate_capex: eDNA costs about $300-800 per sample (candidate's figure; I remember commercial lab pricing in the same range), and protocol surveys run about $5-30k per site-season (my estimate). Both are cheap compared with the entitlement cost. The base hit rate is not low: banks are sited inside known ranges and critical habitat mapped by CNDDB, where I estimate presence probability is high (above 30-50%). So the lever (at most 1/hit rate) is under 3x, and it acts on a cost line that is a small share of total capex. ML cannot cut overall capex anywhere near 10x.

name: Medicare Secondary Payer Claim Assignments
one_line_reason: Discovery is cheap database matching and collection is expensive litigation, which inverts the 95/5 frame. The core data is private PHI, Section 111 reporting already legibly records primary payers, and MSP Recovery's collapse shows the step-up does not materialise.
fatal_flaw: The value is captured by collecting from adversarial, well-funded insurers, not by discovery. The outcome is already partly summarised in Section 111 mandatory insurer reporting to CMS, and incumbent subrogation vendors already work the MA side. MSP Recovery/LifeWallet is the empirical proof: it booked tens of billions in assigned 'paid value', collected pennies, and its equity collapsed more than 99% from its SPAC valuation.
step_up: The unproven right is usually assigned for a contingent split, often about 50% of recoveries, with little or no cash up front (recalled from MSP Recovery's assignment structure; I could not verify it here). So the 'price' is near zero, but that is a profit share, not a $1/ha purchase. A proven-but-uncollected claim is worth its face amount times the odds of collecting it. Double damages give at most 2x the conditional payment. Paid amounts on trauma claims run roughly $5k-$50k (my estimate). The headline step-up is large only because the starting price is near zero. The realistic proven-claim value is about 3-10x the expected value of an unproven one, not 10^3-10^4. MSP Recovery's own record (recalled, not verified): it booked tens of billions in 'paid value' and collected single-digit to low tens of millions, i.e. pennies on the dollar.
hit_rate_capex: I estimate the base hit rate is low: perhaps 5-15% of trauma-coded claims have an identifiable liable primary payer. That leaves an ML lever of up to about 10x on discovery in theory. But identifying the claim is not the expensive step. Proving it is: attorney time, filings, and fighting causation and coverage, plausibly $5k-$50k+ per contested claim (estimate). ML does not cut that cost. Discovery itself is already cheap: it is database matching. All figures are estimates; my web search budget ran out before I could source them.

name: Antitrust Claims of Dead and Small Businesses
one_line_reason: This is a crowded claims-aggregation arbitrage. Administrators already know claim volumes from defendant data, filing is cheap and rarely fails, and the step-up is about 3-10x rather than 10^3-10^4, so ML has almost no discovery lever.
fatal_flaw: The outcome is already legible. In the largest settlements, the administrator computes each claim's value from defendant or card-network transaction data and pre-populates or allocates it. Proving is therefore close to free, has a high hit rate, and is not driven by discovery. What is left is a crowded race to reach and contract owners, already run by established claims-trading funds, with step-ups of only about 3-10x.
step_up: Estimate, not sourced. An unproven claim sells to an aggregator for about 5-20% of its expected payout, typically as an upfront payment on interchange. Once the administrator accepts it, it trades at about 50-80% of payout, per the candidate's own figure. That is a 3-10x step-up. It reaches 100x+ only for tiny claims bought for nominal sums, and those are capped at a few hundred to a few thousand dollars each. Nowhere near 10^3-10^4 on meaningful dollars.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate. Filing costs very little: a claim form, roughly tens to hundreds of dollars of labour each. Acceptance rates for legitimate members are high, likely more than 70%. The real constraint is the low share of eligible members who file. Class-action claim rates are often in the single digits, per the FTC's 2019 consumer class action report, which put the median at about 4-9%. That gap is about reaching owners, not about proving claims. So the ML lever on proving cost is small: the base hit rate is already high, and 1/hit-rate is at most 1.5x. No web numbers were gathered because the shared search budget was exhausted.

name: Revenant Corp / Zombie Entity Recovery
one_line_reason: Cheap rights and cheap proving, but the answer is already searchable, the payout is a fixed debt rather than a 10^3x re-pricing, the ML lever is small, and there is no ladder up a real production chain.
fatal_flaw: The outcome is already written in a legible public field. MissingMoney/state UP databases list owner and holder, so anyone, including the selling shareholder, can see the prize for free. And the 'proven' value is a fixed debt owed to you, not an asset that a capitalised buyer re-prices 10^3x. It is collection arbitrage with finder-fee caps and murky ownership of dissolved entities, not a discovery step-up.
step_up: Unproven: residual interest bought for $100-2,000 (candidate's figure). Proven: the cash claim itself, at face value. Most corporate UP holdings are small. Typical UP accounts are under $100, and NAUPA reports that states hold about $70B+ in total (from memory, not verified this session). Hits worth $10k-100k exist but are rare. On a hit the multiple is about 5-50x, not 10^3-10^4, and finder-fee or assignment limits in many states (roughly 10-35%, from memory, e.g. CA 10%, FL 20%) can cap the share you keep if the deal is treated as a finder agreement rather than a true equity purchase. No search numbers verified.
hit_rate_capex: Estimates only; searches were unavailable. A proving attempt is cheap: database searches cost close to nothing, and reinstatement plus filing is about $500-3,000 including legal time. Because the main UP data is searchable, the hit rate on targeted deals is high once you pre-screen (estimate 30-60%). Low capex and a high base hit rate mean ML has little to cut: the lever is at most about 2-3x, not 10x.

name: Newsroom Morgue Holdings: defunct-newspaper photo archives
one_line_reason: Scanning is the dominant cost and discovery is a small part of the work. The step-up is about 10x before costs and about 1x after. Copyright checks mostly prove images are in the public domain. Historical stock licensing is a crowded, shrinking market.
fatal_flaw: Proving does not create the step-up; it often destroys value. Checking notices and renewals mostly proves that published images are in the public domain, so anyone can copy them. The remaining value sits in unpublished negatives, and getting at it requires costly per-frame physical scanning, which is the dominant cost. That makes this the coal-mine geothermal case, at roughly 10x gross and about 1x net of scanning, in a stock-photo market with collapsing prices.
step_up: Unproven: $5-20k per archive (the candidate's own figure; it matches my memory of eBay and estate sales of press-print morgues, unverified). Proven: an archive is worth its licensing income. Stock licence prices have collapsed (my memory: Alamy's average fee is in the tens of dollars per sale, and most archive images never sell). A well-captioned regional archive might be worth $50-300k as a library, or bring in a few $k-$10s of k a year (estimate). That is about 3-15x before scanning cost, and roughly 1x after it. AI-training licences pay cents per image (estimate). Nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: There is no low-hit-rate proving step to improve. Almost every archive 'hits' in the sense of holding some licensable images, so the base hit rate is high and 1/hit-rate gives ML little room. The cost of each attempt is the scanning, which is proportional to the number of frames: about $0.5-2.5M for a 500k-negative morgue at $1-5 per frame (estimate). ML captioning reduces labour, but not by 10x on the dominant cost, which is physical handling.

name: Orphan Typeface Rights + Usage Discovery
one_line_reason: Cheap, legible detection plus a hard legal step to monetise each hit, in a small market, makes this a weak copyright-enforcement play rather than a Terranox-style discovery play.
fatal_flaw: Typeface designs cannot be copyrighted in the US, so detecting a glyph does not prove infringement, and the font name is already readable in the CSS, PDF and APK metadata. That leaves ML with no discovery edge. What remains is a litigation-heavy enforcement business in a market of about $1B with no 10^3 step-up.
step_up: Unproven: orphan or estate font libraries change hands for about $5k-$50k (the candidate's own figure, not verified). Proven: consolidator deals I recall without checking: Monotype paid about $50M for Bitstream's font business (2012) and about $15M for FontShop (2014), and Monotype as a whole went private for about $825M (HGGC, 2019). Those prices are for libraries with brand names and live licensing revenue, not orphans. My estimate: a small library with a documented unlicensed base might sell for 3-10x its purchase price, or bring a few hundred thousand dollars in settlements. That is nowhere near 10^3. The candidate's 100-1000x is not supported.
hit_rate_capex: The proving step is a cheap compute scan, not an expensive attempt that usually fails. Crawling HTTP Archive or Common Crawl for a font costs a few dollars to a few thousand dollars of compute (my estimate). So ML has no costly step to make more likely to hit, and there is no 10x capex cut to buy more shots. The real cost and risk is converting each hit into a payment, which works like copyright enforcement. My estimate: well under half of demand letters pay, and the money depends on legal process, not on detection accuracy.

name: Bankrupt-Brand Digital Asset Revival
one_line_reason: This fails the gold rubric: the right is bought at fair value in a marketed auction, demand proof is cheap and legible to everyone, the realistic step-up is 2-10x rather than 10^3x, and the value is realised by operating the brand, not by discovering it.
fatal_flaw: The proving signal (residual traffic and search demand) is already legible: Ahrefs, SimilarWeb and Trends measure it, and auction agents like Hilco Streambank put it in front of the very revival buyers who bid at the same 363 auctions. There is no information discount to capture and no expensive, mostly-failing proving step for ML to cheapen. The real work, and the real risk, is operating the relaunch, which repeats the coal-mine geothermal failure.
step_up: From memory, not verified this run (the web search budget was used up). Large bankrupt-brand IP sales clear in the low millions to tens of millions at competitive auction: Bed Bath & Beyond IP went to Overstock for about $21.5M (2023); Pier 1 IP went to Retail Ecommerce Ventures for about $31M (2020); Modell's IP went for about $3.6M. Those prices come out of a marketed auction, so they are fair value, not near-zero. Small dead DTC brands sold through assignment-for-benefit-of-creditors processes probably clear at $5k-250k (my estimate). Resale of a bundle "proven" by traffic data is maybe 2-10x the purchase price at best, and often under 2x, because the buyer looked at the same traffic. The candidate's 40-400x has no comparable behind it.
hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs very little: roughly $0-500 of SEO/traffic tooling plus the auction bid (my estimate). Because nothing about proving is expensive or mostly failing, ML has nothing to cut. Base hit rate on a "does residual demand exist" check is high and observable before buying. Caveat: the real failure point comes after purchase, in the relaunch, and ML does not change that. So the 1/base-hit-rate cap gives roughly a 1-2x lever, nowhere near 10x.

name: Installed-Base Rescue: discontinued robot lines
one_line_reason: This fails the rubric the same way geothermal in coal mines does: finding the installed base is easy, since it comes in the acquired customer records, and keeping orphaned hardware running is hard. The proven franchise sells at about 3-10x the purchase price at ordinary service-business multiples.
fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. The installed base comes with the acquired CRM and serial records, and the real work and risk is the physical, engineering-heavy job of supporting obsolete hardware. Proving is a small share of the rung, the base hit rate is high, and the step-up is about 3-10x at service multiples, not 10^3-10^4.
step_up: Unproven: assets of failed robot companies tend to go to a single strategic buyer or a liquidator at token prices, low single-digit millions or less. Past examples from memory, not checked this session: Rethink Robotics' assets went to HAHN Group in 2018; Jibo's to NTT Disruption; Anki's to Digital Dream Labs in 2019. Proven: field-service businesses are typically valued at about 0.5-2x revenue or 6-10x EBITDA (estimate). If the base supports $2-5M a year of service revenue, the proven franchise is worth about $2-10M. That is roughly 3-10x on the purchase price, below the candidate's 10-50x claim and far from 10^3. The step-up also builds up over months of service delivery rather than arriving on a single hit.
hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving attempt like a drill hole. The proving step is a pilot support contract that costs maybe $50-250k in engineering and technician time (estimate). Whether a line has a live installed base is known with fairly high probability before purchase: the OEM's CRM, warranty records and serial-number registry usually come in the data room. The base hit rate is high, so the lever (capped at 1/hit rate) is small, maybe 1.5-2x, not 10x. No sourced hit-rate figure exists. All numbers are my estimates.

name: Abandoned Brand Revival: legacy media mastheads and trademarks
one_line_reason: This fails the frame test, much like geothermal in coal mines. Relaunch is the real work, roll-ups buy royalties not attention, and the right and the outcome are both legible and free to copy.
fatal_flaw: No proving test turns a dormant mark into a buyer-priced asset. Value only appears after a bespoke relaunch, so discovery is a small share of the work. On top of that, abandoned marks are free first-come ITU filings, not cheap purchases, and the outcome (status, attention) is already in legible fields.
step_up: Unproven: an abandoned mark costs a USPTO filing fee of about $350 per class plus legal fees, so roughly $1-5k all-in. Residual goodwill from a defunct publisher runs roughly $1k-50k (my estimate). Proven, with no revenue: there is no market price, and a mark with only search or attention signals resells at maybe 2-10x (my estimate). Proven with revenue: brand IP from bankruptcy has sold for $5-30M+, for example Hilco Streambank and Gordon Brothers auctions of retail brands. That jump needs a relaunch and years of operating, not one proving test. On a pure discovery basis the step-up is about 3-10x. Note: I could not verify this live because the web search budget was used up. Figures are from prior knowledge or are estimates.
hit_rate_capex: I estimate that 5-15% of revived dormant brands reach meaningful licensing revenue, from the anecdotal record of River West Brands and Retrobrands-style revivers. Each attempt costs about $50k-$1M+ (product, marketing, legal; my estimate). The expensive, mostly failing part is the relaunch itself. ML can rank which marks carry latent attention, but it does not cut the relaunch cost, so the lever on total capex is well under 10x. The cheap part (filing fees) is the only part ML touches, and it is already cheap.

name: Expiring-Exclusivity Biologic Patent Picker
one_line_reason: Litigation is the proving step, it is expensive and slow, and the evidence it needs is confidential, so discovery is far below 80% of the rung. The only buyer is the defendant in a settlement, and the Purple Book now publishes the patents that matter.
fatal_flaw: Proving value depends on infringement and validity litigation, not discovery. That costs about $4M+ per case over 2-4 years, and its key evidence (confidential manufacturing and CMC details) is not in public data. ML can only pick which patents to buy; it cannot cheapen or de-risk the step that creates the step-up. Since 2021 the Purple Book also publishes BPCIA patent lists, which legibly flags the patents that matter. This is patent-troll economics with a better screen, not a Terranox-style frame.
step_up: These are my estimates; no live search was possible. On the secondary patent market (brokered lots tracked by Richardson Oliver Insights), a typical patent asks roughly $100k-$300k. Obscure biologic process patents held by small biotechs or CDMOs probably trade at $10k-$200k, or for the cost of the maintenance fee if abandoned. A proven patent that reads on a blockbuster can settle for a royalty-bearing licence worth $10M-$100M+; AbbVie's Humira patent thicket of about 130 patents produced entry-delay settlements worth billions. That is a 100-1000x step-up only in rare cases, and it arrives after years of litigation, not at the moment of the hit. The expected step-up per patent bought is far lower, about 3-10x after costs (estimate).
hit_rate_capex: Again my estimates; no live search was possible. Patent assertion has a low base hit rate. Pharma and biologic patents challenged at the PTAB are found wholly or partly unpatentable about 40-60% of the time once instituted. Process-patent infringement on biologics is rarely shown. Cost per proving attempt: the AIPLA economic survey puts patent litigation with more than $25M at risk at roughly $4M+ through trial, plus about $0.5M per IPR. ML only improves the cheap screening step, choosing which patents to buy. It cannot raise the hit rate of the expensive step, because infringement depends on confidential manufacturing (CMC) details. So the 10x capex cut does not apply. At best ML cuts screening cost, which is maybe 5% of total capex.

name: Prior-Art Priority Owner: early university patents reading on commercial biologics and devices
one_line_reason: Discovery is not 80%+ of any sellable rung, because value only appears after expensive adversarial litigation. The data is legible and already mined, university sellers are sophisticated, and the ladder only leads to patent assertion.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is litigation, not discovery. Turning the licence into a proven asset takes $3-5M+ and 3-5 years of adversarial work (Markman, IPR, trial) with roughly coin-flip-or-worse odds. Discovery, which ML would speed up, is a small part of that cost and work, and the sellers (university tech transfer offices) already read the same data.
step_up: Unproven: exclusive licence for about $10-100k upfront plus a revenue share (from the candidate brief, not verified). Proven, meaning it has survived Markman and IPR: settlements on biologics or devices can reach $10M-1B. Precedents from memory, not searched this run: Carnegie Mellon v. Marvell, $1.17B verdict, settled for $750M; Caltech v. Apple/Broadcom, $1.1B verdict, later vacated. That is roughly 100-1000x on a hit, but only after 3-5 years and litigation. Right after the proving step this candidate proposes (a claim chart), the market value of the asset rises maybe 2-10x (my estimate).
hit_rate_capex: Base rates from memory, not verified this run. Patent holders win at trial roughly a third of the time (PwC patent litigation studies). The PTAB invalidates all or some challenged claims in a majority of IPRs that reach a final decision. AIPLA economic surveys put median cost through trial for cases with more than $25M at risk at about $4M or more. The $50-150k chart is a cheap screen; the expensive step ($3-5M+) is litigation. Its outcome depends on judges, juries and prior art, which ML can only partly predict. ML can lower screening cost, but screening is not where the cost sits. Realistic lever: under 2x on total cost to reach a proven asset.

name: Lazarus PMA: orphaned Class III approvals
one_line_reason: Discovery is a database lookup and the value comes from bespoke restarts of commercially failed devices, so there is no 95/5 frame, no 10^3 step-up and only a weak ML lever.
fatal_flaw: Adverse selection plus a physical restart. Orphaned PMAs are orphaned because the economics, clinical results or liability failed. Proving value means rebuilding manufacturing (the hard 80%), not discovering something. And the legal status the ML would 'confirm' is already a structured field in FDA's PMA database.
step_up: Unproven: the candidate says PMA plus DHF from an estate costs $10k-500k (my estimate agrees that dormant regulatory files sell cheaply in 363 sales). Proven: a strategic buyer pays for revenue and share, not for the approval. A restarted Class III line with no installed base, no surgeon relationships and lapsed reimbursement momentum is probably worth 1-5x restart cost, so about $2-10M (my estimate). Gross step-up on purchase price is about 10-100x. Net of $0.3-1.5M proving cost plus $1-3M of validation and inventory (my estimate), the step-up on capital deployed is about 2-5x. Nothing like 10^4. Medtech acquirers usually buy at about 3-6x revenue, so value tracks restarted sales, not the restart itself (my estimate). Search budget was exhausted, so none of these are sourced figures.
hit_rate_capex: The proving step does not mostly fail at random. If the device is unchanged and the CM is competent, a site-change supplement probably gets approved more than 50% of the time (my estimate). So the ML lever (capped at 1/hit rate) is under 2x. The real reason an attempt fails is economic: the product was orphaned because it lost commercially, clinically or on liability, and that cannot be read from filings. Cost per attempt: the candidate gives $0.3-1.5M. From memory, the FDA 180-day supplement user fee is about 15% of the PMA fee, roughly $80k in FY2025-26. Validation and inspection readiness add more, my estimate $0.5-2M all-in. ML does not cut that cost 10x, because it is manufacturing work, not search.

name: Article 95 Rescue: abandoned EU biocide dossiers
one_line_reason: The coal-mine-geothermal pattern again: finishing a biocide dossier costs millions in tox studies and takes years, while choosing the dossier is easy and already legible from ECHA status fields. The step-up is only about 2-10x on capital, against the 10^3-10^4 the rubric needs.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is not discovery. It is millions of EUR of bespoke study work and years of regulatory process. Approval outcomes and hazard blockers already sit in legible BPC and CLH fields. And the review-programme data protection that would make an Article 95 listing licensable expired on 31 Dec 2025 (from memory, unverified). So no frame exists where discovery is 80%+ of the work, and ML has no hit-rate lever.
step_up: Unproven: the candidate claims a takeover costs about EUR 50-300k. Proven: a listed AS/PT earns letter-of-access income, and those letters typically sell for tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand EUR per product supplier (my estimate from industry knowledge; I could not check it). Most of the value has to be built by spending millions on studies, so this is a cost-plus regulatory asset, not a value jump on a single hit. Realistic step-up is about 2-10x on total capital invested (my estimate), not 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: approval once a full dossier reaches the BPC is fairly high, so failure is not the main cost. Dossiers usually get withdrawn for economic reasons or because hazards trigger exclusion criteria (CMR or endocrine disruptor), and both are visible in public CLH and BPC records. Cost per attempt: completing an active substance dossier is commonly put at about EUR 1-5M+ in studies, plus ECHA approval fees in the low hundreds of thousands of EUR per substance (my estimates from industry knowledge; I could not check them). Because the base hit rate is already high, ML can raise it very little (the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate), so the 10x capex cut does not happen. The cost is study generation, not choosing badly.

name: Alternate Label: pesticide registrations bought ahead of EPA cancellations
one_line_reason: FIFRA lets anyone cheaply register an off-patent alternative, and EPA cancellations are slow, public and closely watched, so there is no step-up, no low-hit-rate proving step and no illegible-data edge.
fatal_flaw: The right is not scarce and the outcome is legible. A me-too registration for an off-patent alternative costs about a PRIA fee and a few months. Cancellations are telegraphed for years in public EPA dockets that buyers' own regulatory teams already watch. So there is no hidden information to extract, and buyers replicate the right instead of paying a 10^3 premium.
step_up: No transaction comps found, because the search budget ran out. My estimate from FIFRA mechanics: a dormant Section 3 me-too registration of an off-patent AI is worth about its replacement cost. That is a PRIA fee, roughly $5-15k with a 4-8 month decision, plus annual maintenance fees of about $4-5k per product. After a competitor's AI is cancelled, a buyer could pay a time-to-market premium of perhaps $100k-$1M for a label already in hand. Starting from a $20-100k cost basis, that is about 3-10x at best, not the 30-500x claimed. The $1-50M deals in this sector are for product lines with sales, not bare registrations.
hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving step. The 'proof' is an EPA action that happens or does not, on a public timeline. Registration review runs on a 15-year cycle with a published schedule, proposed interim decisions are posted for comment, and cancellations usually take years and are telegraphed (chlorpyrifos: petition in 2007, tolerances revoked in 2021). The cost per attempt is about $5-15k in fees plus maintenance (estimate). Base predictability is high, so ML has little room to raise the hit rate, and the 1/base-hit-rate cap on the lever is small.

name: Vehicle Vault: dormant IDIQ/GWAC seat holders
one_line_reason: Proving a seat is sales and service delivery rather than discovery. The step-up is about 10x at most and tied to revenue, the outcome is already legible in FPDS, and size or 8(a) status, which is the value of the seat, disappears when it is sold to the stated buyer.
fatal_flaw: The asset does not hold its value through a sale. Size-status seats lose set-aside eligibility once acquired by a non-small buyer (13 CFR 121.404(g) recertification; SBA approval needed for 8(a) ownership changes). And the "proving" step is winning plus performing labor-based services, not discovery. On top of that, the outcome of each seat is already a legible FPDS field that GovWin and similar tools index.
step_up: From my own knowledge, because the web search budget was used up (no numbers fetched this run). A dormant small firm holding a seat but no revenue sells for roughly the cost of its paperwork, about $0.1-0.5M (estimate). Govcon services firms usually sell at about 0.5-1.5x revenue or about 8-12x EBITDA (industry-typical, estimate). With $5-20M of backlog and maybe 8-10% margins, the firm might be worth $2-10M. That is a 5-30x step-up at best, nowhere near 10^3-10^4. And much of it comes from performing the contracts (revenue), not from the seat being proven.
hit_rate_capex: From knowledge, not searched. Yes, many seat holders win little or nothing: GSA cancels MAS schedules with under $25k of sales over 5 years, and a large share of small seats on multiple-award vehicles sit idle (estimate: 30-60% show negligible obligations). But the failures come from missing past performance, BD capacity and incumbency, not from bad targeting. A competitive task-order proposal costs roughly $50-300k in BD and proposal labor (estimate), and pWin for a new entrant without incumbency is about 10-25% (estimate). ML targeting might lift pWin modestly, maybe 1.5-2x. It cannot deliver 10x, because the binding limits are past performance, price and incumbency, which public data does not fix.

name: Orphan FMS Sustainment
one_line_reason: This is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern in defense: finding an orphaned fielded system is easy from structured DSCA, FPDS and SIPRI data, while qualifying and sustaining the line is the real cost. The step-up is about 3-10x over years, and incumbents like Ontic and TransDigm already buy these lines.
fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. The proving step is the bespoke manufacturing, qualification and ITAR sustainment of the line, and the signal (DSCA, FPDS, SIPRI) is already legible and already used by well-capitalised incumbents who buy these lines (Ontic, Heico, TransDigm, VSE). That leaves no information edge, no purchase discount and no step-up of 1,000x or more.
step_up: My estimate, not sourced, because the shared web search budget ran out before any search returned. Orphaned or licensed legacy aerospace and defense lines usually change hands at roughly 0.5-2x revenue (licensing deals or small carve-outs). Aftermarket consolidators value proven sole-source lines at roughly 3-6x revenue, or about 15-25x EBITDA in TransDigm and Heico-style deals. That is about 3-10x, and you only get it after years of running the line. The candidate's own "10-50x" looks optimistic. Nothing jumps immediately when a hit lands; the value builds up through contract awards and margin.
hit_rate_capex: There is no single costly proving attempt that usually fails. The cost of each attempt is the cost of buying and requalifying the line: by my estimate $1-10M and 1-3 years for each line, covering acquisition, tooling, first article testing and ITAR setup. The base hit rate is fairly high (my estimate 30-60%) when you pick lines with known demand, because DSCA notices and FPDS awards already show which systems are still fielded. Since the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, ML can improve it by about 2-3x at most, not 10x. Capex is set by requalification, not by discovery.

name: Decontrol Arbitrage: ITAR-to-EAR commodity jurisdiction
one_line_reason: The value uplift is roughly 2x on companies bought at full price, the rulings are rule-predictable and already published, and the main cost is the acquisition, which ML does not cut. This is not a Terranox-shaped frame.
fatal_flaw: The step-up is a small multiple, about 1.2-3x on the value of an operating business (2-10x at best), not 10^3-10^4 from near zero. The CJ outcome is also predictable from published rules and the public DDTC list of CJ determinations, and owners or their counsel can file it themselves for $10-50k. So the arbitrage is small and has no data edge.
step_up: About 1.2-3x, and on revenue multiples, not from near zero. This is my estimate from memory: no live search was possible because the search budget for this run was used up. An ITAR-only niche defense line might trade at about 1-2x revenue or 6-10x EBITDA. The same line free to export might reach about 1.5-3x revenue, and only if real foreign demand exists, which takes years of sales work to capture. The candidate itself claims about 2-10x. Even the top of that range is about 10^1, three orders of magnitude short of the 10^4 benchmark. A new export license does not change the earnings on day one, so a strategic buyer will not pay the uplift up front.
hit_rate_capex: The CJ filing costs roughly $10-50k in counsel fees (the candidate's figure, which matches my understanding), and DDTC answers in about 60 days to a year. That cost is tiny next to the price of buying the product line, which is likely $1-20M (my estimate). So the expensive "attempt" is the acquisition, not the ruling. My recollection, which I could not verify here, is that after the 2013-2016 Export Control Reform a large share of CJ rulings, possibly a majority, came out EAR, because the order-of-review and "specially designed" release rules (22 CFR 120.11 / 120.41) make outcomes fairly predictable for experienced export-control counsel. If the base hit rate is about 30-60%, the most a better predictor could improve it is about 2-3x (1/base rate), not 10x. Capex does not fall 10x either, because the acquisition dominates and ML does not make it cheaper.

name: Franchise Seats: dormant exclusive municipal service franchises
one_line_reason: This is a standard waste or ambulance roll-up dressed up as discovery: exclusivity is a signed, known, published contract, operations dominate the work, and the step-up is about 2x, not 10^4.
fatal_flaw: There is no information asymmetry. The exclusive franchise is a signed contract the seller knows about and that the city publishes, so it is already in the purchase price. The step-up is a 1.3-2x multiple arbitrage that PE roll-ups and consolidators' own M&A teams already capture, not a jump of 10^3 or more.
step_up: About 1.3-2x on enterprise value (my estimate, not sourced: the search budget ran out before I could check). Small private haulers typically sell for roughly 4-7x EBITDA. Consolidators pay roughly 7-10x for tuck-ins, and public majors trade around 12-15x. Exclusive franchise routes do command a premium over open-market routes, but it is a multiple uplift, nowhere near 10^3. The candidate's own "~2-10x" is generous. A rate reset can lift EBITDA, but cities have to approve it and often cap it at CPI-linked formulas.
hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive proving attempt that usually fails. Confirming exclusivity means a lawyer reads one franchise agreement and ordinance, about $5k-25k per target (my estimate). The base rate of "hidden exclusivity" is probably high among operators that hold a contract, so ML has little to improve. The real cost is the acquisition itself, about $1M-20M per small operator (my estimate), and ML does not cut that tenfold.

name: Dormant Type Certificate Holdco
one_line_reason: The fleet data is already in structured FAA records, the step-up is a slow 3-10x from operations rather than an instant jump on a discovery hit, and most of the work is certification, support and liability rather than discovery.
fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Fleet size, AD burden and TC holder are already legible in the FAA registry, DRS and the FAA's orphaned-aircraft list, and the value of the asset comes from running a certified airworthiness-support and parts business with liability attached. There is no proving event that produces an immediate 10^3x step-up. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: finding the asset is easy and operating it is hard.
step_up: I could not find any priced deals: web search budget was exhausted, so every number below is my estimate from background knowledge. Unproven: dormant GA and light-twin TCs reportedly change hands for roughly $10k-$500k, often as part of an estate or bankruptcy (the candidate's own range). Proven: a TC with a live fleet and a parts business sells as an operating company at about 1-3x revenue. Small TC-holder support businesses (Univair-type, or the holders of the Aerostar, Lake, Ercoupe and Stinson TCs) are plausibly $1-20M businesses. There is no hit event that moves value 1000x immediately. Value builds slowly through parts sales and support contracts, so a realistic step-up is about 3-10x over years, not 10^4 on a hit. The candidate's own ~10-100x is optimistic.
hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly failing proving step like an exploratory drill. The proving step is a TC transfer through FAA paperwork, which costs roughly tens of thousands of dollars in legal and engineering work (my estimate) and almost always succeeds once a deal is agreed. The risk is commercial (will the fleet buy parts and support?), and the commercial facts are mostly knowable in advance. Because the base hit rate of the proving step is already high, ML can only raise it slightly: the cap of 1/base rate is about 1-2x, nowhere near 10x.

name: Feedstock Freighters
one_line_reason: Eligibility is mostly evident from legible fleet data, and the hit rate is already high. Value comes from a costly physical conversion, not discovery, so the step-up is under 3x and ML has nothing to lever.
fatal_flaw: The value comes from a $4-6M physical conversion, roughly the price of the airframe itself, that waits on scarce converter slots. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example in aviation form. Finding the right airframe is the easy, high-hit-rate, already-solved part; the bespoke physical step is the hard part. The step-up is also only about 1.2-2x, the sellers are sophisticated, and the deciding data is private, not public.
step_up: Estimates; no searches completed. A 737-800 bought as feedstock costs about $8-12M in 2023-25, against about $5-8M at part-out value, which is only 1.3-2x. A converted 737-800SF is worth about $16-20M, but you must put in about $5M of conversion to get there. A321 feedstock runs about $12-15M; a converted A321P2F is worth about $25-30M after about $6M of conversion. The net step-up is about 1.2-2x, not 10^3-10^4. The candidate's own figure of ~2-5x is optimistic.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate: most 737-800s, A321s and A330s of the right age and cycles are eligible. The base hit rate for 'records support conversion' is probably 60-80%+. A records audit and pre-purchase inspection costs about $50-250k per tail (estimate), which is tiny next to the airframe price. With a base hit rate that high, the lever is capped at 1/0.7, about 1.4x. ML cannot cut discovery capex 10x, because discovery is not where the capital goes.

name: Retired-Iron Grid Bank: decommissioned large power transformers
one_line_reason: The real lead-time shortage makes this a reasonable used-equipment brokerage, but it inverts the Terranox rubric: discovery is cheap and already legible, the physical step dominates, and the step-up is only single-digit.
fatal_flaw: Inside the rung, the physical step dominates: rigging, heavy haul, refurbishment and spec-matching are bespoke and cost about as much as the gain. Finding the units is easy, because retirements sit in legible EIA-860 fields and dealers and utilities already canvass them. The step-up is about 3-10x, not 10^3.
step_up: Unproven: a ~100-300 MVA unit sold for scrap is worth about $0.1-0.4M (estimate: roughly 20-40 t of copper plus steel and oil). Proven: a refurbished used LPT probably sells for $1-4M, against $3-10M+ new. The new-price range rests on the DOE 2014 LPT report ($2-7.5M), raised for the roughly 60-80% price inflation since 2020; both figures are from memory, not verified this run. The gross gain is about 3-15x, and closer to 2-5x net once $0.5-1.5M of haul, rigging and refurbishment is subtracted (estimate). The candidate's own claim of 10-50x is too high. That puts this far below the 10^3-10^4 band.
hit_rate_capex: Proving a unit means a DGA oil sample (about $100-500), Doble power factor tests, FRA and turns-ratio tests (roughly $5-30k per unit on site), all my estimates. Proving is cheap. The base hit rate is probably 30-60% of retired units being serviceable, but many are 40-60 years old and were retired near end of life (estimate). Because proving is already cheap and fails less than half the time, ML can cut proving capex by at most about 2-3x, nowhere near 10x.

name: Vested Fuel-Use Rescue: dormant gas stations as EV charging sites
one_line_reason: Physical and utility work outweighs discovery. The step-up is 1.5-3x on the parcel. Zoning and grid capacity answers are legible or utility-controlled. And charging does not need the vested fuel right, so the core asymmetry is illusory.
fatal_flaw: The "vested fueling use" premise does not hold up. EV charging generally does not need the grandfathered gasoline-dispensing right, because it is permitted or accessory in commercial zones and states are streamlining it. So the lapsing right protects nothing the buyer needs. The real constraint is grid capacity, which the utility decides and partly publishes in hosting maps, and which is cured with capex, not found by discovery. There is no 10^3 step-up and no low-hit-rate proving step for ML to lever.
step_up: No price data was retrieved because the shared web search budget was used up. All figures here are my estimates. A closed-station parcel in a secondary market might trade at about $300k-1.5M. A charger-ready version would gain perhaps 1.1-1.5x as land, since charging operators typically pay site-host rent (about $10k-50k per year per site, my estimate) or revenue share, not a land premium. An option might go from about $10k to about $50-150k assignment value (5-15x) in the best case, but option assignments to CPOs are not an established market. The candidate's own "1.5-3x on parcel" is the honest figure. That is far below 10^3.
hit_rate_capex: My estimates, unsourced because search was unavailable. A zoning check costs about $1-5k (a letter or a review by an attorney). A utility will-serve or capacity study costs about $5-25k and takes 3-12 months. The base hit rate for "commercial parcel near a highway can get charging zoning" is high, perhaps 70-90%, because EV charging is a permitted or accessory use in most commercial zones and several states (for example California AB 1236) require streamlined approval. The hit rate for "existing service is enough for 1+ MW DCFC without upgrade" is low, but that is fixed by spending on upgrades, not by discovery. A 1/base-hit-rate cap of about 1.1-3x means ML cannot cut capex 10x.

name: Misgraded EV Salvage
one_line_reason: Salvage-auction arbitrage in an efficient, legible market. The step-up is a few x at most, the hit rate is already high and the physical work is heavy, so it fails the Terranox 10^4, discovery-dominant test.
fatal_flaw: The step-up is about 1.5-3x into a commodity market, not 10^3-10^4. The asset is sold in a highly efficient, legible, competitive auction where the key signals (damage codes, starts/drives, flood brand, photos) are already structured fields read by thousands of professional bidders. The pack hit rate is already high (estimate about 50%+), so ML's lever is capped near 2x.
step_up: Estimate, no live search possible: salvage EVs typically clear at roughly 15-40% of ACV on Copart/IAA. A Model 3 pack might sell used for roughly $3k-8k against about $13-20k new. Buying a lot at around $5-10k and parting out the pack plus the car might return 1.3-2.5x gross on a good hit, before labour and fees. The candidate's own ~2-5x is optimistic, and the real number is far below 10^3. Proving the pack lifts the price from discounted to fair, not from zero.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate: most totalled EVs are written off for body/structural damage or because pack replacement looks uneconomic to the insurer, not because the pack is dead. So the share with usable packs is probably high (estimate 50-70%), and the proving step (a $100-300 diagnostic, per the candidate) is cheap. With a base hit rate around 0.5, the lever is capped near 2x, not 10x. Each mistake costs the vehicle price (thousands of dollars), not an expensive drill. ML can only shave misgrading at the margin.

name: Dormant CON bed rights bank
one_line_reason: The outcome is already a legible regulatory status field, the market is brokered and priced, the step-up is about 3-10x at best, and proving is legal paperwork with a high hit rate rather than a costly, low-hit-rate shot. It is a weak fit for the rubric.
fatal_flaw: There is little discovery to do. Whether a bed right exists and who holds it is already in legible state bed-inventory and need-table status fields and in CMS POS/HCRIS. Holders and brokers already price these rights in a known market. So there is no near-zero-to-10^4 mispricing for ML to unlock. On top of that, the asset can be made worthless by policy, through CON repeal or expiry of banked beds.
step_up: I could not check numbers: the shared web-search budget ran out before I made any query. What follows is my estimate from background knowledge. In moratorium or CON states (for example Ohio, Michigan, Kentucky, North Carolina, New York), SNF bed rights are reported to trade at roughly $5k-$30k per bed through brokers and in operator deals. An estate or closed operator that knows what its beds are worth sells near market. The candidate's '$0-2k/bed' entry price would only hold for distressed or unaware holders, which gives about 3-10x at best (I scored C2 a 1, toward the low end, because most holders know the price). It does not go from near zero to 10^3-10^4. In many cases beds that have lapsed or expired are simply void, so their value is zero rather than a mispriced option.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate, not sourced (no searches ran). Proving means a legal and regulatory check: chain of title, whether the banking period has run out, and whether the state will allow relocation. It costs roughly $5k-$50k in lawyer and consultant time per transfer (estimate). This is not an expensive, mostly-failing shot in the way an exploratory drill hole is. Once a bed shows as banked or licensed in the state inventory, the base hit rate is probably over 50%. So the 1/base-hit-rate lever is capped at about 2x, not 10x.

name: Stranded cannabis licence plus compliant-site packager
one_line_reason: This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure: siting is about 15% of the work while permits, capital and politics are about 85%, the outcome sits in legible regulator fields, the step-up is roughly 5-15x and needs a costly buildout, and the MSO buyers are shrinking.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is not discovery. Compliant parcels are easy to find with legible GIS and ordinance text, and are already mapped by cannabis real-estate brokers. What strands a licence is municipal SUP and opt-out politics, landlord refusal, buildout capital and transfer restrictions on social-equity licences, and ML touches none of these. The licence status is already a public field, and the MSO buyers are retrenching.
step_up: Unproven: a stake in a conditional licence (for example Illinois's 2021 lottery conditional adult-use dispensary licences, or NY CAURD) without a site. My estimate is about $50k-300k, and many are close to worthless near expiry. Proven: a licence converted and sited but not yet operating. My estimate is about $0.5-2M, and operating dispensaries in limited-licence states trade at a few hundred thousand to several million dollars, on revenue multiples that have compressed. That is roughly 5-15x, at the low end of the candidate's ~10-30x claim, and it requires the expensive buildout and permitting. All figures are from memory, not searched: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran, so I had no live sources.
hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate for finding a buffer-compliant parcel is high once a willing landlord exists. Failures come from municipal opt-outs, SUP denials, landlord refusals and money running out, not from failing to find parcels. Illinois's conditional adult-use dispensary cohort (192 licences, 2021-22) had deadlines extended several times, and only a minority were operating years later (from memory, roughly 20-40%; not verified). Cost per attempt is dominated by lease deposits, legal and SUP fees, and buildout, my estimate about $100k-1M+, and ML does not lower any of it. The lever on the discovery part is under 2x.

name: Revivable pocket liquor licences
one_line_reason: This is legal arbitrage on a regulator-legible status field, with a high base revival rate and only a 2-5x step-up. Neither the discovery-dominant frame nor the ML hit-rate lever applies.
fatal_flaw: The outcome is already legible and priced in. Licence status sits in public regulator databases (NJ POSSE, PLCB licence search, which shows safekeeping and expired), and the 12.39 revival is a routine, mostly-granted legal process. So there is no low-hit-rate proving step for ML to improve, and owners and brokers already price pocket licences near market value. That leaves a step-up of about 2-5x, not 10^3-10^4.
step_up: The candidate claims about 5-20x ($20-100k in, up to a full market licence out). All figures below are my estimates from memory; none were verified this run. NJ plenary retail consumption licences in quota-constrained towns trade around $300k-$1M+, and pocket licences already trade near that because buyers price the 12.39 risk. MA Boston and suburban all-alcohol licences trade around $300-600k. PLCB auctions of expired restaurant licences (Act 39, 2016) have cleared at about $100k-$700k+ depending on county. A truly distressed licence with an unclear renewal chain might trade at a 30-70% discount to full value, so the realistic step-up is about 2-5x. That is nowhere near 10^3.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate, not verified: the base hit rate looks high, not low. NJ ABC routinely grants 12.39 rulings when good cause is shown (for example, an active search for a site or a pending sale), so most licences that are actually alive get revived. Each attempt costs about $5-30k in legal fees plus 3-12 months of time (estimate). With a base hit rate around 50-80%, the ML lever is capped at about 1.3-2x, not 10x. The real constraint is supply and owner pricing, not the hit rate.

name: Landmark Air: landmark transferable development rights
one_line_reason: The unused floor area is already visible in PLUTO and known to owners, and the hard part is legal approval tied to a specific adjacent site. That makes it a thin brokerage-style arbitrage with a 1.5-3x step-up, not a Terranox-style discovery rung.
fatal_flaw: The outcome is already summarised in a legible public field (PLUTO built FAR versus maximum FAR), and owners already know and price their air rights. Value comes from the adjacency of a receiving site and a slow discretionary approval (LPC, CPC, ULURP), not from discovery. So there is no near-zero-to-10^3 jump: the step-up is about 1.5-3x, and ML's lever on a high base hit rate is under 2x.
step_up: No new data: the shared web search budget was used up before any search ran, so these figures are from memory and estimates. Manhattan air rights have generally traded at roughly $150-$450/sf of buildable area. Landmark transfers have historically cleared at a discount to as-of-right merger rights. In East Midtown (2017 rezoning), landmark transfers carried a minimum contribution to a public fund, set around $61.49/sf, and reported sales such as St. Patrick's Cathedral to JPMorgan were reported in the low hundreds of dollars per sf. The key point is that the unproven right is not near zero. Owners already know they hold unused FAR and price an option at a large share of the proven value. My estimated step-up from option to certified sale is about 1.5-3x, not 10^3. It only gets bigger where the owner is unaware or distressed, and that is rare for Manhattan landmarks.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate, not sourced. Telling whether a landmark has unused FAR is close to free and nearly always right, because PLUTO lists maximum FAR and built FAR. The expensive, uncertain step is the legal one: title and zoning-lot work at roughly $25k-$150k per lot, plus a special permit that costs $0.5-2M in counsel, consultants and time. Approval odds once a receiving site is lined up are moderate to high, perhaps 50-70%. The base hit rate on discovery is therefore already high, so ML's lever (capped at 1/hit rate) is under 2x, not 10x. ML does not shorten the approval process.

name: Reclass: closed shellfish areas proven clean
one_line_reason: This fails C4 hard. Regulators already sample these waters and publish the classification, the right is a nominal first-come state lease, and the step-up is about 10-100x in small dollars sold to thinly capitalised oyster growers with no big ladder above.
fatal_flaw: The proving step belongs to the state regulator, and its result is already published. State shellfish authorities sample every growing area routinely and publish the classification and fecal-coliform statistics, so the outcome sits in a legible public field. The proof cannot be run privately to capture an asymmetry, and the unproven right is a near-free first-come state lease rather than something bought cheaply from uninformed owners.
step_up: Estimate, not verified this run (no searches were available). Virginia VMRC leases state bottom at about $1.50/acre/yr, assigned by application. An unproven closed lease is worth about $0-50/acre. Proven Approved leased ground in productive Chesapeake areas plausibly trades at about $500-5,000/acre. WA private tidelands with good oyster ground could reach about $10k-50k/acre, but most of those are already Approved and owned by growers. Realistic step-up is about 10-100x in raw terms, but in small absolute dollars per acre, and the buyer gets it only after it adds the real work of seeding and growing for 2-3 years.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate. A sampling series plus sanitary survey costs about $20k-100k per area (about $100-300 per sample run over 15-30+ runs, plus staff and boat time over 12-24 months). The base hit rate for a closed area passing is low where the closure has a reason (WWTP outfalls, marinas and nonpoint runoff persist). Closures are largely driven by nonpoint sources and rainfall, which do not go away. The state already samples its classified waters routinely (NSSP requires annual reviews and triennial re-evaluations), so the easy wins are captured by the regulator for free. The ML lever is capped by state monitoring already surfacing the improving areas.

name: Riparian: NJ tidelands-claim title clearing
one_line_reason: This is title-cure arbitrage. Discounts are small, the hit rate is already moderate, the state claim layer and grant index are already legible and checked at every closing, a slow legal and bureaucratic step dominates the work, and the market is finite and stuck in one state.
fatal_flaw: The step-up is tiny (about 1.2-3x realistically) because the clouded discount equals roughly the cost of a riparian grant or SNI. Clearing is a routine, legible service that NJ title companies and riparian attorneys already provide, so there is no 10^4 jump and no information asymmetry to exploit.
step_up: Estimate, not sourced, because the search budget was used up. In the clouded parcels that trade (through a title exception or a seller who must get a grant), the discount is usually small. Buyers price in the cost of a riparian grant or an SNI, roughly in the thousands to low six figures, not a wipeout of the whole parcel's value. The candidate's '10-40% of value' purchase price is plausible only for parcels that are fully or mostly claimed and undevelopable. The realistic step-up is about 1.2-3x, and 2-10x is the optimistic ceiling. That is nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate. The proving cost per attempt is about $5-25k (survey, title or riparian counsel, and the NJDEP application fee, which is in the hundreds to low thousands). Hit rate: on parcels where a claim looks clearly wrong after the historical analysis, SNIs are probably granted more often than not, at a guessed 40-70%. With a base hit rate that high, ML can improve the hit rate by at most about 1.5-2.5x. The proving step is not expensive and mostly failing; the cost is time and the legal process.

name: Canopy Title: timber on heirs' and absentee parcels
one_line_reason: Discovery is cheap and almost never fails because the timber is visible, the step-up is about 2-3x rather than 10^3, and the hard part is acquiring the title, so it fails C2, C3 and C4 and stands as the calibration counter-example.
fatal_flaw: Timber is visible from the sky. Merchantable stands show up in free NAIP imagery and LiDAR, and existing forest maps already summarise them, so there is no hidden discovery. Proving rarely fails (hit rate about 90%), so the ML lever is about 1.1x. Because the land always has bare-land value, the step-up is only about 2-3x.
