The real bottleneck is title clearing on heirs' property, which is the physical-step-dominates failure from the geothermal counter-example. It works well as a calibration counter-example.
step_up: Estimate, not sourced, because the search budget was used up before any search ran. Southern US bare or cutover land sells for about $1,500-2,500/ac. Timberland with a merchantable pine stand sells for about $2,500-4,500/ac, and the stumpage on a mature stand is worth about $1,000-3,000/ac. So proving the timber takes an asset worth ~1x to ~1.5-3x. Nothing in this goes from near zero to 10^3. The land always has bare-land value, so the floor is high and the uplift is small. That fits the candidate's own "~2-4x" figure.
hit_rate_capex: A cruise costs about $5-15/acre (from the candidate brief, and consistent with standard forestry consulting rates). Once imagery has been checked, the cruise almost always confirms the timber, so the base hit rate is roughly 80-95% (my estimate). The rubric caps the ML lever at 1/base hit rate, which here is about 1.1-1.25x. There is no 10x drop in capex to win. The expensive and uncertain part is acquisition and title, not proving.

name: AMD Sludge Rights / Sludge Royalty
one_line_reason: Cheap, high-hit-rate assays and a published pH/Al proxy leave ML no lever. The step-up is from a small disposal liability to a small positive value, and processing, not discovery, dominates the work.
fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Proving grade costs a few hundred dollars by ICP-MS and is largely predictable from pH and Al that DMRs already report. The value sits in processing low-grade wet sludge into concentrate, which is bespoke chemical engineering. That is the same failure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example, and the proven asset is still only worth about $10-50 of contained REE per dry ton.
step_up: Unproven: sludge is a disposal liability today. Treatment operators and states pay to landfill or bury it, so it is worth about $0/t or less (estimate, roughly -$5 to -$30/t wet for disposal). Proven: AMD sludge runs about 300-1,000+ ppm TREE on a dry basis (WVU/Ziemkiewicz literature, recalled). At a ~$30-50/kg oxide basket that is roughly $10-50 of contained value per dry ton. A separator pays only a fraction of that for low-grade, wet, chemically variable feed, likely a few $/t at most (estimate). The step-up goes from a small negative to a small positive. It is roughly 1-10x on a near-zero base in a tiny dollar amount, nowhere near 10^3-10^4, and the candidate's own '~10-100x' is generous.
hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap and mostly succeeds. A commercial ICP-MS REE panel costs about $50-300 per sample (estimate from typical lab pricing), so even a thorough multi-sample site characterisation is a few $k. The candidate's $2-40k range overstates it. The hit rate is not low: the literature shows REE enrichment follows simple chemistry. Low-pH, high-Al, high-Mn discharges concentrate REE, and all three are already reported in DMRs. If the base hit rate is about 30-50% with a pH/Al screen, the ML lever is capped at about 2-3x on an already trivial cost. There is no expensive failing shot for ML to make cheaper.

name: Dormant Research-Reactor Irradiation Rights
one_line_reason: This is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern: suitability is already legible from flux and power fields, the proving step is heavy licensing and physical work with a high, knowable success rate, and the step-up is only about 3-30x, so ML has nothing to discover.
fatal_flaw: There is no discovery problem to solve. Whether a reactor is suitable is decided by flux and power, which are already legible public fields. Most 'dormant' university reactors are idle because their flux is too low to be commercially useful, not because nobody has read the data. The rung is mostly physical and regulatory work: licence amendments, hot cells, GMP handling and logistics. It is also crowded out by high-flux and power-reactor supply (MURR, Bruce/Isogen) and by accelerator routes. At heart it sells irradiation services to radiopharma incumbents.
step_up: All of these are my estimates from domain knowledge, not checked sources; no searches ran because the budget was used up. Unproven: a lease of spare flux time at a small university TRIGA reactor, plausibly tens to low hundreds of thousands of dollars a year. Proven: a supply contract for irradiated targets worth perhaps $0.5-5M a year, and only if the reactor has enough flux. That is roughly 3-30x on the lease and about 1x on the reactor itself. Nothing jumps 10^3-10^4 the moment a 'hit' happens. Value builds slowly through capex, licensing and operations.
hit_rate_capex: Again my estimates, unverified. There is no low-hit-rate search here. Whether a given reactor can make a given isotope is decided mainly by flux, which is in a public field. Commercially useful Lu-177 (Lu-176/Yb-176 routes) and Mo-99 by neutron capture need high flux, around 10^14 n/cm2/s or more. That is found at MURR (10 MW), MIT (6 MW), NIST, HFIR and ATR. Most of the roughly 30 US research reactors are TRIGA-class units under 1 MW, with flux around 10^12-10^13, which is too low for commercial quantities. The proving step itself is an NRC licence amendment plus engineering, probably $1-5M and 1-3 years each, and it mostly succeeds once flux is adequate. With a base hit rate that is high and already knowable, ML has close to zero lever (the cap is 1/base rate, around 1-2x).

name: Deadhead Timber / Sunken Stock: sunken old-growth log-drive logs
one_line_reason: Finding the logs is cheap and their locations are already known. The physical, regulatory work and the scattered market killed every Wisconsin permittee, and there is no ~10^3 step-up or capitalised buyer for a proven field.
fatal_flaw: Wisconsin BCPL's own program document says every entity that applied for a submerged logging permit has gone out of business, most administratively dissolved or bankrupt. The hard part is recovery, permitting, drying and milling, not finding the logs (the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure pattern). On top of that, the state owns the logs and takes 30%.
step_up: Unproven: a WI permit costs a $500 application fee plus a bond of at least $10k (2011 MI analysis citing WI; 1999 BCPL handbook). Proven: no market for a proven permit or field. Value only shows up as lumber. Sinker cypress sold for about $7-10/bf wholesale and dried in 2012 (forum quotes), against roughly $1-3/bf for fresh rough cypress. That is about 3-5x per board foot, not 10^3. The state owns the logs and keeps 30% of stumpage value.
hit_rate_capex: I found no published base hit rate. Logs sit in known places (boom sites, sorting gaps, river mouths, mill ponds), and side-scan sonar finds them cheaply (my estimate: $20-60k per stretch, as the candidate states, unverified). Finding them is not the bottleneck, so the ML lever is probably below 2x.

name: Ghost Spur Track Easements
one_line_reason: The value sits with the railroad's consent and the land, not the dormant easement. Proving is cheap legal work, ML adds no hit-rate lever, and the realisable step-up is a 10-50% land premium, not 10^3-10^4x.
fatal_flaw: The railroad, not the easement holder, decides whether a site is rail-served. Industry-track agreements are typically terminable by the railroad on short notice and cannot be assigned without its consent. Spur track can be removed without STB abandonment approval (49 U.S.C. 10906). So a 'proven' dormant right does not deliver rail-served status, and the railroad gives that status away for free through its own site programs to win carload volume.
step_up: From memory, as no searches ran: new industry track costs roughly $1-3M per mile including turnouts (each turnout roughly $150-300k). Those figures are commonly cited by railroads and economic-development agencies. Rail-served industrial land typically sells at a modest premium over truck-only land, my estimate 10-50%, not orders of magnitude. The unproven easement costs close to nothing to assign. But the proven easement is not worth much on its own, because the value sits in the land plus the railroad's willingness to serve. The realisable uplift to an easement holder is maybe the avoided cost of a new right-of-way corridor, $10k-$500k (estimate). In ratio terms against a $0 basis the multiple looks huge, but against the land value it lifts it is under 3x. On honest terms that is C2 = 1.
hit_rate_capex: The proving step today is a title search plus an inquiry to the railroad. That is cheap, roughly $2-10k per site for an abstract and attorney review (estimate). It is not an expensive, mostly failing physical shot like a drill hole. The base rate of a dormant ITA still binding the railroad is likely very low (estimate <5%). ITAs are usually terminable by the railroad on 30-90 days' notice and usually cannot be assigned without railroad consent. Under 49 U.S.C. 10906, spur and industry track can be removed without Surface Transportation Board (STB) abandonment approval, which makes it unlikely that dormant rights survive. ML does not raise that rate, because survival is a legal fact that depends on the railroad, not a hidden signal. There is no 10x capex lever on a step that is already cheap.

name: Terroir Proving: AVA petition land
one_line_reason: This fails the rubric: soil and climate data are already legible, AVA approval is near-certain and adds little value, and the 10-100x premium comes from planting plus decades of brand building, sold to buyers who are shrinking.
fatal_flaw: No discrete proving event creates value. An AVA petition is a near-certain administrative filing that adds little immediate value. The real premium comes from planting capex plus decades of brand reputation, so physical build-out and time, not discovery, are 90%+ of the work. That is the coal-mine-geothermal failure pattern.
step_up: From memory, not verified in this run: California rangeland or dry farmland sells for about $3-10k/acre (USDA/ASFMRA ranges). Planted vineyard values range from about $20-60k/acre in Paso Robles and Lodi, to $100-150k in Sonoma, to $300k-1M+ on the Napa valley floor. The gap between rangeland and Napa looks like 10-100x, but almost all of it comes from planting capex, decades of brand equity and scarcity. An AVA designation alone does not cause it. New AVAs such as Petaluma Gap (2017) and the 11 Paso Robles sub-AVAs (2014) brought no documented immediate land repricing that I know of. The immediate step-up from the AVA alone is estimated at under 2x on unplanted land. Also from memory: the 2024-25 grape oversupply has pushed down vineyard values in Sonoma, Lodi and the Central Coast, and growers are removing vines.
hit_rate_capex: Approval of TTB AVA petitions is high. From memory, nearly all well-documented petitions are eventually approved (about 275+ US AVAs), though it takes 1-4 years and costs about $20-100k in consultants (my estimate). With a base hit rate near 1, the ML lever is capped near 1x. Test plantings cost about $30-60k/acre and take 3-5 years for vines, and a quality verdict takes longer. These are not cheap, repeatable shots. ML on soil and climate cannot cut that cost 10x, because vines still have to grow.

name: Head Rights: senior water rights at non-powered dams
one_line_reason: Discovery is a minor share of a build-dominated small-hydro project; the right's status is already in legible state databases, so the step-up on proving is roughly 2-10x and there is no 80%+ discovery rung with a buyer paying 10^3x.
fatal_flaw: The value is in building the hydro project (about $4-10k/kW, licensing and fish passage), not in proving the right. Seniority and status are already recorded in legible state water-rights fields. So the step-up on proving is about 2-10x, not 10^4, and incumbent IPPs already screen the structured NPD inventories. It is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example again.
step_up: I could not get real numbers because the shared web-search budget was used up, so everything here is my estimate. Unproven dormant mill/power right plus parcel: $1-50k, per the candidate. A proven, adjudicated, non-abandoned non-consumptive power right at a small NPD (most are under 1 MW) is plausibly worth about $50-250k, because the asset only pays after $4-10M/MW of construction. A typical 300 kW site makes about 1.3 GWh/yr, roughly $65-100k/yr in revenue at $50-80/MWh. That cannot carry a large premium for the right. Realistic step-up is about 2-10x, not 10^3-10^4. The value sits in the energy project, not the right.
hit_rate_capex: My estimate, not re-searched: a seniority and non-abandonment check is a title-and-records exercise. A water-rights attorney or engineer opinion costs about $5-30k, and ownership records plus decree search are cheap. The base hit rate is not the problem: many old rights are on record. What usually kills these projects is economics (head, flow, build cost), not whether the right is valid. Proving is neither very expensive nor mostly failing, so ML gives at most a 2-3x cost cut on paralegal work, far short of 10x.

name: Small Closed Landfill Methane Rights
one_line_reason: This fails like geothermal in a coal mine: the hit rate is high and already predictable from legible EPA data, the step-up is under 5x, and capex goes into building wells and a flare, not into finding gas.
fatal_flaw: There is nothing to discover. Gas yield follows predictably from public tonnage and age data (EPA LMOP plus LandGEM), almost every landfill makes gas, and value is created by the $1-3M physical build and selling cheap credits, not by a proving step. No frame exists where discovery is 80% or more of the work.
step_up: About 1-5x at most (estimate; I could not verify it because the shared web search budget was used up). The unproven right is a lease on a closed small landfill, worth close to zero and often obtainable for a royalty. A proven, flaring project on a small site might make 10k-50k tCO2e/yr at voluntary landfill-methane prices of roughly $2-8/t (from memory; landfill credits are among the cheapest). That is about $50k-400k/yr of revenue against $1-3M of capex, with output falling each year after closure. Any value step-up is mostly the return on capex, not a jump in the value of the right. Nothing like the 10^4 from $1/ha to $10,000/ha.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is high, not low (estimate). Nearly every closed municipal landfill makes methane, and LandGEM predicts the volume well enough that a project fails on economics, not on whether gas is there. Cost per attempt is $1-3M (candidate figure), and most of that is build cost, not discovery. A cheap flux or probe screen costs about $10-50k (estimate) and already removes the unknowns. ML would at best cut that screening cost; it cannot change the $1-3M build. The lever, capped at 1/hit rate, is about 1.2-2x, not 10x.

name: Lapse-Rescue Life Settlements
one_line_reason: This fails the gold rubric on its core point. The policy's value lives in private medical files, not public illegible data. Each proving attempt costs only hundreds of dollars, and incumbents like Abacus and Coventry already run this exact lapse-rescue origination under a regulated auction market.
fatal_flaw: The data that sets the value (the insured's private medical records and LE) is non-public and consent-gated. There is no public-but-illegible corpus for ML to exploit. Proving is cheap and already done by specialist LE firms, and regulated broker auctions compete away any purchase discount. Discovery is not 80% of the rung.
step_up: Unproven: a lapsing term policy has a cash surrender value of $0. A UL near lapse has a small one. The insured would otherwise walk away for nothing. Proven: a converted policy on an insured with a short LE typically trades at about 10-25% of face, and LISA says settlements pay about 4-8x the cash surrender value. Both figures are from memory of industry materials, and I could not verify them this session. Against a $0 surrender value the multiple looks unlimited. But the price is cleared by competing brokers running auctions, and the buyer must also pay conversion premiums, often 3-8% of face per year (estimate). So the step-up you can actually capture as the purchaser is about 1.5-5x on cash invested (estimate), not 10^3.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: roughly 10-25% of submitted policies close (my estimate; providers decline most cases for long LE, small face or high premiums). Cost per proving attempt: an LE report is about $300-600, plus medical record retrieval of about $100-300 (estimates). That is cheap, so raising the hit rate saves little. ML on public data cannot predict LE better than underwriters reading private medical files. Lever: about 1.2-2x at most.

name: Liquidating Trust Residuals / Unclaimed Bankruptcy Distributions
one_line_reason: Fails the Terranox rule. The step-up is roughly 2-10x and capped by face value, not 10^4. Proving rarely fails and costs little, so ML has no hit-rate lever. Recoveries are already summarised in disclosure statements and priced by established claims buyers.
fatal_flaw: The asset's face value caps the step-up at a few x, and the outcome is already in legible fields (the disclosure statement's recovery table and the trustee reports) that a crowded professional claims-trading market prices within days. The trust interests, the most attractive target, are often non-transferable under the trust agreement.
step_up: Unproven claims typically trade at about 1-30 cents on the dollar, and a realised recovery is typically about 5-60 cents. That is usually 2-10x, with rare 20-100x outliers when a large D&O or avoidance settlement comes in late (my estimate from general knowledge of the claims market; not checked by search this run). Nothing like the 10^4x land re-rating in the Terranox model, because the claim's face value caps the upside. The candidate's own figure of '~5-100x; slow' is an upper bound. Payouts often take 2-5 years, which drags the IRR down.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: high, not low. Most allowed general unsecured claims in a confirmed liquidating plan pay something, maybe 60-80% of them (my estimate). The proving attempt is reading one docket, about $50-500 of analyst or PACER time (my estimate; PACER is $0.10/page, capped at $3 per document). That attempt is cheap and usually succeeds, so ML has no costly failure rate to cut. The lever (capped at 1/hit rate) is roughly 1.3-2x, not 10x. ML would mainly add throughput on claims too small for anyone to bother with.

name: Forgotten Foreclosure and Tax-Sale Surplus
one_line_reason: This fails the rubric. The value is known and legible ahead of time, fees are capped by law, the buyer is a county paying face value, the hit-rate lever is small, and there is no ladder up to a very large company.
fatal_flaw: The outcome, meaning who is owed and how much, is already printed in public county surplus lists, and statutory fee caps of about 10-33% limit the step-up. So there is no hidden value for ML to reveal and no 10^4 revaluation: it is a crowded collections business.
step_up: I could not check any numbers live: the shared web-search budget ran out on my first query, so everything here is from memory or my own estimate. The asset is never near zero. The county publishes the dollar amount, so the claim is worth face value from day one. The finder's take is capped by law. From memory: California Rev & Tax Code 4675 caps assignment and finder fees at about 10% of the excess proceeds; Florida's surplus statutes (Ch. 45 and s.197.582 regime) cap fees and need court or clerk approval; several states cap fees at 20-33%; and some states void assignments made within a window after the sale. Typical realised economics: get 10-35% of a known amount for a few hundred to a few thousand dollars of effort. That is roughly a 3-10x return on effort cost. It is not a 10^3-10^4 revaluation of the asset itself, because the value is fixed and already visible.
hit_rate_capex: Each attempt is cheap (my estimate): about $50-500 per lead for skip-trace and outreach, plus legal filing costs for contested or judicial claims. The base hit rate is moderate, not tiny. Industry folklore suggests roughly 10-30% of contacted leads sign and pay out. With a base rate around 0.2, ML can improve it by at most about 5x. The bottleneck is persuading heirs and competing with other agents, not finding the signal, so ML does not cut discovery capex 10x. I could not source these numbers live.

name: Food-contact substance notification (FCN) arbitrage for PFAS-free packaging
one_line_reason: Discovery is a small share of the work, the right is non-exclusive and replicable, and the FDA inventory already exposes the outcome. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mine failure applied to packaging chemistry.
fatal_flaw: There is no illegible, scarce, cheaply buyable right with a big step-up. FCNs are non-exclusive and replicable in about 120 days. The FDA inventory already states the substance and its intended use in legible fields. The work is in formulation, scale-up and converter qualification, not discovery. So the 95-5 discovery frame does not exist, and the step-up is roughly 10x rather than 10^3-10^4.
step_up: Estimate, not sourced (the search budget ran out): an unproven small-firm FCN plus know-how might change hands for about $0.1-1M. Getting a new FCN through FDA is commonly quoted in the industry at roughly $50k-$300k plus 120 days. A proven PFAS-free barrier with a major converter's qualification might be worth $5-30M as a licence or acqui-hire. That is about 10-30x at best, nearer 3-10x against the cost of simply filing your own FCN. The step-up is capped because FCNs are non-exclusive for the substance and a competitor can file its own in about 120 days.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate: a Kit/TAPPI bench test costs about $200-$2,000 per sample at a contract lab, and a pilot coater trial about $10-50k. Bench hit rates are not low, because many PFAS-free chemistries (PVOH, latex/acrylic dispersions, waxes, biopolymers) already pass Kit 8-12 at the right coat weight. The binding problems are cost per tonne, repulpability and heat resistance, not finding the needle. With a base hit rate perhaps above 20%, the lever is capped at about 5x, on a step that is already cheap.

name: Recontactable Protective-Variant Carrier Network
one_line_reason: Genuinely illegible public data, but no ownable right, no asset that revalues on a hit, a bespoke non-abstracted proving step gated on IRBs and individual re-consent, and the buyers already do it in-house at biobank scale — it is a service business dressed as an asset play.
fatal_flaw: The right cannot be bought, owned, or made exclusive — human research participants are not mineral title. A recontact agreement is revocable, non-assignable and contingent on IRB approval and individual re-consent, so there is no asset that revalues on a hit and nothing to hold while it appreciates. Compounding this, the counterparty you buy from (the paper's own authors) is the single best-informed reader of the data, so the information asymmetry the model depends on does not exist, and the buyers you would sell to (Regeneron Genetics Center, Amgen/deCODE) already run this exact play in-house with consent-at-enrollment recontact rights across million-person biobanks.
step_up: Estimate, unsourced. The "unproven right" is quoted at $20-100k for a data-use/recontact agreement. A validated protective-target package (human genetic LoF evidence plus phenotyped carriers) is worth somewhere in the $1-20M range as a pharma deal, which on paper is ~10-100x. But that comparison is unsound: the $20-100k agreement is not the asset — it is permission to attempt work, and the proving step (re-consent, blood draws, deep phenotyping on 5-50 geographically scattered people, assay development) is itself a seven-figure, multi-year cost that dwarfs the right. Net of true proving cost, the step-up is roughly 3-10x at best, and the holder of the asset (the academic cohort owner) captures most of it because they can re-trade with any buyer. Scored 1-2; I give 1 because there is no moment at which a "hit" revalues a thing you own.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate, unsourced. Base rate of a published rare-LoF observation becoming a validated, pharma-purchasable protective target is very low — single-digit percent at best, which superficially looks like a good ML lever. But the cost per proving attempt is dominated by non-ML, non-parallelisable items: IRB amendment and local ethics (months of calendar time, not dollars you can throw 10x more of at), investigator goodwill (a strictly rationed, non-purchasable input), and clinical phenotyping. ML can raise the shortlist quality — the literature-mining part is genuinely automatable — but the binding constraint is consent and institutional access, so cutting the discovery step 10x buys you almost no extra shots. The lever caps on the scarce input, not the base hit rate. Also the main buyers (Regeneron Genetics Center, Amgen/deCODE, Novo, Lilly) already run exome/genome biobanks in the hundreds of thousands to millions of participants with recontact consent built in at enrollment — they have solved the access problem structurally rather than deal-by-deal.

name: Indication Expander: new-indication 510(k)s on dormant clearances
one_line_reason: Fails the core rubric. The right is non-exclusive and not needed, the regulatory and clinical work is most of the cost rather than discovery, 510(k)s mostly succeed so there is no hit-rate lever, and the step-up is about 10x at best and can be copied.
fatal_flaw: A 510(k) gives no exclusivity: anyone can cite any cleared device as a predicate without owning it, and a new indication usually needs clinical data rather than MAUDE or off-label evidence. So the bought right has no scarcity value, the proving step rarely fails, so ML has no hit-rate lever, and the cleared output is easy for competitors to copy, which leaves no 10^3-10^4 step-up.
step_up: Estimates, not sourced (the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent could search). Dormant 510(k)s with no revenue usually change hands as part of small asset sales, often well under $50k, and many are simply abandoned. A cleared new indication with no sales, no quality system and no reimbursement probably sells to a strategic for $0.3-3M at most, about 10-60x the candidate's own $5-50k figure, and only if the indication is defensible. The value is not exclusive: once you are cleared, any competitor can file its own 510(k) citing your device as the predicate. So the proven asset is a reference point anyone can copy, not a scarce right. Strategics pay for revenue, IP and data, not for clearance letters.
hit_rate_capex: These are estimates from general knowledge; no web search was run. The FDA user fee is about $24-26k (FY2025/26 standard), and a full submission costs about $100-250k without a clinical study, or $1-10M+ with one. Most 510(k) submissions that reach a decision are found substantially equivalent, roughly 70-85% after AI rounds, with withdrawals as the main failure. So the proving step does not mostly fail today. The low hit rate is in commercial value, not regulatory success, and ML over MAUDE has nothing to raise. The lever is capped near 1/0.75, about 1.3x, not 10x.

name: Predicate Bank: dormant surgical and medical-robot 510(k) clearances
one_line_reason: Owning a 510(k) gives no exclusive right, because predicates can be cited by anyone for free. The SE outcome is already public, about 80% of 510(k) decisions are SE so the hit-rate lever is roughly 1.25x, and the hard part is DHF and QMS work, so there is no 10^3 step-up or discovery-dominated rung.
fatal_flaw: Predicate status is a free public good. Anyone may cite any legally marketed device in their own 510(k) without owning or licensing it. A strategic avoiding De Novo therefore gets the whole benefit from the public database for free. The bought 510(k) is worth something only for marketing the identical device, and that device is the defunct product that already failed. On top of that, the SE outcome is already a legible public field.
step_up: I could not verify this. The web search budget was used up before any query ran, so these numbers are my estimates and are not sourced. The candidate claims an unproven 510(k)+DHF costs $20-200k. A clearance on its own, separated from a manufacturing operation, sells for very little because the buyer cannot use it for a different device. Clearances that do sell usually go inside distressed asset or IP sales and are priced on the technology, team and inventory, not the clearance. A "proven" mapping adds nothing a buyer cannot get for free. Any legally marketed device can be cited as a predicate by anyone, with no ownership or license required (21 CFR 807.92/807.100). My estimate of the step-up is 1-3x, and it is not a 10^2 to 10^4 jump. Avoiding De Novo is worth roughly the gap between De Novo and 510(k) costs: FY2025 MDUFA fees of about $160k versus about $24k, and program costs of about $1-3M versus about $0.2-1M (estimate). That saving comes from the public predicate, not from owning the clearance.
hit_rate_capex: The proving step does not fail often. My estimate, from memory of FDA reporting, is that about 75-85% of 510(k) final decisions are SE, so the hit-rate lever is capped near 1/0.8, about 1.25x, and is nowhere near 10x. Cost per attempt is about $24k in FDA fee plus testing and consulting, which I estimate at $200k-1M for a robotic system. ML predicate-selection tools already exist and target the same step: Basil Systems, RegDesk, and many regulatory consultants. None of this was verified, because the search budget was used up.

name: HCPCS Ghost Codes: DMEPOS codes with dead suppliers
one_line_reason: The answer can be read off structured public lists (DMECS plus FDA), the right is not exclusive, proving is cheap and usually succeeds, and the value comes from making and selling the product, not from discovery.
fatal_flaw: A HCPCS code is not an exclusive right. Any maker can get an equivalent product verified by PDAC, at low cost and with a high hit rate. The "ghost code" gap is visible in public structured data (DMECS joined to FDA registration). So there is no hidden discovery to do, nothing scarce to own, and no step-up on a hit. What is left is ordinary manufacturing and distribution work.
step_up: I estimate about 1-5x on the right itself. The candidate's own guess is 10-30x, and I could not support that. Live web searches were refused because the shared search budget for this turn was exhausted, so the numbers below are from my own knowledge and are not sourced. Distributors such as AdaptHealth and Medline buy products at a markup over manufacturing cost. They do not pay a premium for a coding verification, because the verification is not exclusive. The step-up happens only through operating margin on units sold, not through the asset being repriced as soon as a hit lands. A dormant 510(k) for a low-risk DME device probably trades in the low tens of thousands of dollars or less (my estimate). Many DME items are 510(k)-exempt Class I or II devices (manual wheelchairs, many orthoses, canes), so the 510(k) often carries little value at all.
hit_rate_capex: I put the base hit rate of PDAC verification at high, likely over 70% for a product that truly matches a code's description (my estimate). Rejections are usually fixed by resubmitting. The cost of a PDAC review is close to zero: as I understand it there is no application fee, only staff time. The $50-200k in the candidate is mostly manufacturing restart and quality-system cost, not proving cost, and ML does not lower it. Since the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, it is about 1.4x at most. That is not 10x. These figures are not sourced (search budget exhausted).

name: Stalled PMN Rescue: abandoned TSCA new-chemical submissions
one_line_reason: A regulatory-delay play, not a discovery play. The base clearance rate is high, the outcome is public and legible, ownership after listing is weak, the step-up is about 1-5x, and scale-up and customer qualification dominate the work.
fatal_flaw: The proven asset is not ownable and is not a discovery. Clearing a PMN puts the substance on the public TSCA Inventory, where anyone can make it. Most PMNs clear anyway, so ML adds only about 1.1-1.5x, and the determination is already written into legible EPA fields. There is no 10^4 step-up to capture.
step_up: Unproven: a stalled dossier plus test data at the candidate's assumed $50-200k (not verified). Proven: a cleared PMN is not a separately traded asset with a market price. Once the Notice of Commencement is filed, the substance goes on the public TSCA Inventory and any company can make it for non-exempt uses, subject to any SNUR or consent order. So the cleared right is mostly non-exclusive. The value that can be captured comes from CBI-masked identity, know-how and customer qualification, not from the clearance. My estimate is a 1-5x uplift on dossier cost for a resale to a specialty maker. The candidate's own ~10-30x looks optimistic, and it already notes weak ownership after listing. Nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: most PMNs eventually clear. Historically about 80-90% end with a 'not likely' determination or with an order/SNUR; the remainder are withdrawn, often after EPA signals concerns. This is from memory and could not be checked (searching unavailable). Cost per attempt: EPA PMN fee is about $37,000 (2024 fee rule; about $6,480 for small businesses) plus about $20k-$500k+ of testing when EPA asks for data (my estimate). Review takes 1-2+ years against a statutory 90 days. Because the base hit rate is high, the lever (capped at 1/base) is only about 1.1-1.5x. The real pain is delay, not failure, and ML does not shorten EPA's queue.

name: Predicate Bank (tobacco): grandfathered nicotine product status
one_line_reason: Proving grandfathered status creates no exclusive, ownable asset, and the step-up is about 3-20x, not 10^3. In practice this is regulatory consulting to a shrinking industry.
fatal_flaw: Predicates are non-exclusive. The law lets any applicant cite any grandfathered or SE-cleared product without owning it, so proving status creates no ownable asset to sell for a step-up. The price falls to the cost of producing evidence, which makes it a consulting service, not an owned asset. The high-value buyers (big tobacco) already have predicates, and the segment with the strongest demand (ENDS) has none.
step_up: Unverified estimate. The candidate says a dormant pre-2007 line plus its records costs $10-50k. A proven, documented predicate is worth roughly the cost a buyer avoids by not doing a PMTA instead of an SE: PMTA $1-10M+ (FDA's own deeming-rule cost estimates, from memory) versus SE about $50-300k. That puts the ceiling for a proven predicate at maybe $100k-$1M, but only where no substitute predicate exists. That is about 3-20x, not 100-1000x. And because predicates are not exclusive, the price falls toward the cost of producing the evidence (consultant fees).
hit_rate_capex: Unverified estimate. Proving a predicate is not a low hit-rate gamble. Documents like invoices, catalogues, TTB permits and state MSA listings either exist or they do not, and checking costs about $5-30k in consultant and legal time. FDA's NSE and refuse-to-accept outcomes mostly come from differences between the new product and its predicate or from missing data, not from failing to find a predicate. For example, in 2021 FDA refused large batches of applications covering millions of deemed products on content grounds (from memory). Base hit rate on predicate status is probably above 50% when records exist, so the ML lever is capped at about 2x. It is not a 10x lever.

name: Coastwise Hulls: Jones Act eligibility in scrap-bound hulls
one_line_reason: The answer is already printed on the hull's COD, sellers know it, and the value lies in shipyard conversion rather than discovery, so there is no 95/5 frame and no ML lever.
fatal_flaw: Coastwise eligibility is already a public, legible endorsement field on the USCG Certificate of Documentation, and it is usually intact (high base hit rate), so discovery adds almost no value. The step-up comes from heavy, bespoke conversion capex, which is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode.
step_up: Estimate only; my search budget ran out, so none of these numbers are sourced. A hull bought at scrap value (light ship weight x roughly $300-500/LT for US domestic scrap) might be worth 1.5-3x that as a coastwise-eligible hull before conversion. The candidate's ~10-50x step-up appears only after a multi-million-dollar conversion, and that is a build margin, not a discovery step-up. Remember that the 2016-2021 OSV downturn sent many fully coastwise-eligible US Gulf OSVs to scrap or cold stack. That suggests eligibility alone carries little premium when the conversion or operating economics fail.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate. The base hit rate is high, not low. Most US-built, US-flag hulls headed for scrap still have their coastwise endorsement, because losing it takes a foreign rebuild, foreign registry or sale to a non-citizen under 46 USC 12132 and 46 CFR 67.177, and those events are uncommon and recorded. A proving attempt costs a records review plus a USCG rebuild determination request, maybe $5k-50k in counsel and survey time. Because the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, ML can improve it by about 1.2-2x at most, not 10x.

name: Obsolete IC Surplus Lots matched to military demand
one_line_reason: This is a crowded broker business. The discovery step (reading printed part numbers against structured DIBBS data) is already easy and done by others. The value depends on traceability and authentication testing, which ML cannot supply, and DoD counterfeit rules work against untraceable surplus.
fatal_flaw: Provenance, not identification, is what creates the value. Military buyers discount parts with no traceability back to the original manufacturer, and DFARS 252.246-7007/7008 plus DLA QSLD restrict buying them. Reading the markings (the ML step) is easy and already widespread among brokers and harvesters. Authenticating parts with no chain of custody is the expensive step, ML on photos does not improve it, and it is the main counterfeit risk area that the rules exist to keep out.
step_up: My estimate, no searches ran. Scrap e-waste and mixed surplus boards or reels sell for roughly $1-20/lb. Authenticated EOL military-grade ICs can sell for about $20-500+ per unit, and some rare line items for more. Per hit line item the multiple can be 100x or more, but averaged over a lot it is closer to 10-100x. Most of a typical lot is commodity or worthless parts, and the testing cost of about $1k-5k per part number (estimate) comes out of the gain. The 100-1000x figure only holds for the rare item. The asset's value does not jump because of identification alone: unidentified-provenance parts trade at a discount even after they are identified.
hit_rate_capex: My estimate, no sources. Identification is cheap and already common: brokers and harvesters read markings by eye or with basic OCR and check them against NetComponents, IC Source and ERAI. Lots are bought for a few hundred to a few thousand dollars, and identifying what is inside costs labor-hours, not drill-level capex. The expensive and often-failing step is authentication: AS6171 test suites cost about $1k-5k+ per part number (estimate), and non-traceable lots often fail or come back inconclusive. ML on photos does not raise the authentication pass rate, because whether a part is counterfeit or a reclaimed pull is decided by lab tests (X-ray, decap, XRF), not by the markings. The lever on the costly step is about 1-2x, not 10x.

name: Shuttered Cleanroom Shells
one_line_reason: This fails C1-C4. Fab shells are a few hundred known, legible assets sold by sophisticated owners at fab-aware prices, so the step-up is under 3-10x, the hit rate is already high, and the hard part is the physical refit, not discovery.
fatal_flaw: There is no information gap and no discovery-dominated rung. Fabs are a small, fully catalogued set of assets whose owners and buyers know their value. Proving revivability is a bespoke physical refit, not a cheap test that mostly fails. This is the coal-mine geothermal pattern, plus the powered-brownfields problem of no purchase discount.
step_up: About 1.5-3x, maybe 3-10x in the best case (my estimate). Closed fabs do not sell at warehouse prices because the buyers already know what a fab is. From memory, not searched this run: TI bought Micron's Lehi fab for about $900M in 2021; ON Semi bought GlobalFoundries' East Fishkill fab for about $430M; TI bought Qimonda Richmond tools for about $172.5M in 2009. Prices like these already include most of the revival value. I could not verify any warehouse-price fab sale.
hit_rate_capex: The proving step has no low base hit rate. Whether a known fab can be revived is mostly decided by a site visit and engineering review, so the hit rate is already high (estimate: more than 50% of marketed fabs are revivable at some cost). That puts the lever near 1/0.5 = 2x at most. The real cost of proving is a recertification and utilities refit, roughly $10M-$100M+ (my estimate), and ML does not lower that cost.

name: Stalled NEVI Award Rescue
one_line_reason: Fails the Terranox test: the build, not the discovery, dominates; the step-up is about 2-5x; site status is already in public status fields; and grant assignment is gated by the state DOT.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is not discovery. The value is unlocked by about $1M of physical construction per site plus a non-assignable federal grant needing state DOT approval, and the site status is already published in legible NEVI reports. That leaves no hidden-signal arbitrage and a step-up of only about 2-5x, which is politically fragile.
step_up: My estimate (no sources were reachable this run): a stalled package of an award, a site lease and a pending utility application might trade at about $25-150k, with heavy uncertainty, because there are no sold comps. A site that is energized or ready to build might sell to a charging operator for about $150-400k as a developer premium, on top of reimbursing what has been spent. That is roughly a 2-5x step-up. It is not 10^3, and it only shows up after the build capital has been spent. The step-up is also politically fragile: FHWA suspended state NEVI plan approvals in February 2025, and courts and new guidance in 2025 only partly undid that.
hit_rate_capex: Most awarded sites probably do energize in the end, so failures mean delay rather than a dry hole. I would guess well over 50% eventually energize. With a base hit rate that high, the lever is capped at under about 2x, because the maximum is 1/base hit rate. The candidate puts the cost of the proving step at $20-50k per site (its own number, unverified). However, the money that is actually at risk is the roughly $1M build, and better site selection does not reduce that.

name: Curb-Power Rights: municipal curbside charging franchises
one_line_reason: This is build-heavy infrastructure. Rights are tendered and non-assignable, grid and demand data are legible, and the step-up is about 1-3x once build capex is counted. It repeats the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure.
fatal_flaw: The asset's value comes from building and operating it, not from discovering it. Getting a curbside site energised needs hardware, civils and grid works at roughly 1x the proven value, and rights are allocated by competitive council tender, not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data. That leaves no 80%-discovery rung, no 10^3 step-up, and no illegible-data edge.
step_up: Unproven: a dormant pilot permit or encroachment consent is worth roughly $0 to a few hundred dollars per site (my estimate; it is a revocable licence, not property). Proven: an energised lamppost or kerbside charger is typically valued at roughly replacement cost plus a modest premium. That is about £3-6k hardware plus installed cost for a lamppost unit and £8-15k for a kerbside post (my estimate, from UK industry figures recalled from memory, not verified this session). Once you count the capex you spend to get there, the value gained is about 1-3x the money put in, not 10-30x. The candidate's 10-30x compares against the permit's nominal cost and leaves out the build cost.
hit_rate_capex: The proving step (DNO connection offer plus utilisation) is not mostly failing. Most low-power lamppost and kerbside connections are approved, because the load is 3-7 kW and runs off existing street-lighting or LV supply. Utilisation risk is real (UK on-street average utilisation is often cited at roughly 5-15%; estimate, not verified), but a failed site loses the hardware cost, about $5-15k (estimate), not a cheap probe. If the base hit rate is about 50%+ (estimate), the ML lever is capped at under 2x. The expensive step is the build, not the guess.

name: Latent Permit: dormant limited-entry fishing permits
one_line_reason: The 'proving' step is uncontrollable rulemaking, not discovery. Allocation is history-based and already legible to holders and regulators, and latent permits are what councils deliberately cut out, so there is no 95-5 frame and no hit-rate lever.
fatal_flaw: The value is set by a slow political allocation that rewards catch history the seller already knows about. A dormant permit almost by definition has no history, so it gets near-zero quota. Control dates and latent-licence removal exist precisely to stop this kind of speculation, and no discovery problem exists that ML could solve.
step_up: This is my estimate from general knowledge and is not verified. Latent permits trade for about $1-10k. A permit with heavy catch history going into a catch share can turn into quota worth $100k to several million dollars (for example Gulf red snapper IFQ shares, Pacific trawl IFQ, Alaska crab rationalisation). But allocation is almost always based on catch history in qualifying years, so a permit with no recent landings gets about zero, or at most a small equal-share slice. For the permits this strategy can actually buy, the expected step-up is about 1-3x, or a loss if the permit is cancelled. The rare upside of 10-100x mostly goes to permits with history, and their holders already know that and price it in.
hit_rate_capex: There is no repeatable proving attempt that ML could make cheaper. Each fishery gets one allocation decision, made by council vote. Cost per 'attempt' is the permit price plus holding costs (annual renewal fees, about $100-1k per year, my estimate) over 5-15 years. Councils publish control dates specifically so that history built up after the date does not count, and they often remove latent licences outright: the Alaska groundfish and crab LLP latent licence actions of about 2008-2011 are examples, from memory and not verified. So the base 'hit rate' for a latent permit getting a meaningful allocation is low, but it is set by policy, and better prediction does not raise it. The ML lever is about 1x.

name: CatalystCell: buried refinery catalyst landfills
one_line_reason: Fails the frame test, like coal-mine geothermal. Finding the catalyst is easy and already partly recorded in RCRA manifests. Excavation, hazardous treatment and inherited liability are most of the cost. What is buried is low-value Ni-Mo-Co, not PGM, so the step-up is near break-even from a negative start.
fatal_flaw: The valuable PGM catalysts were reclaimed, not buried. What sits in refinery landfills is low-grade Ni-Mo-Co diluted in hazardous mixed waste. Excavating and treating it costs about as much as the metal is worth or more. The cell cannot be bought as a cheap right without inheriting CERCLA and RCRA post-closure liability. So discovery is not the bottleneck and there is no 10^3-10^4 step-up.
step_up: My estimates, not sourced. Unproven: a closed cell carries 30-year post-closure care plus CERCLA liability, so its value is negative, roughly -$1M to -$10M. Proven: Ni-Mo/Co-Mo hydroprocessing catalyst is worth about $500-3,000/t of contained metal, depending on the Mo price (~$20/lb). It is diluted in mixed sludge, soil and debris. Excavation, hazardous handling and transport cost about $150-400/t before any metal processing. Net value of a proven cell is roughly break-even to modestly positive, not $1-10M per hit. Starting from negative, the move is "less negative," far below 10^3x. Pt/Re/Pd reforming catalysts (0.3-0.6 wt% Pt) were almost always reclaimed under refiner metal-management or leasing accounts, so the PGM upside rarely sits in landfills.
hit_rate_capex: Proving cost $20-50k per cell for test pits, XRF and assay (the candidate's figure; plausible). My estimate is that the base hit rate for "this refinery cell contains catalyst" is fairly high, perhaps 30-60%, because refineries landfilled spent hydrotreating catalyst on site routinely before EPA listed it as K171/K172 hazardous waste in 1998. The rate of hits that are economic after excavation is very low, but ML cannot fix that, because it is set by grade and treatment cost, not by locating the material. The lever is capped at about 1/0.4, roughly 2-3x, not 10x. Proving is also not the expensive step.

name: Sweeps: precious-metal recovery from decommissioned industrial buildings
one_line_reason: This fails the core rubric. The work is physical recovery, not discovery. The business type already identifies the sites, and refiners already sweep them. Value steps up maybe 2-10x, not 10^4, and plating-site liability can wipe out the uplift.
fatal_flaw: There is no information asymmetry and discovery is not the bottleneck. Owners and their refiners already know metal sits in the floors, drains and ducts and routinely harvest it at closure. What remains is labour- and hazmat-heavy physical recovery with environmental liability attached, so the 95-5 discovery frame does not exist.
step_up: I have no sourced numbers, because the shared search budget ran out before my first query and no search ran. Estimates: salvage rights to a demolition-bound plating or jewelry building cost roughly $0 to slightly negative. A large old jewelry or dental plant might recover maybe $20k-$500k of Au/Ag/PGM, and a small plating shop maybe $1k-$30k. After paying for demolition labour, hazmat disposal and refiner charges (a few percent of value plus fees), net value is maybe 2-10x what was spent on the right and the swab. A swab hit does not make the right itself worth 10^3x more, because no market trades swab-proven salvage rights. The candidate's own '10-1000x' is measured against a near-zero base, which inflates it.
hit_rate_capex: Unsourced estimate: a swab and fire-assay campaign costs $5-15k per the candidate, but $1-3k per site is more realistic (fire assay is roughly $30-80 per sample). The base hit rate for 'measurable precious metal' at a known former plating, jewelry or dental site is probably high, maybe 50%+, because the use type itself is the signal. With a hit rate that high, the 1/hit-rate cap limits ML to about 2x, nowhere near 10x. The real uncertainty is how much metal is there and what recovery costs, not whether metal is present.

name: Orphan Source Capital: disused Am-241, Cf-252 and Pu-Be sources
one_line_reason: Discovery is trivial because the sources are registered, while licensed handling dominates the cost. The step-up is about 3-30x on a few thousand dollars, the hit rate is near 100% (so there is no ML lever), and OSRP and the manufacturers already recover these sources.
fatal_flaw: There is no illegible discovery problem. Every disused source is already registered by isotope, activity and holder in NRC GL registrations, NSTS and state licence records, and OSRP already collects many of them for free. The value-adding step is licensed hot-cell and regulatory handling, not finding. That handling caps a step-up of a few thousand dollars per source.
step_up: Rough step-up, all my estimates (I could not verify any of them, see the data field): from about -$2k to -$10k (commercial disposal of an Am-Be gauge source, worse for greater-than-Class-C sources) up to about +$0.5k to $5k resale for a recertified 10-50 mCi Am-Be source. A typical Troxler source is about 40 mCi Am-241, roughly 12 mg of Am. That is a swing of a few thousand dollars per source, i.e. 3-30x at best on small dollars, not 10^3-10^4. The Cf-252 sub-thesis is weaker: Cf-252 has a 2.65-year half-life, so a disused source is mostly decayed and is worth nothing. The Pu-Be sub-thesis is worse: the plutonium is DOE/NNSA-controlled material, which goes back through the Off-Site Source Recovery Program (OSRP) and is not freely resaleable.
hit_rate_capex: The leak and activity tests are cheap (my estimate: about $50-300 per wipe test) and pass most of the time. The base 'hit rate' is near 100% because the source's identity and activity are already known from its registration. So there is no low base rate for ML to improve; the lever is capped near 1x. The real costs are re-encapsulation (my estimate: $5k-50k+ per hot-cell campaign), licensing and transport, and ML does not reduce those.

name: Warbird Registry / Provenance Air: wartime-identity proof for airframe wrecks
one_line_reason: Proving identity is a small, already-crowdsourced part of a bespoke restoration business with a small premium and a tiny market, so it fails C1, C2 and C5.
fatal_flaw: This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure. Buyers pay for the bespoke $1-3M restoration and for the physical airframe, not for the proof of identity. Identity adds only about 1.2-3x, and an obsessive enthusiast community has already worked it out and published it in legible serial databases. The market is also tiny.
step_up: An identity premium exists but it is small. Example: two P-40N-5 combat-veteran projects (one with 3 kill flags) at a combined $895k (Courtesy Aircraft, 2022). That fits the market rate for P-40 projects of that completeness, so I see no 10^3 jump from proven combat identity. Loose data plates sell for a few hundred dollars generic versus about $1,000 with a notable history (WIX, 2005 anecdote), about 2-5x. Identity on a whole wreck probably adds 1.2-3x (estimate). Most of the value comes from the type and the amount of airframe surviving, both of which are visible before any research.
hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap and mostly succeeds already. Researchers, Pacific Wrecks, WIX members and the Joe Baugher serial lists identify most significant wrecks by hand, at an estimated $1-10k of archive time each. Wrecks that can't be identified usually lack plates or stampings, and ML over record cards can't fix missing physical evidence. Base hit rate is high (estimate >50% for intact types), so the 1/hit-rate lever is under 2x. Capex is dominated by recovery and restoration, which ML does not touch.

name: Provenance Wine Vault: estate cellars proven via merchant and château records
one_line_reason: This is a low-multiple wine-arbitrage service. Proving provenance is worth about 1.25-2x, costs hundreds of dollars per bottle in physical work, uses mostly private archives, and runs into auction houses that already do provenance checks for consignors, so it fails C1-C4.
fatal_flaw: No 10^3 step-up. A cellar of unknown provenance already sells at roughly 50-80% of the proven price (my estimate), and proof costs $700-1,200 per bottle in physical inspection that ML cannot remove. Auction houses already do the provenance research free when they take a cellar on consignment.
step_up: I found no matched-lot study of ex-cellar versus unknown-provenance prices. My estimate is that unknown-provenance lots of the same wine sell at a 20-50% discount, so proving provenance is worth about 1.25-2x. The upside is not 10^3. Comparison points: auction prices for Lafite ran 102-294% above trade prices (Decanter), which is an auction-versus-trade gap, not a provenance effect. A Christie's 1973 Stag's Leap lot hammered at $22,500, 275% over its high estimate, but that is a single outlier. The buyer's premium of about 20-27.5% eats a large share of the uplift. The asset never starts near zero: an old Bordeaux cellar already has a liquid market value before it is proven.
hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is high, not low. My estimate is that the large majority of genuine old estate cellars authenticate as authentic. The real variable is condition, which ML on documents cannot change. Cost per proving attempt: Chai Vault priced bottle authentication at $700 per bottle or $1,200 per inspection and report (Decanter, 2015). Bill Koch spends about $800 per bottle on expert inspection plus lab tests (Punch). The cost scales with bottle count, so ML can only remove the archive-research part. That makes the lever about 1.2-2x, nowhere near 10x, and with a high base hit rate the 1/hit-rate cap is also near 1.

name: Relight: dark but alive TV licences for ATSC 3.0 datacasting
one_line_reason: Finding dark licences is a lookup of FCC status fields. The work and the risk are in relighting and in demand, and the uplift is about 2-5x, so this fails C1-C4.
fatal_flaw: There is no discovery problem. Silent status and the 312(g) deadline are legible fields in FCC LMS. The value comes from capex-heavy relighting and from a thin, unproven datacasting lease market, so the step-up is about 2-5x, not 10^4. ML adds nothing over a database query.
step_up: No live numbers: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran, so every figure here is my estimate from memory. Small or mid-market full-power stations normally trade for low single-digit $M. LPTV licences trade for about $50k-$1M. A distressed silent station in a top market might sell at a 30-70% discount to a lit one. After relighting, the value rises by about 1.5-5x, and the candidate's own ~3-20x is the optimistic end. ATSC 3.0 datacasting lease income is small and unproven: Edge Networks and Pearl members mostly use spectrum they already own. That is 10^0-10^1, nowhere near 10^3-10^4. The asset never starts near zero, because a top-market licence is priced off spectrum value (2017 incentive auction clearing prices were tens of $M in large markets, from memory).
hit_rate_capex: There is no low-hit-rate proving step for ML to improve. Relighting is a deterministic engineering job that almost always works if funded: estimated $150k-$1.5M for a full-power transmitter, antenna, site and installation, or about $20k-$150k for LPTV (my estimates; not checked because the search budget was gone). The uncertainty is about the market (will a datacaster pay a lease?) and about regulation (FCC reinstatement or transfer timing). Neither is a discovery problem. The lever, capped at 1/base hit rate, is about 1x.

name: Buildout Rescue: unbuilt auction licences near forfeiture
one_line_reason: This fails the core test the same way geothermal in coal mines does: building out is harder than finding the licence, the data is already legible, and the step-up is roughly 2-5x, not 10^4.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is physical construction (40-80% population coverage under FCC rules), not discovery. The opportunity is fully legible in ULS status fields. And carriers can wait for the licence to terminate and buy it at re-auction, which caps any step-up at a low multiple.
step_up: About 2-5x, and that is my estimate; I found no sourced transaction prices because the web search budget ran out before any search returned. Reasoning: a near-forfeiture licence sells at a distress discount, maybe 20-50% of auction-clearing value. Auction 108 raised about $428M for roughly 7,900 licences (memory, unverified), so many rural licences cleared for tens of thousands of dollars. A built-out licence trades near market $/MHz-pop, which is not orders of magnitude more. The upside is capped hard because the carrier can just wait. A licence that misses its deadline terminates automatically (47 CFR 1.946(c)) and goes back to FCC inventory for re-auction, where the carrier can bid without paying for anyone's build. The candidate's own 3-30x guess looks generous. Nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: There is no low base hit rate to improve. Whether a build-out succeeds is a matter of engineering and money, not chance. If you spend enough on sites to cover 40-50% of the licence area's population, it passes. Cost per attempt (estimate): roughly $50k-$300k per macro or fixed-wireless site including lease, radio and backhaul. A rural county or partial economic area needing 50% population coverage could take several to dozens of sites, so about $0.3M-$5M per licence, likely more than the licence is worth. ML might rank which licences carriers want, but that only saves a little diligence cost. It does not buy 10x more attempts at a big jump. The lever is roughly 1x.

name: ReAuction Picker: FCC defaulted-licence inventory
one_line_reason: This is spectrum arbitrage against informed carriers who are also bidding, using fully legible FCC data, for at best about 2x. It fails C1, C2 and C3.
fatal_flaw: The end buyer is a bidder in the same auction, and every input (inventory, holdings, coverage, bids) is legible structured FCC data. There is no illegible signal and no uninformed seller, so there is nothing to discover and the step-up is about 1-3x, not 10^4. The FCC's anti-collusion and unjust-enrichment rules and the transfer-approval process add cost and delay on top.
step_up: From memory, not freshly sourced: Auction 97 (AWS-3, 2015) cleared about $2.7/MHz-pop on average for $44.9B gross. Later secondary deals for AWS and mid-band spectrum have mostly traded at roughly 0.8-2x the auction-implied $/MHz-pop. A re-auction is thin only if the carriers who need the block stay out. When they do stay out, the block wasn't must-have. When they don't, the price clears at roughly what they'd pay you later. My estimate of the realistic step-up from winning near reserve to selling to a carrier is 1-3x, with a fat left tail when the price clears high or the carrier doesn't buy. That is not 10^3. The candidate's own ~2-10x figure is optimistic.
hit_rate_capex: There is no low base hit rate to improve. Winning is a matter of bidding more, so the 'hit rate' is set by your price, not by skill at finding things. The cost per attempt is the full licence price plus an upfront deposit, typically millions to hundreds of millions per block. Unlike a ~$100k-1M exploratory drill, that capital isn't spent and gone; it is locked in an asset at roughly market price. ML cannot cut the cost of an attempt 10x. At most it sharpens bid shading a little. The 1/base-hit-rate cap is about 1x. These are estimates.

name: Conserved Consumptive Use Credits (Colorado River)
one_line_reason: Fails the rubric. There is no discovery-dominant rung, the step-up is about 1.5x against posted prices, the hit rate is about 100% so there is no ML lever, the outcome is already summarised by public OpenET and Reclamation accounting, and anti-speculation law caps the ladder.
fatal_flaw: Nothing is discovered. Which fields can conserve water and how much is already known, legible and measured by public tools (OpenET, CDSS, Reclamation CU reports). Fallowing succeeds about 100% of the time. Program prices are posted, so the step-up from lease to sale is about 1.2-2x. ML has no hit-rate lever and no information asymmetry to exploit.
step_up: From memory (my web search budget was used up, so I could not check these): the Reclamation Lower Basin IRA/SCPP offers in 2022-23 were about $400/AF for a 1-yr commitment, ~$485/AF for 2-yr and ~$518/AF for 3-yr. The Upper Basin SCPP paid roughly $400-$500/AF in 2023-24. Farmers know these posted prices and want most of the payment to lease. My estimate of the farmer's ask is $250-$400/AF, so the step-up from unproven to proven is about 1.2-2x and the margin is thin. Owning the permanent right would cost about $5k-$40k/AF in Colorado/Arizona (estimate), while the annual conservation payment is ~$400-$500/AF, so owning gives no immediate jump either. Nothing goes from near-zero to 10^3. The candidate's own rough figure (~1.5-3x) is right or even generous.
hit_rate_capex: My estimate: once a field is fallowed, the hit rate for producing conserved consumptive use is close to 100%, because ET drops by construction. Each attempt costs roughly lease plus verification, ~$300-$450/AF (estimate). There is no expensive, mostly failing proving step. The lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, which is about 1x, so ML cannot cut discovery capex 10x. Deficit irrigation adds measurement uncertainty, but that is an accounting problem, not discovery.

name: Unregistered LCFS / Clean Fuel Credit Origination Rights
one_line_reason: The physical and operational work (metering, registration, reporting) is most of the job and finding sites is trivial. The step-up is about 1.1-1.5x on a competitively priced revenue share, not 10^3-10^4, and a near-100% base hit rate leaves ML no lever.
fatal_flaw: There is no discovery problem and no step-up. Every charger qualifies by rule and sits in a public structured locator, so hit rate is near 100% and ML adds nothing. The right is a visible commodity cash flow that hosts keep 70-90% of under competitive aggregator bidding. This is a crowded service and brokerage business (ChargePoint, Enel X, Anew, Element Markets, 3Degrees, Nxu-type aggregators), which falls under the 'sell a service to incumbents' pattern. Its value also rests on volatile, policy-set credit prices.
step_up: From memory, not verified (search budget was used up): CA LCFS credits traded about $50-80/t in 2024-25, down from about $200/t in 2020. A light-duty EV charger yields very roughly 0.5-0.8 credits per MWh (EER about 3.4 versus the CI benchmark). A 10-port workplace L2 site (about 50 MWh/yr) therefore makes about $2-4k/yr, and a fleet depot at 1 GWh/yr makes about $30-60k/yr. Unproven price: an assignment costs nothing up front, but hosts expect a revenue share. Aggregators commonly pass 70-90% of credit value to hosts (my estimate, industry norm). The originator's margin is 10-30% of the stream, and any assignment of that stream is priced near its NPV. Value does not jump 10^3-10^4 on a hit. The upside is roughly 1.1-1.5x on the right's value, or about 10x on a near-zero signing fee at best.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is near 100%. Any operating charger qualifies, and the only real failure is a host who declines or already works with an aggregator. A proving attempt is a sales call plus metering, about $500-5,000 per site (my estimate; a revenue-grade meter or a networked-charger data feed is needed). ML has nothing to raise. The lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, about 1x. ML could at most rank leads, which is ordinary sales targeting.

name: Lapsed-Beneficiary Annuity and Demutualization Recovery
one_line_reason: This is classic heir-hunting. The answer already sits in public unclaimed-property listings, fees are capped at about 10-20% of fixed face values, the ML lever is under 3x, and there is no ladder up. Incumbents such as Kemp & Associates and American Research Bureau, plus many unclaimed-property finders, already work it.
fatal_flaw: The outcome is already written into legible public fields. State unclaimed-property listings name the owner, holder and amount, and the DMF settlements forced insurers to find beneficiaries themselves. On top of that, statutory finder-fee caps of about 10-20% and assignment restrictions limit the step-up to low single-digit multiples, with no capitalised buyer paying a premium.
step_up: From my own knowledge, because the web search budget ran out before any search ran, so none of these numbers is sourced: the unproven right costs about $0 upfront, since heir hunters sign contingency agreements. The proven value is the face amount of the claim, which is usually a few hundred dollars to tens of thousands. The company's own capture is set by finder-fee caps: about 10% in CA and TX, about 15% in NY and up to about 20% in FL. Several states also void finder agreements made within 24 months of the property being reported. Where a claim is bought outright, the discount to face is maybe 20-60% (my estimate). That means the real multiple on capital is about 1.5-5x, not 10^3. Even the candidate's own 10-100x figure measures the fee against near-zero cost, not an asset revaluation.
hit_rate_capex: Estimate only, not sourced: an attempt costs about $50-500 in genealogy and records research plus $500-5,000 in legal and probate work on hits. Once the name is already on a state unclaimed-property list, the base hit rate is high, maybe 30-70%, because the listing itself shows the money exists. That caps the ML lever at about 1.5-3x, not 10x. ML would mainly speed up genealogy, which incumbents already do with Ancestry or LexisNexis tooling.

name: Clean NOL Shells
one_line_reason: The step-up disappears at sale: Section 382 and the continuity-of-business rule zero out a dormant shell's NOL for whoever buys it, and the NOL amount is already in legible tax footnotes.
fatal_flaw: Under Section 382 the buyer's own acquisition of control is the ownership change. A dormant shell's equity value is about $0 and it fails the 2-year continuity-of-business requirement, so its annual NOL limit falls to about $0 at the moment of sale. Proving a clean history therefore creates almost no value a buyer can use; the asset loses its value when it is sold.
step_up: The candidate claims 30-300x on a $25-150k shell. My estimate, not sourced (web search budget was used up): a dormant shell's NOL is worth close to zero to an acquirer. Its equity value is about $0, so the 382 cap times $0 is about $0, and the COBE failure zeroes it anyway. Clean NOL value in the market sits in vehicles that came out of bankruptcy with 382(l)(5) relief and kept an operating business, such as WMIH (the WaMu shell that bought Nationstar) and Signature Group (formerly Fremont). Even those trade at a few cents to the low teens of cents per dollar of NOL, my recollection. For a dormant small shell, the realistic premium over the $25-150k cost of a clean public shell is about 1-3x, not 30-300x.
hit_rate_capex: My estimate, unsourced. A 382 study costs roughly $20-100k from Big-4 or boutique tax firms. Many shells with large NOLs will pass a clean ownership history test, so the base hit rate on "no prior change" is fairly high, maybe 30-60%. A high hit rate leaves ML at most about a 2-3x lever (capped at 1/hit rate), not 10x. The real binding limit is the forward-looking 382 and COBE problem, which ML cannot fix.

name: Surplus Capture: micro-caps with overfunded pension plans
one_line_reason: This is a known financial arbitrage on a disclosed number. It needs control capital, pays a 20-50% excise tax plus corporate tax, and gives at most about 1.1-2x. Discovery is a small part of the work, so ML has nothing to extract.
fatal_flaw: The surplus is already in legible public fields: Schedule SB funding target versus assets, and the ASC 715 funded status in 10-K footnotes. The realisable value is then capped by the 50% IRC 4980 reversion excise tax. The result is a small-multiple capital-markets arbitrage with no discovery step and no 10^3x step-up.
step_up: The step-up is about 1.1-2x on equity, not 10^3-10^4. The step-up is small because the hit is not a new asset. It is cash already shown on the balance sheet that markets discount by some amount (estimate). It shrinks further on the way out. IRC 4980 charges a 50% excise tax on an employer reversion (20% if 25% of the surplus goes to a qualified replacement plan or to benefit increases), plus about 21% corporate tax. So the sponsor keeps roughly 30-60% of the gross surplus (statutory rates; my arithmetic). Annuity buyouts usually price at about 100-105% of the accounting liability (Milliman Pension Buyout Index range, from memory, not re-verified this run). That eats more of the surplus. The candidate's own estimate is 1.5-5x. After excise tax and the control premium I put it at 1.1-2x.
hit_rate_capex: There is no low-hit-rate proving step. Anyone can compute from Schedule SB and 10-K footnotes whether a plan is overfunded. The real uncertainty is execution: whether you win control, the price you pay, and how tax applies. ML does not improve any of that. Each attempt costs the purchase price of a control stake, so for a micro-cap roughly $10M-$100M+ (estimate). On top of that are deal costs: legal, actuarial and termination fees, roughly $0.5-2M (estimate). The capex is the asset price, not a discovery cost, so a 10x capex cut is not possible. The lever is about 1x.

name: EU novel-food authorisations with data protection
one_line_reason: Discovery is a small share of the work, the proving step mostly succeeds already (so ML has little to raise), exclusivity needs costly new studies rather than public data, and the step-up against capital in is at most single-digit.
fatal_flaw: Art. 26 data protection applies only to newly generated proprietary studies, so a dossier mined from public literature, which is the whole ML edge, wins no exclusivity. Getting exclusivity means paying for new tox and compositional studies. Those studies dominate the cost and are not discovery, and the EFSA outcome is already a legible public field.
step_up: The unproven right (a supply or ingredient right to an obscure traditional plant) is cheap. My estimate is $10k-100k for an exclusive sourcing deal. The proving cost is far larger: commonly cited at EUR 0.3-1M+ per dossier (my estimate, matching the candidate's $0.5-2M). The proven asset is 5 years of exclusivity on a niche ingredient. My estimate is that it sells for $1-10M, or 1-5x what went into it. The candidate's ~100-300x compares against the price of the bare right and ignores that the proving step costs 10-50x the right. Measured against capital in, the step-up is under 3-10x. It is also slow (EFSA assessments typically run 2-4+ years) and expires after 5 years.
hit_rate_capex: My estimate is that the base hit rate is high, not low. Most applications that reach a complete EFSA assessment get a positive opinion. Failures are mostly withdrawals or 'safety cannot be established' opinions caused by missing data, not by a wrong pick. ML cannot do much for a step that already succeeds roughly 50-80% of the time: 1/hit-rate caps the lever at about 1.3-2x, nowhere near 10x. Each attempt costs EUR 0.3-2M, and that cost comes from new studies ML cannot replace. I could not check these figures because the shared web-search budget was used up.

name: Secrecy-Order Inventions
one_line_reason: The idea fails because secrecy is the barrier, not illegibility. Without seeing the claims you cannot pick or price which applications to buy, the flow is tiny and mostly government-owned, and the "proven" patent is often obsolete and still has to be licensed or litigated before it is worth anything.
fatal_flaw: The asset's content is legally classified and unpublished until rescission, and rescission makes it fully public. No point exists where you can read the signal and others cannot. On top of that, only about 30-60 rescissions happen a year, mostly on government-funded inventions you cannot buy.
step_up: Unproven: a pending application under a secrecy order cannot be published or licensed abroad, so its market value is close to zero. A token price might be $1k-10k (my estimate; I know of no market for these). Proven: most issued patents sell on the secondary market for about $50k-250k per asset (my estimate from broker-market knowledge from before this task). A rare patent that reads on a current product could be worth $1M+. That is about 10-100x typical, and it only happens if the claims still matter. Many secrecy-ordered inventions are old military technology. Their 20-year term runs from the filing date, although 35 USC 154(b)(1)(C) gives some term adjustment for secrecy-order delay. So what is left after rescission is often obsolete or short-lived.
hit_rate_capex: Base rates from memory of FAS/USPTO FOIA data, not checked in this run: about 5,900-6,000 secrecy orders were in effect around FY2020-2024. New orders run about 70-130 a year, and rescissions about 30-60 a year, so the yearly flow is tiny. Each proving attempt costs roughly $20k-50k in prosecution (my estimate) plus years of waiting. The binding constraint is the agency deciding to rescind, not a hit rate that ML could predict and improve. Rescission timing is set by agency classification review. ML cannot cut the cost of a proving attempt, and with a flow this small there are few shots to take anyway.

name: Grandfather Clause: 510(k)s bought ahead of device up-classification
one_line_reason: This fails: a 510(k) is a predicate anyone can cite without owning it, and under 515(i) up-classification forces existing holders to file a PMA rather than grandfathering them, so the predicted hit lowers the asset's value.
fatal_flaw: Both premises are false. (1) A clearance is not a scarce pathway, because any 510(k) is a public predicate that anyone can cite without owning it. (2) Up-classification destroys value instead of grandfathering it. Under 515(i), and in the final orders that moved device types up to Class III (for example metal-on-metal hips in 2016 and surgical mesh for pelvic organ prolapse in 2016, whose remaining 510(k)-cleared products FDA ordered off the market in 2019), existing holders must file a PMA. Owning a 510(k) at the moment its device type is up-classified is a liability.
step_up: No real step-up. Prices are my estimates, because web search was unavailable (the shared turn budget was used up). Dormant 510(k)s sell through brokers and asset deals for roughly $10k-$250k. That price is capped by the cost of a fresh 510(k): the FDA fee is about $24k for a standard filer (FY2025), and all-in cost is about $50k-$300k plus 3-12 months. The candidate's 10-300x assumes clearances become scarce after up-classification, and they do not. Realistic uplift, my estimate: 1-3x, from saving time.
hit_rate_capex: There is no costly physical proving attempt. The bet is a prediction about FDA, and one dormant clearance costs about $10k-$100k (my estimate). FDA reclassifies only a handful of device types a year, often years after a panel meets. When a type is moved up to Class III, current holders must file a PMA or leave the market, so a 'hit' cuts the asset's value instead of raising it. ML has no 10x discovery cost to cut.

name: EVP Ready: dormant EPA antimicrobial registrations for outbreak claims
one_line_reason: The answer comes from a published rule plus public EPA lists, there is no low hit rate to improve, the registration has little scarcity value, and an outbreak rewards supply chain rather than rights. This fails the Terranox test.
fatal_flaw: The outcome is already legible and published: EPA's EVP rules decide qualification from existing label virus claims, and EPA lists the qualifying products by reg number (List Q, N, G). So there is no hidden signal for ML to find. The value in an outbreak sits in manufacturing and supply, not in the registration.
step_up: Unproven: a dormant antimicrobial registration costs roughly one PRIA maintenance fee a year (low thousands of USD per registrant, my estimate from memory of the PRIA schedule), and registration transfers are cheap paperwork. Proven: an EVP-qualified registration has little standalone resale value outside outbreaks, because a new registration or an EVP label amendment can be obtained through PRIA in months for an estimated $5k-$50k including testing.
