During COVID (List N, 600+ products) the shortage was in supply and manufacturing capacity, not registrations. My estimate is about 2-5x on the right itself even in outbreak years, and 1-2x otherwise. The candidate's 10-100x applies to product revenue, not to the right.
hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: close to 100% predictable from the label. A registration whose accepted efficacy data includes a small non-enveloped virus claim qualifies for EVP tiers by rule, so there is no low base rate for ML to improve, and the lever (capped at 1/base hit rate) is about 1x. Cost per proving attempt: an EVP label amendment PRIA fee in the low thousands of USD, plus about $10k-$30k per virucidal efficacy test (GLP lab, surrogate virus) if new data is needed. Both figures are my estimates, not sourced; the web search budget was exhausted, so none of them were verified this run.

name: Lapsed-Registration Airframe Recovery
one_line_reason: This is a low-margin restoration-and-flip business: the discovery step is a small share of the work, the step-up is about 2x, the hit-rate lever is small, and the status data is already legible in the FAA's free registry download.
fatal_flaw: The physical step dominates and the outcome is already legible. Making an abandoned airframe airworthy (engine overhaul, corrosion, annual, $10-45k) dwarfs the find, which is the coal-mine-geothermal failure. Lapsed or deregistered status is already a structured field in the free FAA registry download. And the step-up is about 2x net of restoration, three orders of magnitude short of the 10^4 the rubric needs.
step_up: I estimate about 1.5-3x gross, and less than 1.5x net of restoration (the candidate itself says ~2-5x). Example from memory, not sourced: a derelict Cessna 172 with lapsed registration and an unclear lien history might trade at $15-30k as a project. Once it is clean-titled and airworthy with a fresh annual it might sell for $60-90k. But the uplift mostly pays for the physical work: a sitting airframe often needs a $25-45k engine overhaul plus $3-15k of annual and corrosion work. Clearing the title alone (the actual discovery step) adds maybe 1.2-2x. That is nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
hit_rate_capex: These are estimates only; no web search ran. A title search through the specialist aircraft title firms costs roughly $100-300 per tail number. A pre-buy or annual inspection costs about $1.5-5k. The hit rate of "can this title be cleared" is probably already high, maybe 50-80%, because FAA liens and probate are clearable with an attorney and time. The real uncertainty is the airframe's condition, which ML on registry data cannot see. So 1/base hit rate caps the lever at about 1.5-2x, not 10x.

name: Grandfathered gaming-entitlement parcels
one_line_reason: Fails the frame: the outcome is a public mapped field, sellers are sophisticated, the step-up is about 3-10x, nothing expensive is failing that ML could improve, and the value sits in building the casino.
fatal_flaw: Gaming eligibility is a statutory, mapped zoning designation that sellers already price in, so there is no illegible signal to find. The only way to create new value is a political petition, not discovery, and building the casino rather than finding the site is where all the work lies.
step_up: No verified numbers; the search budget ran out before any price search returned results. My estimate: off-Strip Las Vegas commercial land trades at roughly $0.5-3M per acre, and land eligible for gaming in GED, corridor or Strip-adjacent areas at roughly $3-15M+ per acre (Strip sales in 2022-23 were reportedly around $10M+ per acre, from memory). That is about a 3-10x premium, which matches the candidate's own figure, and it applies only where the eligibility is not already priced in. It is far below 10^3.
hit_rate_capex: There is no costly proving step that usually fails. Confirming gaming eligibility means checking a zoning map, a title report and a land-use attorney's opinion, roughly $5-50k per parcel (my estimate). A petition for a new site costs a hearing and lobbying, and it fails or succeeds on politics and neighbourhood opposition, which ML cannot predict better from the record. Base hit rate is not meaningful. ML gives no cut in discovery capex because discovery is not where the money goes.

name: Thorium Legacy to Pb-212 Feed
one_line_reason: This is a radiochemistry processing business, not a discovery business. The hit rate is about 100% and the outcome is legible from licence files plus decay math. Yield is only about 0.11 Ci Th-228 per tonne of Th-232, and the value is captured by whoever builds the separation plant, which incumbents like Orano and DOE already have.
fatal_flaw: There is nothing to discover. Th-228 ingrowth is deterministic decay physics from a known separation date, and holders already declare quantities in licence files, so the hit rate is about 100% and ML has no edge. Value comes only from a bespoke radiochemistry separation plant processing tonnes of material for about 0.1 Ci of Th-228 per tonne. That plant is the dominant cost and risk, which is exactly the geothermal-coal-mine counter-example. On top of that, Orano already holds captive thorium, and the DLA stockpile was disposed of.
step_up: The unproven right is legacy thorium taken as a liability, so its value is about zero or negative. Disposal costs avoided are an estimate, roughly tens of $/kg. The gamma assay itself does not raise the value much. Physics (my calculation): Th-232 specific activity is 4.06 kBq/g, and at secular equilibrium (more than about 25-30 years since separation) Th-228 activity equals that. So one tonne of aged thorium holds only about 4 GBq, or about 0.11 Ci, of Th-228, spread through tonnes of material. Value appears only after chemical separation and purification. The ratio looks large only because the starting value is negative, and that uplift comes from processing, not from proving. On proving alone I estimate under 3x. I could not verify current Th-228 market prices because the search budget was used up.
hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is effectively about 100% (my estimate, from physics): any thorium more than about 25 years from its last chemical separation is in Th-228 equilibrium, and the separation date is usually known. A gamma-spec assay costs on the order of $100s-$1,000s per sample (my estimate). Nothing is failing, so there is nothing for ML to raise. The 1/base-hit-rate cap gives a lever of about 1x. The real capex is the separation hot cell and licensing, which I estimate at $10M+ (unsourced), and ML does not reduce it.

name: Ghost SRECs: unregistered behind-the-meter solar
one_line_reason: Discovery is a trivial list diff against a legible regulator status field, the step-up is about 1.5-2x because owners can self-register for free, and the market is a few hundred DC systems. This is a sales business, not a discovery business.
fatal_flaw: There is no information asymmetry for ML to resolve and no 10^3 step-up. Whether a system is certified is already written into the public DC PSC/GATS list. The owner can self-register for free, so the right cannot be bought near zero. NJ and MA legacy programs are closed to retroactive registration. What remains is a tiny DC pool where the bottleneck is door-knocking (customer acquisition), not discovery.
step_up: Estimates only; the web search budget was used up, so these numbers come from prior knowledge, not fresh sources. DC SRECs trade around $400-450/MWh, below an SACP of about $500/MWh. A typical 6-8 kW DC rooftop makes about 7-9 MWh/yr, so roughly $3k-4k/yr of SRECs. An upfront lump-sum buyout from an aggregator usually pays about 40-70% of the discounted strip. If you buy the right from the owner at 0.5x and sell or monetise at 1.0x, the step-up is about 1.5-2x, not 10^3-10^4. The 'unproven' right is not near zero: the owner can register for free in an afternoon through SRECTrade and similar sites, which sets a floor on what you must pay. NJ legacy SREC closed to new registrations in 2020 (replaced by TREC/SuSI ADI, which need pre-registration). MA SREC I/II are closed and SMART needs pre-qualification. So older ghost systems in NJ and MA mostly cannot be registered retroactively, which leaves only DC open.
hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving step. A detection-vs-list diff costs pennies per parcel and should hit most of the time for systems that really are unregistered. The real cost is customer acquisition, which I estimate at $300-1,500 per signed residential owner, in line with residential solar and SREC-aggregator CAC. The 'failure' is owners refusing, already being registered under an installer/aggregator name that does not match the address, or systems being ineligible (vintage, interconnection, data). ML does not cut that cost by 10x. The lever is about 1x.

name: Orphaned ZEV / GHG Credit Banks of Defunct Automakers
one_line_reason: This is a legal and brokerage arbitrage on assets that are already legible and already priced. No discovery rung exists, the step-up is about 2-5x, and the hit-rate lever is about 1x.
fatal_flaw: The balances are already published by regulators and listed in bankruptcy schedules, so there is nothing to discover and no ML edge. On top of that, the policy rollbacks in the US and Canada and the doubtful transferability in the UK and EU cap the step-up at about 2-5x, with only a few buyers who set the price.
step_up: From memory, all estimates (no web search ran: the shared search budget was used up). Trustees already know a credit balance is an asset and list it in the estate schedules, so the price paid to the estate is probably 20-60% of market, not near zero. That gives roughly 1.5-5x on resale at best. Price references: the UK ZEV mandate fine is about £12k per missing car after the April 2025 change, and traded credits sit well below that, likely about £3-8k (estimate). US CARB/GHG credit value collapsed after the 2025 federal changes: CAFE penalties set to zero, and California's waiver revoked by a CRA resolution. Canada EVAS was paused in 2025. Nothing about this asset goes from about $1 to $10k.
hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving step. Finding a balance is close to certain because regulators publish balances by manufacturer. Most failures come from legal rules on transferability or credit expiry, which ML cannot change. Cost per attempt is legal fees, about $10k-100k per estate (estimate). Because the base hit rate is high, the 1/base-hit-rate cap on the lever is about 1-2x.

name: Claim Harbor: contractors with unasserted REA/CDA claims
one_line_reason: This fails on every axis that makes Terranox work. Proving the claim is lawyering, not cheap discovery; the evidence is private, not public and hard to read; the right costs a whole company at going-concern value, not $1/ha; and a win returns about 2-5x, not 10^4.
fatal_flaw: The proving step is bespoke legal litigation that takes years, not a trivial physical step, and the evidence is private to the contractor. On top of that, the claim cannot be assigned, so you have to buy an entire operating company at full price from owners who already know their own claims. That leaves no information asymmetry, no cheap right and no 10^3 step-up.
step_up: No step-up from near zero. To get the claim you have to buy an operating contractor at a normal SDE/EBITDA multiple (about 2-4x SDE for a small GovCon, my estimate), so most of the price pays for the business, not the claim. If you pay about $0.2-0.5 per expected claim dollar (estimate), the step-up on that slice is 2-5x on a win and 0 on a loss. Litigation funders typically price a CDA claim at 10-40% of face before it is adjudicated (estimate, unsourced). The candidate's own figure of ~10-100x assumes the claim is free, which it is not once you buy the entity.
hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is not low. Contractors who file a certified claim recover something in most cases: from memory of ASBCA annual reports, most appeals end in settlement or withdrawal, and decided appeals are sustained in whole or part at a rate around 30-50% (estimate, not verified this run). Each proving attempt costs about $50k-$1M+ in legal and claim-consultant fees plus 1-4 years (estimate). The problem is not a low hit rate. It is that the contractor never filed, which is a matter of choice and relationships (fear of losing future work), not missing information. So the ceiling on the ML lever (1/base hit rate) is about 2-3x, not 10x.

name: Tritium Sign Harvest
one_line_reason: This is recycling, not discovery. The outcome (curies) sits in legible fields, every attempt "hits", and the gas recovered barely pays for licensed processing, so there is no 10^3 step-up and no ML lever.
fatal_flaw: There is no discovery problem. The tritium content of every sign is printed on its label and in NRC registrations, and it decays on a fixed schedule. The hit rate is about 100% and the step-up is about 1x, while licensed reverse logistics is the whole job. It is a regulated recycling service with tiny volumes, and the manufacturers already run it.
step_up: About 1x or less, often negative (all of these are my estimates; the search budget was used up and no live searches ran). A new sign holds about 10-25 Ci, and an expired 15-20-year-old sign has about 3-8 Ci left. At roughly 9,600 Ci per gram and roughly $30k per gram of tritium, that is about $3 per Ci, or about $10-25 of tritium per sign. Accumulated He-3 is a few mL STP per sign, at about $2-20 per mL, so roughly $10-70, and some of it has already leaked out. Owners pay about $100-300 per sign for take-back (my estimate, and this is the "negative cost"). The fee covers reprocessing, so the gas recovered is worth about as much as the processing costs. There is no jump from near zero to 10^3.
hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is about 100%: every registered sign contains tritium in a known, declining amount. There is no failed proving attempt for ML to avoid, so the lever is capped at 1/1.0 = 1x. The cost per attempt is collection plus licensed processing, about $50-150 per sign (my estimate).
